sources: INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED, from MIW verification record QP2602/Q5 which read the provision: Merchant Shipping Act 1958, section 334 'Unseaworthy ship not to be sent to sea'. Sub-section (1) makes it an offence to send or attempt to send an Indian ship to sea from any port in India 'in such an unseaworthy state that the life of any person is likely to be thereby endangered', unless the person proves he 'used all reasonable means to insure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state' or that sending her to sea in that state was 'under the circumstances, reasonable and justifiable'. Sub-section (2) applies the offence to a master who 'knowingly takes' such a ship to sea, with only the second defence. Sub-section (3) permits a person charged to give evidence. Sub-section (4) provides that no prosecution shall be instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government. The section describes the state itself: a ship is unseaworthy when 'the materials of which she is made, her construction, qualifications of the master, the number, description and qualifications of the crew including officers, the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast, the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service'.

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED, same record: Merchant Shipping Act 1958, section 335 'Obligation of owner to crew with respect to seaworthiness'. Sub-section (1) implies into every contract of service, express or implied, between the owner of an Indian ship and the master or any seaman, and into every contract of apprenticeship, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, an obligation that the owner, the master and every agent charged with loading the ship or preparing her for sea or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship for the voyage at the time when the voyage commences, and to keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage. Sub-section (2) empowers the Central Government, at the owner's request or otherwise, to arrange a survey of the hull, equipment or machinery by a surveyor.

INTERNAL REUSE VERIFIED, same record: Merchant Shipping Act 1958, section 336 'Power to detain unsafe ship and procedure for detention'. Sub-section (1) describes an unsafe ship as one which 'by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, [is] unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended'. Clause (a) empowers the Central Government to order provisional detention for survey on complaint or otherwise; clause (b) requires a written statement of the grounds to be served forthwith on the master; clause (c) requires reference to a court of survey, or to a competent person appointed to survey and report, upon which the ship is released or finally detained.

QP2410 Q9 - seaworthiness in its third legal life, as a matter of marine insurance and carriage rather than of criminal statute

blocks.h: (a) The meaning of an unseaworthy vessel — 5 marks
1. What the Act means by an unseaworthy vessel

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 gives no definition of unseaworthiness in a definitions section. The description sits inside section 334 itself, which treats a ship as unseaworthy where the following are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service:

ul: the materials of which she is made, and her construction;
the qualifications of the master;
the number, description and qualifications of the crew, including officers;
the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast;
the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery.

blocks.p: Two features carry the marks in this limb. First, the test is relative. The Act does not ask whether the ship is in good condition in the abstract; it asks whether she is fit for the proposed voyage or service. A ship perfectly adequate for a sheltered coastal run may be unseaworthy for a North Atlantic passage in winter, and the same ship may be seaworthy on Monday and unseaworthy on Tuesday because the intended service has changed. Second, the concept is far wider than material condition. An undermanned ship is unseaworthy. A ship whose officers hold the wrong certificates is unseaworthy. A mechanically perfect ship with badly stowed cargo or ballast is unseaworthy. The Act puts people and stowage on the same footing as steel, and a candidate who treats unseaworthiness as a hull-and-machinery question has read only half the section.

blocks.h: 2. The offence the section creates, and the defences it allows

ul: Section 334(1) — every person who sends or attempts to send an Indian ship to sea from any port in India in such an unseaworthy state that the life of any person is likely to be thereby endangered is guilty of an offence, unless he proves that he used all reasonable means to insure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state, or that sending her to sea in that state was, under the circumstances, reasonable and justifiable.

Section 334(2) — a master who knowingly takes such a ship to sea is likewise guilty, but with only the second defence open to him. The master cannot say he used all reasonable means; if he knew, he is answerable.
Section 334(3) permits a person charged to give evidence in his own defence.
Section 334(4) — no prosecution shall be instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government.

blocks.p: Liability is therefore not automatic, and the section is more carefully balanced than it first appears. The threshold is danger to life, not mere unfitness. The burden of the defence lies on the accused — he must prove it. But the standard demanded of him is reasonable means, not a guarantee of result, so a latent defect that diligence would not have found does not convict him. And the requirement of Central Government consent keeps the section from being used as a private weapon in a commercial dispute.

blocks.h: (b) The difference between an unseaworthy ship and an unsafe ship — 6 marks

blocks.p: This is the heaviest limb on the question, and it asks for a comparison, not for a second definition. Establish what an unsafe ship is first, because the difference cannot be stated until both concepts are on the page.

blocks.h: 3. What an unsafe ship is, and the power it triggers

blocks.p: Section 336 is directed at a different problem altogether — stopping the ship rather than punishing anybody. A ship is unsafe where, by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, she is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended. The procedure is staged, and the stages are the safeguards:

ol: the Central Government, having reason to believe on complaint or otherwise that she is unsafe, may order her provisionally detained for the purpose of survey;
a written statement of the grounds must be served forthwith on the master;
the matter is referred to the court of survey for the port, or a competent person is appointed to survey the ship and report;
on that report she is either released or finally detained.

blocks.h: 4. The difference between the two, on five axes

blocks.p: State the difference on more than one axis. One sentence will not earn six marks; five short propositions will.

rows: A state of the ship, described by the Act
A condition that triggers a power in the Government
Criminal liability for sending her to sea, or for a master knowingly taking her
Provisional and then final detention. Nobody is punished
Backward-looking — it punishes a decision already taken
Forward-looking — it prevents the voyage from happening
Wider — expressly includes crew numbers and qualifications, and the stowage of cargo and ballast
Narrower — a closed list: hull, equipment, machinery, overloading, improper loading
The life of any person is likely to be endangered
Unfit to proceed without serious danger to human life
A court, on a prosecution the Central Government has consented to
The Central Government itself, subject to survey and the right to be told the grounds

blocks.p: Then close with the asymmetry, which is the observation that shows you have understood rather than memorised. A ship that is unsafe within section 336 will invariably also be unseaworthy within section 334 — but the converse does not hold. A ship one certificated engineer short of her safe manning document is unseaworthy under section 334, because crew qualifications are expressly part of the test; she is not unsafe under section 336, because that section's causes are confined to hull, equipment, machinery and loading. The two provisions overlap; they are not two names for one idea.

blocks.h: (c) The obligations of owners to crew with respect to seaworthiness — 5 marks
5. The owner's obligation to the crew

blocks.p: Section 335 converts seaworthiness from a matter between owner, cargo and underwriter into a duty owed to the people on board. In every contract of service, express or implied, between the owner of an Indian ship and the master or any seaman, and in every contract of apprenticeship, there is implied — notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary — an obligation that the owner, the master and every agent charged with the loading of the ship, or preparing her for sea, or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship for the voyage at the time when the voyage commences, and shall keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage.
Three consequences follow, and they are the marks in this limb:

ul: The duty is non-excludable. The words ‘notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary’ mean a term in the crew agreement purporting to waive it is void. A seafarer cannot sign away his right to a seaworthy ship.

It is a due-diligence standard, not a warranty of result. The obligation is to use all reasonable means. The owner does not guarantee that the ship is seaworthy; he guarantees that he tried properly to make her so.

It is continuing. The duty is owed at the commencement of the voyage and throughout it. It is not discharged at the pilot station, which is where the marine-insurance doctrine of a voyage-policy warranty would stop.

blocks.p: It also reaches beyond the registered owner. The section names the master and every agent charged with loading the ship or preparing or sending her to sea, so a shore manager or loading agent whose act renders her unseaworthy is inside the obligation, not outside it.

blocks.h: 6. How the obligation is policed, and the statute in force on the day

blocks.p: Section 335(2) allows the Central Government, at the owner's request or otherwise, to arrange a survey of the hull, equipment or machinery by a surveyor. In practice the obligation is policed through the wider system rather than through that sub-section alone: classification and flag State statutory survey and certification, ISM auditing of the safety management system, and port State control inspection — with the section 336 detention power as the last resort when inspection finds a ship that should not sail.

One point of currency should be stated rather than assumed, because it is the standard way this question is lost. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 was the operative statute on this examination date, and at this sitting it stood unopposed. There was no replacing Act, and there was not even a Bill before Parliament: the Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 was introduced in the Lok Sabha only on 10 December 2024, two months after this paper was sat. Sections 334, 335 and 336 are therefore not merely the correct answer — at this sitting they are the only answer available.

The examiner has printed the structure for you, and the marks are not evenly split. 5 + 6 + 5 means the middle limb is the largest single block of marks on the question, and it is the limb candidates most often skip — they define unseaworthy, define unsafe, and never actually state the difference. Answer in the printed order, label the limbs (a), (b) and (c) so the marker can find them, and give limb (b) more paper than either of the others.

Within limb (b), do not settle for one sentence. A comparison stated on five axes — what each one is, what follows from it, which direction it looks in, how wide its causes are, and what threshold it sets — is five scoreable propositions where ‘one is an offence and the other is detention’ is one. Finish with the asymmetry, because it is the sentence that shows you have read both sections rather than remembered a slogan.

blocks.h: Why the Act splits one idea into two sections

blocks.p: A criminal offence needs fault, a trial and proof, and it operates after the event — which is no use at all to the crew of a ship that is about to sail. An administrative detention power needs only a reasonable belief and can act within hours, but it punishes nobody and it is open to abuse. The 1958 Act therefore does both: section 334 attaches consequences to a decision, and section 336 supplies the fast preventive lever, with the survey, the court of survey and the right to be told the grounds in writing as the safeguards against its misuse. Seeing that the two sections exist to solve different problems is the whole of the distinction, and it is worth more in limb (b) than any amount of re-quoting.

blocks.h: Seaworthiness has three different legal lives — keep them apart

ul: Statutory and criminal — MSA 1958 s.334. A state of the ship, punishable when she is sent to sea in it, with a due-diligence defence. This is limb (a).
Contractual, owed to the crew — MSA 1958 s.335. Implied, non-excludable, and continuing through the voyage. This is limb (c).

Insurance and carriage — a warranty or a duty of due diligence depending on whether the policy is a voyage or a time policy and on the terms of the contract of carriage. Under Indian law that is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, not the English Act of 1906, and a breach affects recovery rather than attracting a penalty. This is not asked here — do not import it.

blocks.p: Most wrong answers to this question are right answers to the third bullet. The word ‘warranty’ is the tell.

ul: Defining both terms and never stating the difference. Limb (b) is six marks and it asks for one thing.
Treating unseaworthiness as a hull-and-machinery question. The section expressly includes the master's qualifications, the crew's number and qualifications, and the stowage of cargo and ballast.
Forgetting that the test is relative to the proposed voyage or service, and writing as though seaworthiness were an absolute condition.
Answering limb (c) with the English marine-insurance warranty of seaworthiness instead of section 335's implied contractual obligation.
Saying the owner guarantees a seaworthy ship. He does not: the standard is all reasonable means.
Stopping the section 335 duty at departure. It continues during the voyage, and those three words are worth a mark.
Naming the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. At this sitting it did not exist in any form.
Quoting a penalty figure for the section 334 offence. Get it wrong and you have volunteered an error; the section can be answered fully without one.

blocks.p: ‘Give me an example of a ship that is unseaworthy but not unsafe.’ A ship sailing one certificated engineer short, or with an officer holding the wrong certificate of competency. Crew qualifications are expressly inside section 334 and are outside the closed list of causes in section 336. This is the discriminating answer and it is the reason the asymmetry matters.

‘Who can prosecute under section 334?’ Nobody, without the Central Government. Section 334(4) provides that no prosecution shall be instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government.

‘Your owner tells you the charterer accepted the ship in her present condition and signed a waiver. Are you covered?’ Not as against the crew. Section 335 implies the obligation notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, so a waiver in a crew agreement is void. And a charterer's acceptance is nothing to the point in a section 334 prosecution, where the threshold is danger to life.
‘Which Act applies?’ The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. At an October 2024 sitting there was no competing candidate at all — see the currency note below.

ul: Which section describes unseaworthiness, and why is it not in the definitions? Section 334; the Act describes the state inside the offence provision.

Name four things the section takes into account. Materials and construction; the master's qualifications; the crew's number, description and qualifications; the weight, description and stowage of cargo and ballast; the condition of hull, equipment, boilers and machinery.

What are the two defences to section 334(1), and which of them is open to the master? All reasonable means used, and reasonable and justifiable in the circumstances. Only the second is open to the master under s.334(2).
What are the causes of unsafety in section 336? Defective hull, equipment or machinery; overloading; improper loading.

Walk me through a detention under section 336. Provisional detention for survey; written grounds served forthwith on the master; reference to the court of survey or an appointed competent person; release or final detention on the report.
Can an owner contract out of section 335? No — it is implied notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary.
When does the section 335 duty end? It does not end at departure; it continues during the voyage.
Which Indian Act governs marine insurance, if this had been an insurance question? The Marine Insurance Act, 1963.

blocks.p: 334 — 336 — 335, which is also (a), (b), (c). Read the numbers as STATE — POWER — PROMISE. State: what the Act says she is (steps 1 and 2). Power: what the Government may do about her (steps 3 and 4). Promise: what the owner owes the people on board (steps 5 and 6). For limb (a)'s list, the elements run outside inwards and then aft — materials and construction, master, crew, cargo and ballast, hull and equipment, boilers and machinery — and the phrase that ties them together is ‘in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service’. If you can write that one phrase you can rebuild the rest.

ul: Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, section 334 — unseaworthy ship not to be sent to sea; the description of unseaworthiness; the offences under sub-sections (1) and (2); the defences; sub-section (4), prosecution only by or with Central Government consent

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, section 335 — obligation of owner to crew with respect to seaworthiness; implied into every contract of service and of apprenticeship notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary; sub-section (2), survey arranged by the Central Government
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, section 336 — power to detain an unsafe ship; the causes; provisional detention, written grounds, court of survey, release or final detention

Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 — the operative general statute at this examination, unopposed. The Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 10 December 2024, two months after this sitting; the resulting Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026, when section 324(1) repealed the 1958 Act
Marine Insurance Act, 1963 (India) — named only to be set aside. Seaworthiness as an insurance concept is not what this question asks about, and no section of it is asserted

blocks.p: The statutory content of this answer is strong but its provenance must be stated exactly. MIW does not hold the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Sections 334, 335 and 336 were read for MIW verification record QP2602/Q5 in a reproduction of the Act rather than in a current official consolidated print, with section 334 cross-checked against a second independent reproduction and found to agree. The printed question says ‘as amended’, and any later amendment to these three sections is therefore unconfirmed. That is an accepted limitation, declared rather than disguised, and it is the reason no penalty figure and no section number outside 334 to 336 is asserted anywhere in this answer.

The currency position, by contrast, is settled and is simpler at this sitting than at any other in the family. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 — Act No. 24 of 2025, assented 18 August 2025 and brought into force on 15 March 2026 by S.O. 1244(E), its section 324(1) repealing the 1958 Act — is established from the Gazette reading in MIW record QP2607/Q7. Every step of that story lies after this examination, and the first step of all, the introduction of the Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 in the Lok Sabha, came on 10 December 2024, two months after it. So the 1958 Act is stated here without qualification. A candidate revising today should note that this is a historical answer: the 1958 Act is no longer in force, and a paper sat after 15 March 2026 requires the corresponding provisions of the 2025 Act, which MIW has not yet mapped section by section against these three.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three printed demands, separately marked, and they are not three definitions. Limb (a) at 5 asks what the Act MEANS by an unseaworthy vessel - so the answer must come from the statute, not from a general notion of a ship being in poor condition. Limb (b) at 6 - the heaviest limb - asks for the candidate's own analysis of the difference between an unseaworthy ship and an unsafe ship, which is a comparison between two named statutory concepts and must be made on more than one axis. Limb (c) at 5 asks what the owner owes the CREW, which is a different provision again and a different kind of duty: contractual rather than criminal.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as 5 + 6 + 5, reconciling exactly. The middle limb is the largest, which is unusual and is the single most important planning fact on this question: the comparison, not the definitions, is where most of the marks are. Budget roughly a third of the writing time to (a), a little over a third to (b) and a third to (c), and do not let limb (a) expand into the recital of everything known about seaworthiness.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate can work from the Indian statute rather than from general impressions or from English case law; can see that the Act splits one idea into a criminal provision and an administrative one because they solve different problems; and knows that seaworthiness is owed to the crew as an implied and non-excludable contractual term, not merely to cargo interests and underwriters.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - not because the 1958 sections moved, they did not, but because the whole family of donors was authored at sittings where a successor statute was in play, and the temptation to inherit that discussion is strong. The risk is of importing a later statute, not of missing a later one.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW-MEDIUM. The question is expressly Indian and names its own statute, which removes most of the risk. The residual risk is the opposite one - answering from English marine insurance doctrine, where seaworthiness is a warranty, instead of from the Indian criminal and contractual provisions the question actually names.
technical_ambiguities: 'Unseaworthy vessel within the meaning of the Merchant Shipping Act' invites a general essay on seaworthiness. The Act has no definitions entry for it; the description sits inside section 334 and must be quarried from there.

'What according to you is the difference' reads as an invitation to opinion. It is not - it is an invitation to compare two statutory concepts on stated axes, and an answer that gives a personal impression will not score six marks.
'Obligations of owners to crew with respect seaworthiness' is printed without 'to', and could be read as the general duty of care. It is section 335, a specific implied term.

Limb (b) is worth six marks - more than either definition limb - and it asks for the difference, not for a second definition. The second trap is answering from English marine-insurance doctrine, where seaworthiness is a warranty; this question is about an Indian criminal provision and an Indian implied contractual term.

questions.memory_cue: Three sections, three limbs, in numerical order: 334 - 336 - 335. State (1, 2), power (3, 4), promise (5, 6). Or in one line: what she is, what can be done about her, and what is owed to the people on board.
questions.understand_first: The Act is doing two different jobs with one idea, and seeing that is the whole question. A criminal offence needs fault, a trial and proof, and it operates after the ship has sailed - which is no use whatever to the crew of a ship about to sail. An administrative detention power needs only a reasonable belief and can act within hours, but it punishes nobody. So section 334 attaches consequences to a decision already taken, and section 336 supplies the fast preventive lever, with the survey and the written grounds as the safeguards against its misuse. Section 335 then does a third thing again: it turns seaworthiness from something owed to cargo and underwriters into something owed to the people on board, by a term the owner cannot contract out of. Once you see three jobs rather than three definitions, the comparison limb writes itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 treat as making a ship unseaworthy?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 334: the materials she is made of, her construction, the qualifications of the master, the number, description and qualifications of the crew including officers, the weight, description and stowage of cargo and ballast, and the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery - where these are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service.
retrieval_cards.why: The Act has no definitions entry for unseaworthiness; the description lives inside the offence section, and quoting it from there is what distinguishes a statutory answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is an unsafe ship under section 336?
retrieval_cards.answer: One which, by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended.
retrieval_cards.why: The causes are a closed and narrower list than section 334's, which is half of the comparison the six-mark limb is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In one sentence, what is the difference between an unseaworthy ship and an unsafe ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: Unseaworthy is a state to which criminal liability attaches after the ship has been sent to sea; unsafe is a condition that entitles the Central Government to stop her before she goes - so one looks backwards and punishes, the other looks forwards and prevents.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the highest-value sentence on the question. Limb (b) carries six marks and this is the proposition it is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is every unseaworthy ship unsafe, and is every unsafe ship unseaworthy?
retrieval_cards.answer: A ship unsafe within section 336 will invariably be unseaworthy within section 334, but not the converse - a ship one certificated engineer short is unseaworthy without being unsafe, because the section 336 causes are confined to hull, equipment, machinery and loading.
retrieval_cards.why: The asymmetry is the mark-scoring observation, and it also demonstrates that section 334 reaches crew and stowage where section 336 does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does section 335 imply into a crew agreement, and can it be excluded?
retrieval_cards.answer: An obligation on the owner - binding also the master and every agent charged with loading, preparing for sea or sending to sea - to use all reasonable means to ensure seaworthiness at the time the voyage commences and to keep her seaworthy during the voyage. It is implied notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, so it cannot be excluded; a waiver clause is void.
retrieval_cards.why: Non-excludability and continuation through the voyage are the two features limb (c) is worth five marks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Set out the section 336 detention procedure.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Central Government, having reason to believe on complaint or otherwise that the ship is unsafe, may order her provisionally detained for survey; a written statement of the grounds is served forthwith on the master; the matter is referred to the court of survey for the port, or a competent person is appointed to survey and report; and on that report she is either released or finally detained.
retrieval_cards.why: The staged procedure with its safeguards is what makes detention an administrative power rather than an arbitrary one, and examiners ask for the stages.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian merchant shipping statute governed this examination, and what about the 2025 Act?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, unopposed. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 did not exist: the Bill that became it was introduced in the Lok Sabha only on 10 December 2024, two months after this paper, received assent on 18 August 2025 and was brought into force on 15 March 2026, when its section 324(1) repealed the 1958 Act.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the newest Act a candidate has heard of is the standard failure on Indian statutory questions. Here it is not merely premature - the Bill had not even been introduced.

blocks.h: 1. What a charter party is, and what it is not

blocks.p: A charter party is a contract by which a shipowner agrees to place a ship, or part of her carrying capacity, at the disposal of a charterer for reward. It is a commercial contract and nothing else: no convention, code or resolution prescribes its content. Its terms are what the parties agree, subject to the general law of contract and to whatever law and arbitration forum the contract itself chooses. Saying that plainly is worth a mark, because it is the reason no carriage convention should be cited in answer to this question.
Three distinctions complete the definition:

ul: It is not the contract of sale of the goods. That is a separate bargain between seller and buyer, and it is what decides who has to arrange and pay for the carriage in the first place.

It is not the same as a bill of lading. A bill of lading is a receipt for goods shipped, evidence of the contract of carriage, and a document of title. Between owner and charterer the charterparty governs; but once a bill of lading passes into the hands of a third-party holder it operates as a contract in its own right and may attract a mandatory carriage regime that the charterparty, freely negotiated between commercial equals, does not.

It is almost always concluded on an amended standard form. The market uses printed forms — GENCON in dry-cargo voyage chartering, NYPE and BALTIME in time chartering, BARECON for bareboat, SHELLTIME and the common tanker forms in the oil trades — and then amends them with rider clauses, which prevail over the printed text where the two conflict. The printed form is the starting point; the rider clauses are where the negotiation actually is.

blocks.h: 2. The types, and the one question that generates them

blocks.p: The types are not an arbitrary list. They fall out of a single question: how much of the ship's operation has the owner sold? Cost, time and control all follow the same axis, which is why the whole taxonomy can be reconstructed rather than memorised.

rows: A carriage of an agreed cargo between agreed ports
The owner — bunkers, port charges, canal dues
The ship's time for a stated period
The charterer — bunkers, port and canal charges
Carriage of stated quantities over a period, ships nominated later

ul: Voyage charter. The owner sells a single carriage. He keeps the ship, the crew and the whole operation, pays the voyage costs, and is paid freight — usually per tonne of cargo or as a lump sum. Because he is paying for the time, he needs a clock: hence laytime, demurrage and despatch.

Time charter. The owner sells the ship's time. He retains possession, the master and crew, and responsibility for navigation and maintenance; the charterer directs her commercial employment within agreed trading limits and pays hire, usually daily, whatever she is doing. Because the charterer is now paying for the time, he needs a clock that stops: hence off-hire.

Bareboat or demise charter. The charterer takes possession, mans, insures, maintains and operates the ship as disponent owner for the period. The registered owner is close to a financier. This is the type used in leasing and long-term financing structures.

Contract of affreightment. Not a charter of a named ship at all, but a commitment to carry stated quantities over a period, with ships nominated voyage by voyage. It suits a shipper with a continuous programme rather than a single parcel.

Intermediate forms exist and are worth naming: the trip time charter (a time charter for one voyage, so hire is paid but the charterer buys a passage), consecutive voyage charters, and the slot charter in liner trades, where what is bought is container capacity rather than a ship.

blocks.h: (b) The key clauses typically included — 5 marks
3. The key clauses, grouped so they can be recalled

blocks.p: The clause list varies with the form and the trade, so the useful answer describes the families by what they do. Six groups cover almost every charterparty:

ul: The ship. The description clause — name, flag, class, tonnage, dimensions, cargo capacity, gear, and the speed and consumption warranty. Owners warrant the ship as described; a shortfall against the warranted speed or an excess over warranted consumption is what generates a performance claim.

The period or the voyage. For a time charter: place and time of delivery and redelivery, the period and any option, and the trading limits. For a voyage charter: the loading and discharging ports or ranges, and the laycan — the window within which the ship must present, with a cancelling date giving the charterer the right to cancel if she is late.

Money and time. Freight (voyage) or hire (time) and how, when and where it is paid; the owner's right of withdrawal for non-payment of hire; laytime, demurrage and despatch; off-hire; and the bunker clauses governing quantity, grade and price on delivery and on redelivery.

Risk and control. The safe port and safe berth warranty; the employment and indemnity clause, under which the master follows the charterer's employment orders and the charterer indemnifies the owner against the consequences; deviation and liberty clauses; excluded and dangerous cargoes; and the war risks, ice and strikes clauses.

Security and liability. The bills of lading clause, governing what the master may sign and on what terms; lien and cesser, giving the owner a lien on cargo and sub-freights for freight, hire, demurrage and general average contribution; general average and the New Jason clause; the both-to-blame collision clause; and insurance and P&I provisions.

Compliance and administration. ISM and ISPS clauses allocating responsibility for compliance and its costs; sanctions clauses; fuel-quality and emission-compliance provisions, which sit at the join between the charterer's obligation to supply fuel and the ship's obligation to comply; and the arbitration and choice of law clause, which decides where and under what law any of this is fought.

blocks.p: One general point outranks the list. A printed form is only the starting point. Rider clauses added in negotiation prevail over the printed text where they conflict, so a question about ‘typical’ clauses is really a question about what has to be settled — not about the contents page of any one form.

blocks.h: (c) The rights and obligations of both parties — 5 marks
4. Voyage charter - what each party owes the other

rows: Provide the named ship, seaworthy and cargoworthy, at the loading port within the laycan; carry and care for the cargo; proceed with reasonable despatch and without unjustified deviation
Provide the agreed cargo in the agreed quantity; nominate a safe port and safe berth; load and discharge within the laytime
Crew, stores, maintenance, insurance — and the voyage costs: bunkers, port charges and canal dues
The cargo, and the loading and discharging costs so far as the agreed terms place them on him
Freight as agreed; demurrage if laytime is exceeded; a lien on the cargo for freight and demurrage; cancellation or claim if the charterer fails to provide cargo
Carriage of the agreed cargo between the agreed ports; despatch money if the operation is completed inside laytime; the right to cancel if the ship misses the cancelling date

blocks.p: The organising point: under a voyage charter the risk of time sits with the owner. A slow passage, bad weather or congestion at the anchorage is his problem, because he is paying for the fuel and the days. The only relief is the laytime clock — once it has run, delay becomes the charterer's problem in the form of demurrage.

blocks.h: 5. Time charter - what each party owes the other

rows: Deliver at the agreed place and time in the agreed condition; maintain the ship in class and in a thoroughly efficient state in hull, machinery and equipment throughout the period; provide and pay the crew

Pay hire punctually; nominate safe ports and employ her only in lawful trades within the agreed limits; supply and pay for fuel of the agreed specification; redeliver in like good order, fair wear and tear excepted
Crew wages and victualling, stores, lubricating oil, maintenance and repair, class and survey, hull and machinery insurance
Bunkers, port and canal charges, pilotage and towage, cargo handling, agency, and usually hold cleaning

Hire, paid punctually and continuously; the right to withdraw the ship for non-payment; an indemnity for the consequences of complying with the charterer's employment orders; a lien on cargo and sub-freights for hire
The right to direct the commercial employment of the ship within the agreed trading limits; the benefit of the off-hire clause; a claim for underperformance against the speed and consumption warranty

blocks.p: The organising point: under a time charter the risk of time moves to the charterer — except where the owner's own performance fails. That exception is the off-hire clause, which is the pivot of the whole relationship: hire ceases while the ship is prevented from working by a cause falling within it — typically breakdown of machinery, deficiency of crew, damage, drydocking or detention. Note also the division of authority: the charterer directs employment, but the owner and the master retain navigation and safety, and the master may refuse an order that would put the ship in danger.

blocks.h: 6. The comparison, and where the engineer sits in it

blocks.p: The stem says analyse, so close by comparing rather than by summarising:

rows: Who pays bunkers and port charges
Who bears the risk of delay
The owner controls the operation; the voyage is fixed by the contract

blocks.p: One line predicts most of that table: whoever pays for the bunkers has bought the ship's time, and therefore bears the risk of delay. Everything else — demurrage in one, off-hire in the other — is the machinery each side needs to protect itself against that allocation.

Finally, and this is what makes the question a management-level one rather than a legal one: the Chief Engineer meets this contract in three specific places. The speed and consumption warranty, which turns the engine room's daily record into the evidence in a performance claim. The off-hire clause, where a machinery breakdown stops hire and the cause and duration have to be proved. And the bunker clauses, covering quantity and price on delivery and redelivery and the specification and quality of the fuel the charterer supplies — where a poor stem sample becomes simultaneously a commercial dispute and a compliance problem. In every one of those three, the evidence that decides the matter is engine-room evidence: noon reports, logbooks, bunker delivery notes and consumption records.

The marks are 6 + 5 + 5, and the largest limb is the definition-and-types one. That is unusual and it is the planning fact to act on: six marks are not paid for a one-line definition, so the types must be developed properly — four principal types with who pays and who controls, plus the intermediate forms.

Limb (b) is five marks over a dozen or more clause families. That is roughly a line each, so group them. Six named groups, each with two or three examples, is readable and recallable; a random list of fifteen clause names is neither. Limb (c) is four cells, not two — owner and charterer, voyage and time — and a two-column table is the only way it fits in five marks. If you cannot draw a table, use four labelled sub-headings.

blocks.h: The single axis that generates the whole answer

blocks.p: Learn one question and you can derive limb (a) and most of limb (c) from it: how much of the ship's operation has the owner sold?

ul: Sell a carriage → voyage charter. The owner keeps everything and pays the voyage costs, so he carries the risk of time — and needs laytime and demurrage to protect himself.
Sell the time → time charter. The charterer directs employment and pays for the fuel and the ports, so he carries the risk of time — and needs off-hire to protect himself.
Sell possession → bareboat charter. The charterer mans, insures and operates her; the owner is close to a financier.
Sell a quantity over a period → contract of affreightment. No named ship at all.

blocks.p: Notice that demurrage and off-hire are the same idea from opposite sides: each is the protection needed by whichever party is paying for time it is not getting the use of. A candidate who says that has understood the subject rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: Where the engine room meets the contract

blocks.p: This question is set in a management paper, so the examiner is entitled to expect the Chief Engineer's angle. There are exactly three places where the machinery and the charterparty touch, and knowing them converts a competent answer into a strong one:

ul: The speed and consumption warranty in the description clause. An underperformance claim is decided on noon reports, weather data and consumption figures — that is, on the engine room's own record. Sloppy noon reporting loses defensible claims.

The off-hire clause. A breakdown moves money. How much depends on the wording (some clauses are ‘net loss of time’, others operate on a period basis) and on whether the cause and duration can be proved from the log and the planned-maintenance record.

The bunker clauses. Quantity, grade and price on delivery and redelivery; and the specification of the fuel the charterer supplies. A fuel that damages the engine, or that will not meet the ship's statutory compliance obligations, is simultaneously a commercial dispute and a regulatory one — and the bunker delivery note and the retained sample are the evidence in both.
Citing a carriage convention as though it governed the charterparty. No instrument prescribes its terms.
Inventing a clause number, or attributing a term to a named form. Describe what the clause does; do not pretend to quote it.
Answering limb (c) as two descriptions instead of four cells. Both parties, both charter types.
Giving a one-line definition and then racing on. Limb (a) is the biggest limb.
Confusing freight with hire. Freight is for a carriage; hire is for time.
Confusing demurrage (voyage) with off-hire (time), or applying one to the wrong charter type.
Saying a time charterer controls the ship. He controls commercial employment; the owner and master retain navigation and safety.
Forgetting the bareboat charter and the contract of affreightment, which together are worth a mark or two in a six-mark limb.
Quoting a hire rate, demurrage rate or laytime allowance. All are negotiated case by case and any figure is invented.
Writing the whole answer as commercial law with no engineering angle at all, in a management paper.

blocks.p: ‘Your main engine breaks down for three days. Who pays?’ Under a time charter, hire ceases for the period the ship is prevented from working, if the cause falls within the off-hire clause — so the owner effectively pays. Under a voyage charter there is no off-hire at all: the owner simply loses the time, unless laytime was already running, in which case the position depends on whether the delay was at the charterer's risk. Naming both cases is the discriminating answer.

‘The charterer orders you to a port you consider unsafe. What happens?’ The charterer warrants the safety of the port he nominates, and the employment and indemnity clause obliges the master to follow employment orders with the charterer indemnifying the owner. But the master's responsibility for the safety of the ship survives, and he may refuse to enter. The warranty gives a remedy in damages; it does not oblige anyone to run the ship into danger.

‘Who pays for the lubricating oil?’ The owner, under a time charter — even though the charterer pays for the fuel. It is a favourite question precisely because it tests whether the candidate has learned the split or merely assumes the charterer pays for everything consumed.
‘Which prevails, the printed clause or the typed rider?’ The rider clause, where they conflict — the parties are taken to have meant what they specially negotiated.

‘What is the difference between a charterparty and a bill of lading?’ One is the contract for the use of the ship between owner and charterer; the other is a receipt, evidence of the contract of carriage, and a document of title — and in a third party's hands it may attract a mandatory regime the charterparty does not.

ul: Define a charter party. A contract by which the shipowner places the ship, or part of her carrying capacity, at the disposal of the charterer for reward.
Name the principal types. Voyage, time, bareboat or demise, and contract of affreightment - plus trip time and consecutive voyage charters and, in liner trades, slot charters.
Who pays for bunkers under each? Owner under a voyage charter; charterer under a time charter; charterer under a bareboat charter.
What is laytime and what happens when it runs out? The time allowed for loading and discharging; beyond it the charterer pays demurrage.
What is despatch? Money payable by the owner where the operation is completed in less than the laytime allowed, commonly at half the demurrage rate.
What is off-hire? A clause under which hire ceases while the ship is prevented from working by a cause within the clause.
What does the description clause warrant that matters to you? Speed and consumption - and it is the basis of performance claims.
What is the employment and indemnity clause? The master follows the charterer's employment orders and the charterer indemnifies the owner against the consequences.
What does a safe port warranty promise? A port the ship can reach, use and leave without exposure to danger avoidable by good navigation and seamanship, absent an abnormal occurrence.
Who signs the bills of lading and on what terms? The master or an agent, under the bills of lading clause, which limits what may be signed and on what terms.

blocks.p: ONE AXIS, SIX FAMILIES, FOUR CELLS. The axis is how much of the ship has been sold — carriage, time, possession, quantity. The six clause families are SHIP — PERIOD — MONEY — RISK — SECURITY — COMPLIANCE. The four cells are owner and charterer × voyage and time.

And one sentence carries the whole of limb (c) if everything else deserts you: whoever pays for the bunkers has bought the ship's time and bears the risk of delay — owner in a voyage charter, protected by demurrage; charterer in a time charter, protected by off-hire.

ul: No instrument governs a charterparty. It is a contract, and its terms are what the parties agree, subject to the general law of contract and to the law and arbitration forum the contract chooses

Charterparty compared with bill of lading — the charterparty is freely negotiated between commercial parties; a bill of lading in the hands of a third-party holder may attract a mandatory carriage regime. Stated at the level of principle; no article of any carriage convention is cited

Standard forms — GENCON, NYPE, BALTIME, BARECON, SHELLTIME and the common tanker voyage forms are named as forms only. MIW holds none of the wordings, and no clause number and no clause wording is quoted or attributed
Rider clauses prevail over the printed form where they conflict
ISM and ISPS compliance, and fuel-quality and emission compliance, are commonly allocated by express clause. Referred to at regime level only; for the verified regulatory position see this paper's Q8
No Indian statute is named with a section. Neither the Indian Contract Act, 1872 nor the Indian carriage legislation is held, and no proposition here rests on either

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the limits of this answer

blocks.p: There is no primary source for this question and none is invented. A charterparty is a contract; no convention, code or resolution prescribes its content, so the dominant provenance class here is settled commercial practice and that is stated rather than disguised. It would properly be reviewed by a chartering or shipping-law practitioner; a regulatory check would find nothing to check.

MIW holds no charterparty standard form. GENCON, NYPE, BALTIME, BARECON and SHELLTIME are named as forms — which is uncontroversial industry knowledge — but no clause number is asserted anywhere, no clause wording is quoted, and no term is attributed to any particular form. That is a deliberate discipline, because supplying a clause number from memory is the specific way this question goes wrong, and a wrong number is worse than none. The same applies to figures: no hire rate, demurrage rate, laytime allowance or performance tolerance is quoted, since all are negotiated case by case.

Two further boundaries. The interaction with mandatory carriage regimes is stated only at the level of principle — a charterparty is freely negotiated, a bill of lading in a third party's hands may not be — with no article of the Hague, Hague-Visby, Hamburg or Rotterdam Rules cited and no assertion about which applies to any given contract. And no decided case is cited: the propositions here are settled practice rather than contested law, and where a real dispute arises it turns on the wording of the particular contract, not on a general rule. Charterparty law is a genuine gap in the MIW corpus — no other solved question in twenty-eight papers treats it — and that is recorded so a future session knows this answer stands alone.

notes: NO INSTRUMENT BOUNDARY. A charterparty is a contract and no convention, code or resolution governs its content. There is therefore no adopted, in-force or superseded date anywhere in this question, and the answer asserts none.
CHECKED IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AND CLEAR. Nothing in the commercial practice described here changed in 2024, and nothing relied on was superseded before this sitting.

THE ONE DATED ITEM IS DELIBERATELY GENERIC. Charterparties routinely carry clauses allocating responsibility for compliance with the ISM and ISPS Codes and with fuel-quality and emission requirements. Those regimes have dated content, so the answer refers to them at REGIME LEVEL ONLY and asserts no regulation number and no compliance date. Where a fuel or emission requirement matters, the paper's own Q8 carries the verified regulatory position.

NO INDIAN STATUTE IS NAMED WITH A SECTION. The Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the Indian carriage legislation are not held and no proposition rests on them. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 does not arise and does not appear.
NO POST-SITTING MATERIAL APPEARS. No BIMCO clause published after this sitting is named, no later IMO instrument is referenced, and no MEPC or MSC resolution arises.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs, and they climb. Limb (a) at 6 is definitional and taxonomic - define the instrument and explain its types, which is the largest single block on the question. Limb (b) at 5 is a survey - OUTLINE the key clauses, which means breadth with a short explanation each, not depth on three of them. Limb (c) at 5 is the analytical limb: ANALYSE the rights and obligations of BOTH parties under BOTH a time and a voyage charter, which is a two-by-two comparison and must be structured as one.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as 6 + 5 + 5, reconciling exactly. Limb (a) is the largest, which is unusual for a definition limb and tells you the TYPES are expected in real detail rather than as a list of three names. Limb (b)'s five marks over a dozen clause families means roughly a line each - group them or the limb becomes unreadable. Limb (c) must cover four cells - owner and charterer, time and voyage - in five marks, so a table or a disciplined four-part structure is the only way it fits.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate understands the commercial document under which the ship they run actually trades: who pays for the bunkers, who bears the time when the ship breaks down, what a safe port warranty commits the owner to, and why the speed and consumption figures in the description clause end up as a claim on the Chief Engineer's noon reports. The discriminating idea is that all the types are variations on one question - HOW MUCH OF THE SHIP'S OPERATION HAS BEEN SOLD - and that cost, time and control follow that answer.
primary_source_plan: Establish first that NO instrument governs a charterparty, and resolve not to invent one - which for this question means inventing neither a convention nor a clause number.
Name standard forms as forms only, and attribute no term and no number to any of them, because MIW holds none of the wordings.
Quote no hire rate, demurrage rate, laytime allowance or performance tolerance.
Refer to ISM, ISPS and fuel-quality obligations at regime level only, and leave the verified regulatory detail to this paper's own Q8.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW - Charterparty structure is stable over decades. Standard forms are revised occasionally and new rider clauses appear, but the allocation of cost, time and control that this question asks about does not move.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM, and handled by avoidance. Charterparties commonly choose English law and London arbitration whatever the parties' nationalities, so an Indian examination does not automatically make this an Indian-law question. The answer therefore states the choice-of-law and arbitration clause as a feature of the contract rather than asserting which law applies, and names no Indian statute with a section.
technical_ambiguities: 'Define a Charter Party' invites a one-line definition. Six marks with 'explain its different types' attached means the definition is the doorway and the types are the room.

'Key clauses typically included' is form-dependent, and MIW holds no form. The honest answer describes clause FAMILIES by what they do, which is also more useful than reciting one form's table of contents.

'Rights and obligations of BOTH the shipowner AND the charterer under a Time Charter AND Voyage Charter' is four cells, not two. An answer that describes the two charter types without separating the parties has done half of limb (c).
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six steps across three labelled limbs. Limb (a): what a charterparty is and what it is not; then the types arranged along the control axis. Limb (b): the clause families, grouped into about five groups so that five marks' worth of breadth is recallable. Limb (c): voyage charter rights and obligations for both parties; time charter rights and obligations for both parties; then a short comparative close that answers the word 'analyse'.

steps.title: What a charter party is, and what it is not
points: a contract for the use of a ship, or of her carrying capacity, for reward
between the shipowner and the charterer - and no instrument prescribes its terms
not a contract of sale of the goods, and not itself the contract of carriage with a cargo receiver
distinguish it from the bill of lading, which is receipt, evidence of contract and document of title
between owner and charterer the charterparty governs; a bill in a third party's hands may not be freely negotiated
freely negotiated, usually on an amended standard form, with rider clauses prevailing over the printed text

steps.title: The types, and the one question that generates them
points: the axis is simple - HOW MUCH of the ship's operation has been sold
VOYAGE CHARTER - the charterer buys a carriage between named ports; the owner keeps everything else
TIME CHARTER - the charterer buys the ship's time and directs her employment; the owner keeps possession and crew
BAREBOAT or DEMISE - the charterer takes possession, mans and operates her as disponent owner
CONTRACT OF AFFREIGHTMENT - a commitment to carry quantities over a period, ships nominated later
intermediate forms - trip time charter, consecutive voyage charter; slot charter in liner trades
cost, time and control all follow the same axis, which is why the types can be reconstructed rather than memorised

steps.title: The key clauses, grouped so they can be recalled
points: THE SHIP - description, class, flag, tonnage, capacity, speed and consumption warranty
THE PERIOD OR VOYAGE - delivery and redelivery or loading and discharging ports; laycan and cancelling
MONEY AND TIME - freight or hire and its payment; laytime, demurrage and despatch; off-hire; bunkers on delivery and redelivery
RISK AND CONTROL - safe port and safe berth; employment and indemnity; deviation; cargo exclusions; liberty and war risks; ice and strikes
SECURITY AND LIABILITY - bills of lading clause; lien and cesser; general average and New Jason; both-to-blame collision; P&I and insurance
COMPLIANCE AND ADMINISTRATION - ISM and ISPS clauses; sanctions; bunker quality and emission compliance; arbitration and choice of law
the printed form is a starting point; the rider clauses are where the negotiation actually is

steps.title: Voyage charter - what each party owes the other
points: OWNER'S OBLIGATIONS - provide the named ship, seaworthy and cargoworthy, and proceed with reasonable despatch
OWNER BEARS - crew, stores, maintenance, insurance, AND the voyage costs: bunkers, port charges, canal dues
OWNER'S RIGHTS - freight as agreed, demurrage if laytime is exceeded, and a lien on cargo for freight and demurrage
CHARTERER'S OBLIGATIONS - provide the agreed cargo, nominate a safe port and berth, load and discharge within laytime
CHARTERER BEARS - cargo and, according to the terms agreed, the cost of loading and discharging
CHARTERER'S RIGHTS - carriage of the agreed cargo between the agreed ports, despatch money if quicker than laytime
THE RISK SITS WITH THE OWNER - delay at sea or in port is the owner's problem unless laytime has expired

steps.title: Time charter - what each party owes the other
points: OWNER'S OBLIGATIONS - deliver at the agreed place in the agreed condition, and maintain her in class and efficient state throughout
OWNER BEARS - crew wages, stores, lubricating oil, maintenance, class and hull insurance
OWNER'S RIGHTS - hire, punctually and continuously, with a right to withdraw for non-payment; an indemnity for complying with the charterer's orders
CHARTERER'S OBLIGATIONS - pay hire; nominate safe ports; supply and pay for fuel of the agreed specification; employ her lawfully
CHARTERER BEARS - bunkers, port and canal charges, cargo handling, agency
CHARTERER'S RIGHTS - direct the commercial employment of the ship within the agreed trading limits
OFF-HIRE IS THE PIVOT - hire ceases while the ship is prevented from working by a cause within the clause
THE RISK OF TIME MOVES TO THE CHARTERER, except when the owner's own performance fails

steps.title: The comparison, and where the engineer sits in it
points: voyage - the owner sells a carriage and keeps the risk of time; time - the charterer buys the time and takes that risk
voyage - owner pays bunkers; time - charterer pays bunkers. This one line predicts most of the rest
voyage - delay is settled by laytime and demurrage; time - by off-hire
voyage - the owner controls the operation; time - the charterer controls employment, the owner controls navigation and safety
in both, the master remains responsible for the safety of the ship and may refuse an unsafe order
the engineer's exposure - speed and consumption warranty, off-hire for breakdown, bunker quantity and quality on delivery and redelivery
and the evidence that decides those disputes is engine-room evidence: noon reports, logs, bunker delivery notes, consumption data

quick_revision.recall_15s: A charterparty is a contract for the use of a ship — no convention governs it. Types run along one axis: how much of the operation has been sold. Voyage (a carriage), Time (the ship's time), Bareboat (possession and manning), Contract of affreightment (a quantity over a period). Clauses in six families: the ship, the period or voyage, money and time, risk and control, security and liability, compliance and administration. Money line to remember: voyage — owner pays bunkers and bears delay until laytime expires; time — charterer pays bunkers and bears the time, subject to off-hire.
keywords: contract for the use of a ship
critical_numbers: Marks: a) 6, b) 5, c) 5 - the definition-and-types limb is the LARGEST, so the types need real detail
Four principal types: voyage, time, bareboat or demise, and contract of affreightment
Limb (c) is FOUR cells: owner and charterer, under time and under voyage
NO clause number, no hire rate, no demurrage rate and no laytime allowance is quoted - all are negotiated case by case
quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no instrument. A charterparty is a contract, and its terms are what the parties agree, subject to the general law of contract and to the law and arbitration forum the contract itself chooses. Say that plainly — it is a correct and scoring observation, and it is the reason no convention should be cited here. The one legal distinction worth making is that a charterparty is freely negotiated, whereas a bill of lading in the hands of a third-party holder may attract a mandatory carriage regime.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (c) with two descriptions instead of four. The stem says the rights and obligations of both the shipowner and the charterer under a Time Charter and Voyage Charter — that is a two-by-two grid, and an answer that describes the two charter types without separating the parties has done half of it. The second trap is inventing a clause number or attributing a term to a named form: describe what the clause does, and do not pretend to quote it.

questions.memory_cue: One axis carries limb (a) and most of limb (c): HOW MUCH OF THE SHIP HAS BEEN SOLD? A carriage (voyage), her time (time), or the ship herself (bareboat) — steps 1 and 2. For clauses, six families: SHIP — PERIOD — MONEY — RISK — SECURITY — COMPLIANCE (3). For limb (c), one line predicts nearly everything: who pays for the bunkers pays for the time (4, 5, 6).
questions.understand_first:
A charterparty is not a species of regulation and there is no convention behind it. It is a commercial bargain about a ship, and everything in it — the types, the clauses, the disputes — falls out of a single question: how much of the ship's operation has the owner sold?

Sell a single carriage and you have a voyage charter: the owner keeps the ship, the crew and the operation, pays for the bunkers and the port charges, and takes the risk that the voyage runs long — which is why he needs laytime and demurrage, a clock that starts when the ship is ready and charges the charterer once it runs out. Sell the ship's time and you have a time charter: the charterer now decides where she goes and therefore pays for the fuel and the ports, and the owner is paid a daily hire whatever she is doing — which is why the charterer needs off-hire, a clause that stops the clock when the ship cannot work. Sell possession itself and you have a bareboat charter: the charterer mans her, insures her and operates her, and the owner is close to a financier.

Hold that axis and you can derive the answer rather than recall it. And note where the Chief Engineer sits on it: the speed and consumption warranty, the off-hire clause and the bunker clauses are the three places where the engine room and the contract meet — and the evidence in every one of those disputes is engine-room evidence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the charter party question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 What a charterparty is and what it is not. 2 The types, along the control axis. (b) 3 The key clauses in six families. (c) 4 Voyage charter - both parties. 5 Time charter - both parties. 6 The comparison, and where the engineer sits in it.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) is 6 marks and gets two steps; limbs (b) and (c) are 5 each. Limb (c) needs two steps because it is four cells - owner and charterer, time and voyage.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define a charter party, and distinguish it from a bill of lading.
retrieval_cards.answer: A charterparty is a contract by which a shipowner agrees to place a ship, or part of her carrying capacity, at the disposal of a charterer for reward. A bill of lading is a receipt for goods shipped, evidence of the contract of carriage, and a document of title. Between owner and charterer the charterparty governs; a bill of lading in the hands of a third-party holder is a separate contract and may attract a mandatory carriage regime that the charterparty does not.
retrieval_cards.why: The distinction is a standard opening mark and it also sets up the point that a charterparty is freely negotiated while a bill of lading may not be.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four principal types of charter and the one question that distinguishes them.
retrieval_cards.answer: Voyage charter, time charter, bareboat or demise charter, and contract of affreightment. The question is how much of the ship's operation has been sold: a single carriage; the ship's time; possession of the ship herself; or a commitment to carry quantities over a period with ships nominated later.
retrieval_cards.why: Deriving the types from one axis is faster and more defensible than memorising a list, and it makes the cost and risk allocation in limb (c) predictable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who pays for the bunkers under a voyage charter and under a time charter, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: The owner under a voyage charter; the charterer under a time charter. It matters because whoever pays for the fuel is the party who has bought the ship's time and therefore bears the risk of delay - which is why a voyage charter needs laytime and demurrage and a time charter needs off-hire.
retrieval_cards.why: This single line predicts most of the cost and risk allocation in limb (c) and is the fastest way to reconstruct it under pressure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are laytime, demurrage and despatch?
retrieval_cards.answer: Laytime is the time allowed to the charterer for loading and discharging under a voyage charter, running from a valid notice of readiness. Demurrage is the agreed sum payable by the charterer for time used beyond laytime - liquidated damages for detaining the ship. Despatch is the sum, commonly half the demurrage rate, payable by the owner where the operation is completed in less than the laytime allowed.
retrieval_cards.why: These three are the voyage charter's answer to delay, and they exist because under a voyage charter the owner is the one paying for the time.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is off-hire, and why does the time charterer need it?
retrieval_cards.answer: A clause providing that hire ceases to be payable while the ship is prevented from working by a cause falling within it - typically breakdown of machinery, deficiency of crew, damage, drydocking or detention. The time charterer pays hire continuously and is buying the ship's time, so without off-hire he would go on paying for a ship that cannot work.
retrieval_cards.why: Off-hire is the clause a Chief Engineer meets most directly: a machinery breakdown moves money, and how much depends on the wording and on the engine-room record.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a safe port warranty commit the charterer to?
retrieval_cards.answer: To nominate a port and berth at which the ship can reach, use and return from without, in the absence of some abnormal occurrence, being exposed to danger which cannot be avoided by good navigation and seamanship. It is a promise about the port's characteristics, and the master's residual right to refuse to enter an unsafe port survives it.
retrieval_cards.why: It is one of the few charterparty terms that bears directly on the ship's safety, and the interaction with the master's own judgement is exactly what an examiner probes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which convention governs the content of a charter party?
retrieval_cards.answer: None. A charterparty is a contract between commercial parties and no convention, code or resolution prescribes its terms; it is governed by the general law of contract and by whatever law and arbitration forum the contract itself chooses. That is different from a bill of lading in a third party's hands, which may attract a mandatory carriage regime.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying so plainly is a correct and scoring observation, and it prevents the standard error of citing a carriage convention as though it governed the charter.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does the Chief Engineer meet the charterparty?
retrieval_cards.answer: In three places. The speed and consumption warranty in the description clause, which generates performance claims settled on noon reports and weather data. The off-hire clause, where a machinery breakdown stops hire and the cause and duration have to be proved from the engine-room record. And the bunker clauses, covering quantity and price on delivery and redelivery and the specification and quality of fuel the charterer supplies.
retrieval_cards.why: This is what turns a commercial-law answer into a management-level one, and it is the likeliest oral follow-up on the whole question.

The IMO standards for ship manoeuvrability and the class rules for steering arrangements exist and are referred to AT REGIME LEVEL, by function, with NO RESOLUTION NUMBER, NO CIRCULAR NUMBER AND NO NUMERICAL CRITERION ASSERTED - MIW holds neither and inventing a criterion would be a far worse defect than declaring the limitation. NO PERCENTAGE IS QUOTED for any margin, because sea margin, engine margin and light-running margin are all installation-specific and contractual.
sources: ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT, settled naval architecture: directional or course stability as the property of a hull which, when disturbed from a straight course by a transient force and with the rudder returned amidships, settles onto a new straight course rather than continuing to turn. The distinction between straight-line stability, directional stability and positional motion stability, and the fact that stability is judged on the RESIDUAL MOTION after the disturbance ceases, not on the deviation during it.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT, settled naval architecture: the hydrodynamic origin of course instability - a hull at a small drift angle generates a lateral force whose centre of pressure lies FORWARD of the centre of gravity, producing a moment that increases the drift angle; the ship is directionally stable only where the restoring moment from the after body and appendages exceeds that destabilising moment. Hence the role of longitudinal distribution of lateral area.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the design conflict that is the substance of limb (A) - directional stability and manoeuvrability are OPPOSED. A long, fine, deeply skegged hull holds a course and turns slowly; a short, full-bodied hull with a cut-up afterbody turns readily and wanders. Length to beam ratio, block coefficient, trim, and the longitudinal distribution of lateral area are the parameters, and the choice is a trade-off made for the ship's intended service.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: how the attributes are provided - hull form and proportions; skeg, deadwood and after body form; trim by the stern; the rudder as the primary control surface, with area, aspect ratio, section and type (spade, semi-balanced horn, high-lift flap and steerable nozzle) determining lift and stall angle; twin skegs and twin rudders; propeller-rudder interaction and the rudder working in the propeller race; bow and stern thrusters as low-speed devices whose effectiveness falls away with headway; azimuth and podded units; and the autopilot with rate and counter-rudder terms as the closed-loop element that makes a marginally stable ship usable.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT, settled marine engineering: the engine layout and load diagram - power against speed for a slow-speed two-stroke, bounded by the maximum mean effective pressure line, the maximum speed line, the constant-torque or mean-effective-pressure limit at low speed, and the overload region; the layout points L1 to L4 defining the field within which the specific engine is laid out; MCR and the selected service or continuous service rating; and the torque-limit and scavenge-air-pressure-limit curves that constrain acceleration.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the propeller demand curve - for a fixed-pitch propeller in free-running conditions the delivered power varies approximately as the CUBE of shaft speed and the torque as the SQUARE, so the demand curve is a cubic through the origin whose position depends on the propeller and on the resistance of the hull. Its migration with fouling, added displacement, shallow water, heavy weather, towing and ice - all of which move the curve to the LEFT, so more torque is demanded at a given speed. The light-running condition of a clean, trial-condition ship moving the curve to the RIGHT.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the relation the stem asks for - the propeller is designed to absorb the selected service power at the selected service speed, and the engine is rated above that point. The gap is deliberately made up of MARGINS: a sea margin covering the added resistance of fouling and weather; an engine or operating margin keeping the service point below the maximum continuous rating; and a light-running margin so that the propeller is deliberately slightly light when new and clean, allowing the curve to migrate towards the torque limit through the docking cycle without the engine becoming overloaded. NO PERCENTAGE IS QUOTED for any of these.

ENGINEERING JUDGEMENT: the consequences of mismatch - a heavy-running or torque-rich engine reaching its torque limit before its rated speed, so the rated power cannot be developed; high thermal loading, high exhaust temperature, fouled turbocharging and scavenge fires; loss of speed and increased consumption; and the converse light-running case, in which the engine overspeeds before it is fully loaded and the ship never reaches her design power.

REGIME LEVEL ONLY, NO NUMBER ASSERTED: IMO has adopted standards for ship manoeuvrability, applicable to ships above a stated size, tested by defined trial manoeuvres - turning circle, zig-zag, stopping and initial turning ability - and classification societies set requirements for steering gear and may assign optional manoeuvrability notations. THE RESOLUTION NUMBER, THE CIRCULAR NUMBER, THE SIZE THRESHOLD AND EVERY NUMERICAL CRITERION ARE DELIBERATELY NOT ASSERTED: MIW holds neither the standards nor the class rules, and an invented criterion would be a far worse defect than a declared gap.
