blocks.h: (a) Directional stability and manoeuvring, and how they are provided — printed as limb (A), 8 marks

blocks.p: Directional or course stability is a property of the hull, not of the steering gear, the autopilot or the helmsman. The test is simple and should be stated first, because it defines the whole term: disturb the ship from a straight course by a transient force — a gust, a wave, a moment of rudder — then return the rudder amidships and see what she does.

ul: A directionally stable ship settles onto a new straight course. She ends up on a different heading, but she goes straight again without help.
A directionally unstable ship continues to turn. Rudder must be applied to stop her turning, and the helmsman or autopilot is permanently at work.

blocks.p: Note that stability is judged on the residual motion after the disturbance ceases, not on how far she deviated while it acted. A stable ship may swing a long way and still be stable.

Why instability arises at all. When a hull moves at a small angle of drift, it behaves as a low-aspect-ratio lifting surface and generates a lateral force. On most ship forms the centre of that force lies forward of the centre of gravity, so the moment it produces increases the drift angle — it is destabilising. The ship is directionally stable only where the restoring moment generated by the after body and its appendages exceeds that destabilising moment. That is why everything that provides course stability is aft, and why the answer to the second half of this limb is mostly about the stern.

The two attributes named in the question are not two virtues; they are opposed, and saying so is the substance of this limb rather than a refinement of it. Both depend on the same parameter — the longitudinal distribution of lateral area — and they want it in opposite places.

rows: Long and fine, high length-to-beam ratio, low block coefficient
Short and full, low length-to-beam ratio, high block coefficient
Holds a course; turns slowly and widely
Turns readily and tightly; wanders on course

ul: Trim matters as much as form. Trim by the stern moves lateral area aft and improves course stability; a ship in ballast trimmed by the head is markedly worse on course, which every watchkeeper has felt.
Draught and depth of water matter. Shallow water changes the pressure field around the hull and generally increases course stability while degrading turning ability.

The design is therefore a deliberate compromise chosen for the ship's service, and a modern ship is often placed slightly on the unstable side on purpose, accepting a small permanent workload on the steering gear in exchange for a real gain in turning ability — because the autopilot can close the loop and the fuel cost of continuous small corrections is less than the operational cost of a ship that cannot turn.

blocks.p: Answer this in order of priority, because that order is itself worth marks: the property lives in the hull, and everything else modifies it.

ul: Hull form — first and most important. Length-to-beam ratio, block coefficient, and the form of the run aft. A skeg is the single most direct device: it adds lateral area well aft of the centre of gravity and therefore adds restoring moment. Deadwood does the same. Full-form ships may use twin skegs, which also improve the wake field into two propellers.

The rudder — the primary control surface. What matters is area as a fraction of the ship's lateral plane, aspect ratio (a deeper, narrower rudder gives more lift for its area and stalls later), section, and type: a spade rudder for small and fast ships, a semi-balanced horn rudder where the stock must be supported on a large ship, and high-lift flap or fishtail rudders where a large side force is needed at low speed. A balanced rudder places part of its area forward of the stock to reduce steering torque.

The rudder works in the propeller race, and this is the operational point of the whole limb. Immersed in an accelerated slipstream, the rudder develops far more side force than the ship's speed through the water alone would produce. Stop the propeller and the rudder has only the free stream to work with, so steering effectiveness collapses even though the ship still has headway. That is why a ship loses steerage the moment the engine is stopped, and why a rudder behind a stopped propeller is nearly useless.

Low-speed devices. Bow and stern thrusters generate side force where the rudder has no flow at all, but their effectiveness falls away rapidly with headway as the ship's own flow sweeps the jet along the hull. Azimuth and podded units produce thrust in any direction and give a manoeuvring capability nothing else matches.

The control system. An autopilot with rate and counter-rudder terms anticipates the swing instead of chasing it, and an adaptive autopilot tunes itself to the loading and sea state. This is what makes a marginally unstable hull entirely usable in service, and it is the reason designers are willing to accept one.

blocks.p: Finally, the regulatory frame, stated at the level at which it can be stated honestly: IMO has adopted standards for ship manoeuvrability applying to ships above a stated size, assessed by defined trial manoeuvres — the turning circle, the zig-zag, the stopping test and initial turning ability — and classification societies set requirements for steering gear and may assign optional manoeuvrability notations. No resolution number and no numerical criterion is quoted here, because the standards are not held and an invented criterion would be worse than none.

blocks.h: (b) The engine power / engine speed diagram and the propeller demand curve — printed as limb (B), 8 marks

blocks.p: This limb asks you to use a diagram. Draw it. Power on the vertical axis, engine or shaft speed on the horizontal, both usually logarithmic so the curves become straight lines. Mark the engine's permitted field, lay the propeller cubic across it, and label MCR, the service point, and at least two propeller curves — trial condition and service condition. Everything below is what those labels mean.

blocks.h: 4. The engine power versus engine speed diagram

ul: The layout diagram is the field, bounded by the layout points, within which the particular engine may be optimised at the design stage — the manufacturer's offer, before a rating is chosen.
The load diagram is the operating field of the engine as actually rated, and it is the one that matters in service. Its boundaries each mean something physical:
above — the maximum mean effective pressure line, which is a limit on mechanical and thermal loading of the running gear and combustion chamber;
to the right — the maximum speed line, a limit on rotational speed and inertia loading;

to the left at low speed — the torque limit and the scavenge air pressure limit, which together prevent the engine being asked for high torque before the turbocharger can deliver the air to burn the fuel cleanly. This is the boundary that bites in service;
an overload region above the continuous field, permitted only for limited periods and normally only on trials.

blocks.p: MCR — the maximum continuous rating — is the top right corner of the permitted continuous field: the highest power the engine may develop continuously, at its corresponding speed. The service or continuous service rating is a point deliberately placed below and to the left of it, and that deliberate placement is the subject of step 6.

blocks.h: 5. The propeller demand curve, and how it moves

blocks.p: For a fixed-pitch propeller in free-running conditions, the power the propeller demands varies approximately as the cube of shaft speed, and the torque as the square. The demand curve is therefore a cubic through the origin, and where it crosses the engine's field is where the ship actually runs.

Its position depends on two things: the propeller (pitch and diameter) and the resistance of the hull. The second is not constant, which is the whole point of this limb. Draw more than one curve, because the examiner's plural is deliberate:

ul: the curve moves LEFT — more torque demanded at any given speed — with hull and propeller fouling, increased displacement, shallow water, heavy weather and head seas, ice, towing, and damage to a propeller blade;
the curve moves RIGHT when the ship is clean, light and in trial condition — the light-running case;
left is towards the torque limit. That single direction carries most of the operational content of the limb.

blocks.h: 6. The relation the question asks for - the three margins

blocks.p: Now the printed question can be answered directly. The propeller is designed to absorb the SERVICE power at the SERVICE speed. The engine is rated ABOVE that point. The gap is deliberate, and it is made up of three margins.

ul: Sea margin. Added power provided to overcome the added resistance of hull and propeller fouling and of weather accumulated over the docking cycle. Without it a ship could make her contract speed only on the day she left the builder's yard.

Engine or operating margin. The service point is kept below MCR so that the engine runs continuously at a load that is easier on it, more economical in specific fuel consumption, and leaves reserve power available.

Light-running margin. The propeller is deliberately made slightly light when the ship is new and clean — that is, it absorbs slightly less torque than the engine could give at that speed. This is the one candidates find counter-intuitive and it is the most important of the three: because the demand curve only ever migrates leftwards in service, it must be given somewhere to migrate to. A propeller matched exactly in trial condition is already heavy-running the day she leaves the dock.

blocks.p: So the answer to the question as printed is that the maximum rated output of the plant exceeds the power for which the propeller is designed by design, not by accident, and the difference is the sum of those three allowances. No percentage is given here for any of them: sea margin, engine margin and light-running margin are settled between owner, yard and engine builder in the newbuilding contract and vary with trade, hull form and docking interval.

blocks.h: 7. What happens when the match goes wrong

blocks.p: Heavy running, or torque-rich operation. The demand curve has moved left of design — typically a foul hull, a foul or damaged propeller, deep draught, shallow water or persistent heavy weather. The engine now meets its torque limit before it reaches its rated speed, so it cannot develop rated power at all. The symptoms follow directly from that:

ul: high thermal loading and high exhaust temperatures, because the engine is burning a large fuel quantity at a speed at which the turbocharger delivers less air;
turbocharger and gas-side fouling, which makes the air shortage worse and is self-reinforcing;
increased risk of scavenge fire and of exhaust-valve and piston-ring distress;

loss of speed and increased specific fuel consumption — and, as a commercial consequence, a worse operational carbon intensity for the year and a possible underperformance claim under the charterparty.

blocks.p: The remedies are in the same order as the causes: hull and propeller cleaning, correct trim and draught, and — if the condition persists after cleaning — a propeller re-pitch to move the curve back to the right.

Light running is the converse and is a real fault too, not merely a safe margin. If the propeller is too light, the engine reaches its speed limit before it is fully loaded: the ship never develops her design power, the engine is overspeed-limited, and the installation is not delivering what it was paid for.

In both cases the diagnosis is the same, and it is the practical point of the whole limb: plot the actual operating points — power, shaft speed, fuel index — on the engine's own load diagram, and see which boundary the ship is running into. A diagram used that way is a condition-monitoring tool, not a piece of design paperwork.

This is two questions of eight marks joined by a staple. They share no content and they need no linking material — so treat them as two independent answers, label them (A) and (B), and give each half the paper. A candidate who is strong on one and weak on the other should still write both: eight marks are available in each, and half of a well-organised limb beats a rushed whole.

In limb (A), the eight marks are weighted towards the second half. The definition is one mark and the conflict is worth two or three; ‘how are these attributes provided in a ship’ is the biggest single block, and it wants hull first, rudder second, low-speed devices third, control system last. Answering it in that order is itself a scoring decision, because it shows you know where the property lives.

In limb (B) the stem says ‘Using typical engine power versus engine speed diagram and propeller demand curves’. Draw it. A written description of a diagram the examiner explicitly asked for is a weaker answer than the same words with a labelled sketch above them, and the sketch takes ninety seconds.

blocks.h: What to draw in limb (B), exactly

blocks.p: Axes: power vertical, engine or shaft speed horizontal, both on log scales so the curves come out as straight lines. Then, in this order:

ol: the load diagram as a four-sided field — mean effective pressure limit along the top, speed limit on the right, torque and scavenge-air limits sloping up from the left, and a small overload region above;
MCR marked at the top right corner of the continuous field;
the service point marked below and to the left of MCR — and the gap between them labelled with the three margins;
the propeller demand curve in trial condition, passing through or just right of the service point;
a second propeller curve to its left, labelled service or fouled condition, running into the torque limit — this is the one that makes the diagram tell a story;
an arrow between them labelled fouling, weather, displacement.

blocks.p: Six elements. If you can draw those and label them, the prose almost writes itself and every mark in the limb is reachable.

blocks.h: The two ideas that carry the whole question

blocks.p: Limb (A): stability and manoeuvrability are opposed. Both depend on the longitudinal distribution of lateral area, and they want it in opposite places. Everything aft of the centre of gravity — a long run, a deep skeg, deadwood, trim by the stern — makes her hold a course and makes her reluctant to turn. There is no design that maximises both, so a ship is placed on the scale where her service needs her, and modern ships are often placed slightly unstable on purpose because the autopilot can carry the workload and the turning gain is worth having.

Limb (B): the design point and the maximum rating are different on purpose. The engine offers a field of power against speed; the propeller demands power along a cubic; and the gap between MCR and the propeller's design point is not slack but three deliberate allowances. The counter-intuitive one is the light-running margin: the propeller is made slightly light when new because the demand curve only ever moves leftwards in service. Give it nowhere to move and you have built in a heavy-running engine from the first voyage.

ul: Treating directional stability and manoeuvrability as the same virtue. They are opposed, and the question is about the compromise.
Answering limb (A) as ship handling. It asks how the attributes are provided in a ship — a design question.
Starting the ‘how provided’ answer at the rudder. The property lives in the hull; the rudder modifies it.
Forgetting that the rudder works in the propeller race, which is the reason steerage is lost when the engine stops.
Not drawing the diagram in limb (B) when the stem asks you to use one.
Drawing one propeller curve. The plural in the stem is deliberate — trial and service conditions.
Confusing MCR with the propeller design power. They are different points on purpose, and the difference between them is the answer.
Getting the direction wrong: fouling moves the curve LEFT, into the torque limit.
Saying the propeller should be matched exactly on trials. It should be slightly light.
Quoting a percentage for sea margin or light-running margin, or an IMO manoeuvring criterion. Neither can be defended from a held source.

blocks.p: ‘Is a directionally unstable ship unsafe?’ Not necessarily. Many large full-form ships are marginally unstable by design, and the autopilot with rate and counter-rudder terms handles it. It becomes a problem when the control system fails, when the ship is trimmed by the head in ballast, or when close-quarters manoeuvring demands more attention than the bridge team can give.

‘Why do you lose steering when the engine stops?’ The rudder works in the propeller race. Without the accelerated slipstream it has only the free-stream flow, so the side force collapses even with headway on. This is the single most practical consequence of limb (A).

‘Your engine will not make revolutions and the exhaust temperatures are high. What is it?’ Heavy running — the demand curve has moved left and the engine is on its torque limit. Confirm by plotting operating points on the load diagram; then hull and propeller cleaning, trim, and a re-pitch if it persists.

‘Why not match the propeller exactly at trials?’ Because the curve only moves one way afterwards. A perfectly matched propeller is heavy-running from the first month, and the engine cannot then reach rated power for the rest of the docking cycle.

‘What limits the engine at low speed?’ The torque and scavenge-air-pressure limits — you cannot demand high torque before the turbocharger can supply the air to burn the fuel. Naming the scavenge-air limit rather than just ‘the torque limit’ is the better answer.

ul: Define directional stability and tell me how you would test it. Disturb her, return the rudder amidships; a stable ship settles on a new straight course, an unstable one keeps turning.
Why is a hull directionally unstable at all? At a small drift angle the lateral force acts forward of the centre of gravity, producing a moment that increases the drift.
Name three things that provide course stability. Hull proportions and a long run; a skeg and deadwood; trim by the stern.
What determines rudder effectiveness? Area as a fraction of the lateral plane, aspect ratio, section and type - and whether it is working in the propeller race.
When is a bow thruster useless? At any appreciable headway, as the ship's own flow sweeps the jet along the hull.
Name the IMO manoeuvring trials. Turning circle, zig-zag, stopping ability, initial turning ability.
How does propeller power vary with shaft speed? As the cube; torque as the square.
What bounds the load diagram? Mean effective pressure above, speed to the right, torque and scavenge air pressure at low speed, with an overload region above the continuous field.
Name the three margins between MCR and the propeller design point. Sea margin, engine or operating margin, light-running margin.
Which way does fouling move the demand curve, and what does that do? To the left - the engine meets its torque limit before rated speed and cannot develop rated power.

blocks.p: Limb (A): WHAT — CONFLICT — HOW, and inside the how, four things in descending order of importance: HULL, RUDDER, THRUSTER, AUTOPILOT. If you remember only that the property lives in the hull and the rudder works in the race, you can rebuild the limb.

Limb (B): FIELD — CUBIC — MARGINS — MISMATCH. The three margins are SEA, ENGINE, LIGHT. And the direction is the thing to burn in: LEFT IS HEAVY — fouling, weather, displacement and shallow water all push the curve left, towards the torque limit.

ul: No instrument prescribes hull form, appendage design, rudder area, engine selection, or the margins between engine rating and propeller demand. Both limbs are engineering, and the provenance class is stated rather than disguised

Classification society requirements for steering gear, and optional manoeuvrability notations. Described by function; no rule and no notation is cited

Naval architecture references for course stability, the lateral-force mechanism, rudder types and propeller-rudder interaction; marine engineering references for the layout and load diagram, the propeller law, and the sea, engine and light-running margins. No percentage and no diagram boundary value is quoted

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the numbers deliberately withheld

blocks.p: Engineering judgement is effectively the sole provenance class on this question, and that is stated rather than disguised. No instrument prescribes hull form, appendage design, engine selection or the margins, so there is nothing regulatory to verify in either limb and nothing was invented to fill the space. The content is settled naval architecture and marine engineering explained by mechanism, and it would properly be reviewed by a naval architect and an engine specialist rather than by a regulatory check.

The one regulatory touch is deliberately held at regime level. IMO's standards for ship manoeuvrability and the class requirements for steering gear are real and are referred to by function — the trial manoeuvres are named because they are universally known by name — but MIW holds neither the standards nor any class rule, so no resolution number, no circular number, no application threshold and no numerical criterion is asserted anywhere. No advance, no tactical diameter, no overshoot angle, no track reach. An invented manoeuvring criterion would be a far worse defect than a declared gap, and this is exactly the kind of question where one is easy to invent.

Three sets of numbers are withheld on the same principle. No percentage for sea margin, engine margin or light-running margin — all three are contractual and installation-specific, settled between owner, yard and engine builder, and typical values vary with trade, hull form and docking interval. No numerical value for any load-diagram boundary, since those belong to a particular engine's project guide, which is not held. And no numerical course-stability criterion: the concept is explained and the index is not quantified. One further limitation is worth stating plainly — the stem asks the candidate to use a diagram, and this spec carries no figure, so the answer specifies exactly what should be drawn and labelled instead. A candidate in the examination room should draw it.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two lettered limbs of eight marks each, and they are two different subjects joined by the word 'propulsion'. Limb (A) is NAVAL ARCHITECTURE: what directional stability and manoeuvring are, and HOW THEY ARE PROVIDED IN A SHIP - which is a design question, not a ship-handling one. Limb (B) is MARINE ENGINEERING and is explicitly a DIAGRAM question: it names the engine power versus engine speed diagram and the propeller demand curves, and asks for the RELATION between the maximum rated output of the plant and the power the propeller is designed for. That relation is the margins, and the margins are the answer.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as 8 + 8, reconciling exactly. Equal weight, and the two limbs are genuinely independent - a candidate strong in one and weak in the other should still write both. Within limb (A) the 'how are these attributes provided' half is where most of the marks are, because it is the part that requires design knowledge rather than definitions. Within limb (B) the diagram must be DRAWN and LABELLED; a written description of a diagram the examiner asked for is a weaker answer than the same words with the sketch above them.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate knows directional stability is a property of the HULL, not of the steering gear, and that it is in DIRECT CONFLICT with manoeuvrability - so a ship is designed to a compromise chosen for her service. And, in limb (B), that the candidate can draw the layout diagram with the propeller cubic across it, place MCR and the service point, and explain the sea, engine and light-running margins as the deliberate gap between them - then say what happens when the curve migrates left.

technical_ambiguities: 'Directional stability and manoeuvring' are commonly treated as one idea. They are OPPOSED, and saying so is the substance of limb (A) rather than a refinement of it.
'How are these attributes provided in a ship' could be read as ship handling. It is a DESIGN question - hull form first, appendages second, control systems third.

'Using typical engine power versus engine speed diagram and propeller demand curves' is an instruction to DRAW. The plural 'curves' is deliberate: the examiner wants the clean and fouled or loaded conditions shown, not one line.
'The power for which the propeller is designed' is the SERVICE point, not the engine's maximum. Conflating the two is the error the whole limb is testing for.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Seven steps in two labelled limbs. Limb (A): what directional stability is; the conflict with manoeuvrability; and how both are provided, hull first then appendages then control. Limb (B): the layout diagram and its boundaries; the propeller demand curve and why it is a cube law and how it moves; the relation between MCR and the design point through the three margins; and what happens when the match goes wrong.
decomposition_gate.completed: Before research and drafting, against the October 2024 anchor

steps.title: What directional stability is
points: a property of the HULL, not of the steering gear or the helmsman
disturb her from a straight course, return the rudder amidships, and see what she does
directionally stable - she settles on a new straight course, on a different heading
directionally unstable - she continues to turn, and needs rudder to stop turning
stability is judged on the RESIDUAL motion after the disturbance ceases
the origin - at a small drift angle the hull's lateral force acts forward of the centre of gravity
so the moment increases the drift angle unless the after body and appendages restore it

steps.title: The conflict - stability against manoeuvrability
points: the two attributes are OPPOSED, and this is the substance of the limb
a long, fine hull with a deep skeg holds a course and turns slowly and widely
a short, full hull with a cut-up after body turns readily and wanders on course
length to beam ratio, block coefficient, and the longitudinal distribution of lateral area
trim by the stern moves lateral area aft and adds stability
a ship in ballast, trimmed by the head, is markedly worse on course
the design is a compromise CHOSEN FOR HER SERVICE - deep-sea passage against harbour work
and a marginally unstable ship is acceptable if the control system can close the loop

steps.title: How the attributes are provided
points: HULL FIRST - proportions, after body form, skeg and deadwood, twin skegs on full ships
the skeg is the single most direct stability device: lateral area aft of the centre of gravity
THE RUDDER is the primary control - area as a fraction of the lateral plane, aspect ratio, section
type - spade, semi-balanced horn, and high-lift flap or fishtail rudders for greater side force
a balanced rudder reduces steering torque; a horn supports the stock on large ships
the rudder works in the propeller RACE, so it is far more effective with the engine turning
which is why a ship loses steerage the moment the propeller stops
LOW-SPEED DEVICES - bow and stern thrusters, effective only at low headway
azimuth and podded propulsion, which produce side force directly
and the AUTOPILOT with rate and counter-rudder terms, which makes a marginal ship usable
assessed at regime level by IMO manoeuvring standards - turning circle, zig-zag, stopping

steps.title: The engine power versus engine speed diagram
points: power on the vertical axis, engine or shaft speed on the horizontal - usually logarithmic
the LAYOUT diagram - the field bounded by the layout points, within which the engine may be optimised
the LOAD diagram - the operating field of the engine as actually rated
bounded above by the maximum mean effective pressure line
bounded to the right by the maximum speed line
bounded to the left at low speed by the torque and scavenge-air-pressure limits
an overload region, permitted only for limited periods and usually only on trials
MCR - maximum continuous rating - is the top right corner of the permitted field
the SERVICE or continuous service rating is deliberately placed BELOW it

steps.title: The propeller demand curve, and how it moves
points: for a fixed-pitch propeller in free running, delivered power varies as the CUBE of shaft speed
torque varies as the SQUARE - so the curve is a cubic through the origin
its position depends on the propeller pitch and diameter AND on the resistance of the hull
DRAW MORE THAN ONE - the trial condition and the service condition are different curves
the curve moves LEFT with hull and propeller fouling
left with increased displacement, shallow water, heavy weather, ice, towing
left after damage to the propeller or a bent blade
and RIGHT when the ship is clean, light and in trial condition - the light-running case
left means more torque demanded at any given speed - towards the torque limit

steps.title: The relation the question asks for - the three margins
points: the propeller is designed to absorb the SERVICE power at the SERVICE speed
the engine is rated ABOVE that point, and the gap is deliberate, not slack
SEA MARGIN - added power for the added resistance of fouling and weather over the docking cycle
ENGINE or OPERATING MARGIN - service point kept below MCR for reliability and fuel economy
LIGHT-RUNNING MARGIN - the propeller made deliberately slightly LIGHT when new and clean
so the demand curve can migrate left through the docking cycle without hitting the torque limit
a propeller matched exactly at trial condition is WRONG - it is heavy the day she leaves dock
no percentage is quoted here: all three margins are contractual and installation-specific
the answer to the printed question is therefore that MCR exceeds the propeller design power BY DESIGN

steps.title: What happens when the match goes wrong
points: HEAVY RUNNING or torque-rich - the demand curve has moved left of design
the engine meets its torque limit before reaching rated speed, so rated power cannot be developed
high thermal loading, high exhaust temperatures, turbocharger fouling, risk of scavenge fire
loss of speed and increased specific consumption - and a worse operational carbon intensity
the remedies - hull and propeller cleaning, correct trim and draught, propeller re-pitch if persistent
LIGHT RUNNING - the engine reaches its speed limit before it is fully loaded
the ship never develops her design power, and the engine may be overspeed-limited
the diagnosis in both cases is the same - plot the actual operating points against the layout diagram

quick_revision.recall_15s: (A) Directional stability is a property of the HULL. Disturb her, rudder amidships: stable ships settle on a new straight course, unstable ships keep turning. It opposes manoeuvrability — long, fine, deep skeg holds course and turns slowly; short, full, cut-up after body turns well and wanders. Provided by hull form and skeg first, rudder second (working in the propeller race), thrusters and azimuth units at low speed, autopilot to close the loop. (B) Engine layout diagram, propeller cubic across it. Power ∝ N3, torque ∝ N2. MCR is above the service point on purpose — sea margin, engine margin, light-running margin. Fouling moves the curve left into the torque limit: heavy running.
critical_numbers: Marks: A) 8, B) 8 - two independent subjects, equal weight, and limb (B) asks for a DIAGRAM
Power varies as the CUBE of shaft speed; torque as the SQUARE - for a fixed-pitch propeller in free running
THREE margins between MCR and the propeller design point: sea margin, engine or operating margin, light-running margin
NO percentage is quoted for any margin - all three are contractual and installation-specific
NO IMO manoeuvring criterion is quoted - the trial manoeuvres are named, their pass criteria are not
quick_revision.critical_regulation: No instrument prescribes any of this. Hull form, appendage design, rudder area, engine selection and the margins are all engineering and contractual. IMO has adopted standards for ship manoeuvrability, assessed by defined trial manoeuvres — turning circle, zig-zag, stopping and initial turning ability — and classification societies set steering-gear requirements. Refer to both by function; do not quote a resolution number or a numerical criterion you cannot verify.
quick_revision.major_trap: Two, one in each limb. In (A), treating directional stability and manoeuvrability as the same virtue: they are opposed, and the design is a compromise chosen for the ship's service. In (B), confusing the engine's maximum rating with the power the propeller is designed for. They are different points on purpose, and the gap between them — the three margins — is the answer to the printed question.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (A): WHAT — CONFLICT — HOW (1, 2, 3), and inside the how, hull, rudder, thruster, autopilot in that order of priority. Limb (B): ENGINE FIELD — PROPELLER CUBIC — MARGINS — MISMATCH (4, 5, 6, 7). The three margins are SEA, ENGINE, LIGHT, and the direction that matters is LEFT IS HEAVY.
questions.understand_first:
The two limbs look unconnected and they are not, because both are about a compromise made at the design stage that the ship then lives with for twenty-five years.

In limb (A) the compromise is between holding a course and changing one. They pull in opposite directions, and the physics says why: a hull at a small angle of drift generates a sideways force whose centre lies forward of the ship's centre of gravity, so the drift tends to increase itself. Everything aft — the run of the after body, the skeg, the deadwood, the rudder — is there to supply the opposing moment. Add more of it and she holds her course beautifully and turns like a barn door; take it away and she turns in her own length and cannot be left alone for thirty seconds. Neither is right in the abstract. A VLCC on a long ocean passage and a harbour tug want opposite ends of that scale, and a modern ship is often deliberately placed on the marginally unstable side because the autopilot can close the loop and the manoeuvring gain is worth having.

In limb (B) the compromise is between the engine you have and the propeller you gave it. The engine can produce power along a field of speeds; the propeller demands power along a cubic curve, and where those two meet is where the ship actually runs. The essential insight is that the design point and the maximum rating are deliberately different, and that the propeller is deliberately made a little light when new — because the curve is going to march leftwards for the next five years as the hull fouls and the weather does its work, and it must have somewhere to march to. A propeller matched perfectly on trials is a propeller that is overloading the engine before the first drydocking.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the directional stability and propeller demand curve question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (A) 1 What directional stability is. 2 The conflict with manoeuvrability. 3 How both are provided - hull, rudder, low-speed devices, autopilot. (B) 4 The engine layout diagram. 5 The propeller demand curve and how it moves. 6 The three margins between MCR and the design point. 7 What happens when the match goes wrong.
retrieval_cards.why: Three steps for eight marks in (A) and four in (B), which is right because (B) asks for a diagram and an explanation of a relationship rather than a description.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define directional stability, and say how you would test it.
retrieval_cards.answer: The property of a hull which, when disturbed from a straight course by a transient force and with the rudder then returned amidships, settles onto a new straight course rather than continuing to turn. It is judged on the residual motion after the disturbance ceases, not on the deviation during it - a directionally stable ship ends up on a different heading but going straight; an unstable one goes on turning until rudder is applied to stop her.
retrieval_cards.why: The rudder-amidships test is the whole definition, and stating it prevents the standard confusion with how well a ship steers under autopilot.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why are directional stability and manoeuvrability in conflict?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both depend on the longitudinal distribution of lateral area. Lateral area aft of the centre of gravity - a long fine hull, a deep skeg, generous deadwood, trim by the stern - supplies the restoring moment that keeps her straight, and the same area resists the turning moment when you want her to turn. A short full hull with a cut-up after body turns readily and wanders. The design is a compromise chosen for the intended service.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying they are opposed, and why, is the substance of limb (A). An answer that praises both as virtues has not understood the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How are directional stability and manoeuvrability provided in a ship? Give the order of priority.
retrieval_cards.answer: Hull first: proportions, after body form, skeg and deadwood, twin skegs on full-form ships, and trim. Rudder second: area as a fraction of the lateral plane, aspect ratio, section, and type - spade, semi-balanced horn, or high-lift flap - working in the propeller race. Low-speed devices third: bow and stern thrusters, azimuth or podded units, which produce side force where the rudder has no flow. And the control system last: an autopilot with rate and counter-rudder terms, which makes a marginally stable hull entirely usable.
retrieval_cards.why: The order matters. Candidates start at the rudder; the examiner wants the hull first, because that is where the property actually lives.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does a ship lose steering the moment the main engine stops?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the rudder works in the propeller race. With the propeller turning, the rudder is immersed in an accelerated slipstream and generates far more side force than the ship's speed through the water alone would give it. Stop the propeller and the rudder has only the free-stream flow to work with, so effectiveness collapses even though the ship still has headway.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single most practical consequence of the design in limb (A) and a favourite oral question, because it explains why a dead-ship drift is not merely a propulsion problem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do power and torque vary with shaft speed for a fixed-pitch propeller?
retrieval_cards.answer: In free-running conditions, delivered power varies approximately as the cube of shaft speed and torque as the square. The demand curve is therefore a cubic through the origin, and its position depends on the propeller pitch and diameter and on the resistance of the hull.
retrieval_cards.why: The cube law is the reason a small speed reduction saves a large amount of fuel, and the reason a small increase in resistance produces a disproportionate torque demand.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three margins between MCR and the power the propeller is designed for.
retrieval_cards.answer: Sea margin - added power to overcome the added resistance of hull and propeller fouling and of weather over the docking cycle. Engine or operating margin - the service rating is deliberately kept below the maximum continuous rating for reliability and fuel economy. Light-running margin - the propeller is deliberately made slightly light when new and clean, so that the demand curve can migrate left through the docking cycle without meeting the engine's torque limit.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the direct answer to the printed question: the maximum rated output exceeds the propeller design power by design, and these three margins are what fills the gap.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the propeller deliberately made light-running when new?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the demand curve only ever moves one way in service - to the left, towards more torque at a given speed - as the hull and propeller foul, displacement increases and the weather works on her. If the propeller were matched exactly in trial condition, it would already be heavy-running the day she leaves the dock, and the engine would meet its torque limit before its rated speed. The light-running margin gives the curve somewhere to migrate to.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating insight in limb (B) and shows the candidate understands the diagram as a lifetime operating envelope rather than a trial-day snapshot.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The engine will not reach rated speed and exhaust temperatures are high. What is happening and what do you do?
retrieval_cards.answer: Heavy running, or torque-rich operation: the propeller demand curve has moved left of design, so the engine meets its torque limit before reaching rated speed and cannot develop rated power. The symptoms follow - high thermal loading, high exhaust temperatures, turbocharger fouling, risk of scavenge fire, loss of speed and increased specific consumption. Confirm by plotting actual operating points against the layout diagram; then hull and propeller cleaning, correct trim and draught, and if it persists a propeller re-pitch.
retrieval_cards.why: It joins the theory to the engine room, and the diagnosis - plot the points on the diagram - is the answer an examiner is waiting for.

reverify_before_publication.claim: The whole technical content of both limbs
reverify_before_publication.why: ENGINEERING_JUDGEMENT is effectively the sole provenance class on this question. No instrument prescribes hull form, appendage design, engine selection or the margins between engine rating and propeller demand, so there is nothing regulatory to verify and none was invented. The content is settled naval architecture and marine engineering, explained mechanistically, and would properly be reviewed by a naval architect and an engine specialist rather than by a regulatory check.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That the IMO standards for ship manoeuvrability and the class steering-gear requirements are referred to at REGIME LEVEL ONLY
reverify_before_publication.why: MIW holds neither the IMO standards nor any class rule. The trial manoeuvres are named because they are universally known by name, but NO resolution number, circular number, application threshold or numerical criterion - no advance, tactical diameter, overshoot angle or track reach - is asserted anywhere. Inventing a criterion would be a far worse defect than the declared gap. Promote to primary only if the standards are acquired.

reverify_before_publication.claim: That no percentage is quoted for sea margin, engine margin or light-running margin, and no numerical boundary for the layout diagram
reverify_before_publication.why: A deliberate omission. All are installation-specific and contractual, settled between owner, yard and engine builder, and typical values vary with trade, hull form and docking interval. Recorded so that a later editor does not supply figures from a particular maker's project guide as though they were general.

sources: P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, READ AT SOURCE THIS SESSION from the corpus copy of the Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009: ARTICLE 17, Entry into force. The Convention enters into force 24 months after the date on which three conditions are met - not less than 15 States have signed without reservation or deposited the requisite instrument; the combined merchant fleets of those States constitute not less than 40 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; and their combined maximum annual ship recycling volume during the preceding 10 years constitutes not less than 3 per cent of the combined gross tonnage of those same States. Article 17.2 and 17.3 govern instruments deposited after the conditions are met and after entry into force respectively.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ARTICLE 2, definitions - 'Ship' includes submersibles, floating craft, floating platforms, self-elevating platforms, FSUs and FPSOs, including a vessel stripped of equipment or being towed; 'Ship Recycling' is complete or partial dismantling at a Ship Recycling Facility to recover components and materials for reprocessing and re-use; 'Competent Authority' is the governmental authority designated by a Party for duties relating to Ship Recycling Facilities in its jurisdiction; 'Administration' is the flag State government.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ARTICLE 3, Application. The Convention applies to ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party or operating under its authority, and to Ship Recycling Facilities operating under the jurisdiction of a Party. Article 3.2 excludes warships and government non-commercial ships. ARTICLE 3.3 provides that the Convention shall NOT apply to ships of less than 500 GT, or to ships operating throughout their life only in waters subject to the sovereignty or jurisdiction of the flag State - each Party nonetheless ensuring such ships act consistently with the Convention so far as reasonable and practicable. ARTICLE 3.4 requires Parties to apply the requirements to non-Party ships as necessary to ensure NO MORE FAVOURABLE TREATMENT.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ANNEX regulation 4 and APPENDIX 1, Controls of Hazardous Materials. Appendix 1 lists asbestos (new installation prohibited for all ships); ozone-depleting substances (new installations prohibited, HCFCs permitted until 1 January 2020); polychlorinated biphenyls (new installation prohibited for all ships); and anti-fouling compounds and systems 'regulated under Annex I to the International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001 (AFS Convention) IN FORCE AT THE TIME OF APPLICATION OR INTERPRETATION of this Annex' - so later AFS listings are caught dynamically by reference rather than being named in Appendix 1.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ANNEX regulation 5, Inventory of Hazardous Materials. Each new ship shall have one on board, verified by the Administration or an authorised organisation, identifying as PART I the Appendix 1 and 2 materials in the ship's structure or equipment with their location and approximate quantities. Regulation 5.2 - existing ships shall comply as far as practicable NOT LATER THAN 5 YEARS AFTER ENTRY INTO FORCE, or before going for recycling if earlier. Regulation 5.3 - Part I maintained and updated throughout the operational life. Regulation 5.4 - prior to recycling the Inventory shall incorporate PART II for operationally generated wastes and PART III for stores, and be verified.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ANNEX regulations 8 and 9. Regulation 8 - ships destined to be recycled shall only be recycled at authorised facilities; shall minimise cargo residues, remaining fuel oil and wastes before arrival; a tanker shall arrive with cargo tanks and pump rooms ready for certification as Safe-for-entry or Safe-for-hot work or both; shall provide the facility with all available information; shall complete the regulation 5 Inventory; and shall be certified as ready for recycling before any recycling activity. Regulation 9 - a SHIP-SPECIFIC SHIP RECYCLING PLAN developed by the facility, in a language the authorising Party accepts, covering the establishment, maintenance and monitoring of Safe-for-entry and Safe-for-hot work conditions and the management of the inventoried materials, and either explicitly or tacitly approved by the Competent Authority - tacit approval carrying a 14-DAY REVIEW PERIOD after a written acknowledgement of receipt issued within three working days.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ANNEX regulations 10 and 11, surveys and certificates. Four surveys - INITIAL before the ship is put in service or before the certificate is issued; RENEWAL at intervals not exceeding five years; ADDITIONAL after change, replacement or significant repair; and a FINAL SURVEY before the ship is taken out of service and before recycling starts, verifying the regulation 5.4 Inventory, that the Ship Recycling Plan properly reflects it and covers Safe-for-entry and Safe-for-hot work conditions, and that the facility holds a valid authorisation. Regulation 11 - an INTERNATIONAL CERTIFICATE ON INVENTORY OF HAZARDOUS MATERIALS after initial or renewal survey; and, per regulation 8.6 and the final survey, certification as ready for recycling.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ANNEX chapter 3, regulations 15 to 25 - the requirements for Ship Recycling Facilities. Regulation 15 - each Party shall legislate, establish an authorisation mechanism, and establish inspection, monitoring and enforcement including POWERS OF ENTRY AND SAMPLING, and designate Competent Authorities. Regulation 16 - authorisation by the Competent Authority including verification of documentation and a SITE INSPECTION, drawn up in the form of Appendix 5, VALID FOR A PERIOD NOT EXCEEDING FIVE YEARS, suspended or withdrawn if inspection is refused. Regulation 18 - the SHIP RECYCLING FACILITY PLAN, adopted by the board or governing body of the Recycling Company, covering policy, implementation, roles and responsibilities, worker information and training, an emergency preparedness and response plan, performance monitoring, record-keeping, and reporting of discharges, emissions, incidents, accidents and occupational disease. Regulation 19 - procedures to establish, maintain and monitor Safe-for-hot work and Safe-for-entry conditions throughout recycling. Regulation 20 - hazardous materials identified, labelled, packaged and REMOVED TO THE MAXIMUM EXTENT POSSIBLE PRIOR TO CUTTING, with wastes kept separate and transferred only to an authorised waste management facility. Regulations 22 and 23 - worker safety and training, and reporting on incidents, accidents, occupational diseases and chronic effects.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: ARTICLES 10, 11 and 12. Article 10 - violations prohibited by national law, sanctions established under the law of the Administration for a ship and of the Party having jurisdiction for a facility, and 'adequate in severity to discourage violations of this Convention wherever they occur'. Article 11 - all possible efforts to avoid undue detention or delay, with compensation for loss or damage where it occurs. Article 12 - each Party reports to IMO, for dissemination, its list of authorised Ship Recycling Facilities, its Competent Authority contact point, its recognised organisations and nominated surveyors, and an annual list of its ships issued with a Ready for Recycling Certificate.

blocks.h: 1. The Convention, and exactly where it stood at this examination

blocks.p: The Hong Kong International Convention for the Safe and Environmentally Sound Recycling of Ships, 2009 was adopted at a diplomatic conference in Hong Kong, China in May 2009. Begin the answer with its status, because the status governs the tense of everything that follows.
Article 17 makes entry into force conditional, and the condition is a triple one. The Convention enters into force twenty-four months after the date on which all three of the following are satisfied:

ol: not less than 15 States have signed it without reservation or deposited the requisite instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession;
the combined merchant fleets of those States constitute not less than 40 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; and
their combined maximum annual ship recycling volume during the preceding ten years constitutes not less than 3 per cent of the combined gross tonnage of those same States.

blocks.p: The third condition is the interesting one, and it explains the sixteen-year delay better than any commentary. A tonnage threshold alone could have been met by flag States; the recycling-volume threshold made it impossible to bring the Convention into force over the objections of the recycling States themselves. The Convention could not begin until the countries whose domestic industry it regulates agreed to be regulated.

The position at this examination must be stated exactly. The Article 17 conditions were satisfied in June 2023 — which follows from Article 17's own twenty-four-month rule applied to the entry-into-force date. The Convention accordingly enters into force on 26 June 2025. That is eight months after this paper. So at this sitting the Convention is adopted, its conditions are met, its commencement date is fixed and publicly known — and it is not yet in force. No obligation in it binds any ship or any yard today. Everything below is what it will require, and the whole industry is in the final run-up to it.

blocks.h: 2. What it will require of ships

blocks.p: Application. The Convention will apply to ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party or operating under its authority, and to recycling facilities under a Party's jurisdiction. Warships and government non-commercial ships are excluded, and under Article 3.3 it does not apply to ships of less than 500 GT, nor to ships operating throughout their life only in waters under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of their own flag State — Parties being required nonetheless to see that such ships act consistently with it so far as reasonable and practicable. Article 3.4 applies the familiar no more favourable treatment rule to ships of non-Parties.

ul: An Inventory of Hazardous Materials, ship-specific and verified by the Administration or an organisation authorised by it. Part I identifies the listed hazardous materials in the ship's structure and equipment, with their location and approximate quantities, and is maintained and updated throughout the operational life.
Parts II and III added before recycling — Part II for operationally generated wastes and Part III for stores — and the whole then verified.

Control of listed hazardous materials. Appendix 1 prohibits or restricts asbestos (new installation prohibited on all ships), ozone-depleting substances, and polychlorinated biphenyls, and controls anti-fouling compounds and systems by reference to the AFS Convention as in force at the time of application — so later additions to the AFS list are caught automatically rather than being named here.

Existing ships must comply as far as practicable not later than five years after entry into force, or before going for recycling if that is earlier. Applied to 26 June 2025 that gives an inventory deadline of 26 June 2030, which is a date the industry can already plan to.

blocks.h: 3. Survey, certification and the last voyage

blocks.p: The certification regime follows the familiar statutory pattern, with one addition at the end of the ship's life:

ul: an initial survey before the ship is put in service or before the certificate is issued, verifying Part I of the Inventory;
a renewal survey at intervals set by the Administration not exceeding five years;
an additional survey, general or partial, after a change, replacement or significant repair;

and a final survey before the ship is taken out of service and before recycling starts. This one verifies three things: that the Inventory is complete in all three parts; that the Ship Recycling Plan properly reflects it and covers Safe-for-entry and Safe-for-hot work conditions; and that the yard where she is to be recycled holds a valid authorisation.

blocks.p: On the strength of the initial or renewal survey the ship carries an International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials; on the strength of the final survey she is certified as ready for recycling before any recycling activity takes place.

The last voyage itself is regulated. A ship destined for recycling must go only to an authorised facility, must minimise cargo residues, remaining fuel oil and wastes on board beforehand, and, if a tanker, must arrive with cargo tanks and pump rooms in a condition ready for certification as Safe-for-entry or Safe-for-hot work or both. She must give the yard all available information for the ship-specific Ship Recycling Plan, which the yard develops and the Competent Authority approves either explicitly or tacitly — tacit approval running a fourteen-day review period from a written acknowledgement issued within three working days.

blocks.h: 4. What it will require of the recycling facility

blocks.p: This is the feature that makes the Convention unlike almost any other IMO instrument, and it deserves saying plainly: an IMO convention that reaches ashore and regulates a facility on land. It is also why the instrument took sixteen years to enter into force.

ul: Each Party must legislate, establish an authorisation mechanism, and establish inspection, monitoring and enforcement provisions including powers of entry and sampling, and designate one or more Competent Authorities.

Authorisation of the yard by the Competent Authority, following verification of documentation and a site inspection, evidenced by a Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling and valid for a period not exceeding five years. If a yard refuses inspection, the authorisation is suspended or withdrawn.

A Ship Recycling Facility Plan, adopted by the board or governing body of the recycling company, covering worker safety and health policy, a system for implementation and continuous improvement, roles and responsibilities, worker information and training, an emergency preparedness and response plan, performance monitoring, record-keeping, and reporting of discharges, emissions, incidents, accidents and occupational disease.
Safe-for-entry and Safe-for-hot work conditions established, maintained and monitored throughout the recycling, in ship spaces including confined and enclosed spaces.

Hazardous materials identified, labelled, packaged and removed to the maximum extent possible prior to cutting, by properly trained and equipped workers — hazardous liquids and sediments, heavy metals, flammable or toxic coatings, asbestos, PCBs, CFCs and halons.

Controlled downstream management: wastes kept separate from recyclable material, labelled, stored safely, and transferred only to a waste management facility authorised to treat and dispose of them. This is where the real burden falls.

blocks.p: Enforcement is built in. Article 10 requires sanctions under national law, adequate in severity to discourage violations wherever they occur; Article 11 protects a ship against undue delay or detention, with compensation; and Article 12 requires each Party to report its list of authorised facilities and its competent-authority contact point to IMO for dissemination.

ul: India is one of the world's principal ship-recycling States, centred on the Alang-Sosiya yards in Gujarat. Published figures for its share of world recycling differ widely between sources and none is quoted here.

India acceded on 28 November 2019, the Director General of Shipping depositing the instrument at the thirty-first session of the IMO Assembly. That accession was decisive rather than symbolic: it took the count to the required fifteen States and contributed heavily to the recycling-volume condition, which was the condition no group of flag States could satisfy.

Domestically the Convention is given effect by the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019, which apply Convention standards to ships recycled in India. India therefore legislated some six years ahead of entry into force, and its yards have been upgrading against that standard since.
The maritime administration is the competent authority, authorising yards and dealing with ship recycling plans.

Note the statutory architecture: Indian ship recycling is governed by its own separate Act, not by the general merchant shipping legislation. The general statute standing alongside it at this examination is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

blocks.p: The stem says ‘benefit or be impacted’. That is not an invitation to choose; it is an instruction to argue both sides and reach a view.
How India stands to benefit

ul: Legitimacy, and access to better tonnage. Owners who have avoided South Asian yards on reputational grounds will be able to send ships to an authorised Indian facility with a defensible answer, which should raise both the volume and the quality of tonnage arriving.

A level playing field. Once the Convention bites, competing recycling States must meet the same standard. The money Indian yards spent upgrading ahead of entry into force is then rewarded rather than punished on price.

Worker safety and environmental gain. Enforceable Safe-for-entry and Safe-for-hot work requirements, training, protective equipment and controlled waste handling address directly the fatality and contamination record that has defined the industry's reputation.

Downstream industry, investment and financeability. Formalisation supports the steel re-rolling and second-hand equipment trades, and a certified yard is easier to finance and to contract with on longer terms.
First-mover advantage. Because India legislated in 2019 and the Convention begins only in June 2025, Indian yards reach the start line with six years of compliance investment already made.

blocks.p: How it stands to be impacted

ul: Cost of compliance. Impermeable floors, containment, lifting equipment, and hazardous-waste storage and treatment are capital-intensive. Smaller operators may not be able to afford them, so the industry consolidates and some yards close.

Downstream waste capacity is the binding constraint. The obligations do not end at the yard gate: treatment and disposal capacity for asbestos and other hazardous waste must exist, or compliance becomes documentary rather than real.

Price and leakage. Higher costs mean a lower price per light displacement tonne offered to owners, which creates an incentive to recycle elsewhere — including by changing flag before the last voyage to a State outside the Convention. Article 3.4's no-more-favourable-treatment rule limits this but does not close it.

Convention compliance is not European acceptance. The Convention does not expressly prohibit beaching; it regulates how recycling is done, not how the ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation maintains its own list of approved facilities on stricter terms, so an Indian yard may be fully Convention-compliant and still not be EU-listed.
Enforcement is the credibility test. Authorisation has to be inspected and enforced. A documentary-only regime would incur the cost and forfeit the reputational gain that is the main prize.

blocks.p: The balance. On the position as it stood at this examination, entry into force on 26 June 2025 is net positive for India. It converts an early and expensive investment into a competitive advantage, legitimises an industry that has been under external criticism for decades, and gives Indian yards a head start over competitors who have not yet spent the money. The gain is conditional, and honestly so: it depends on downstream waste infrastructure and on real enforcement keeping pace with certification. Without those, the cost is incurred and the reputational benefit is not.

Three tasks are packed into one running stem and candidates routinely answer only the first. Budget the paper deliberately: roughly a third on the Convention and two thirds on India, split between benefit and impact. The command is evaluative, and evaluation questions are marked on whether a reasoned conclusion actually appears — so leave room for the final paragraph and do not let the machinery recital eat it.

One structural decision does more work than any other here: state the status in the first three lines. If the examiner reads ‘adopted May 2009, conditions met, enters into force 26 June 2025, not yet in force’ at the top of the answer, everything that follows is read as correctly tensed. If the status appears only at the end, or not at all, the whole script reads as though it were describing a live regime.

blocks.h: The date is the question — and this is the hardest kind of temporal trap

blocks.p: This topic has a hard boundary running through it, and at this sitting the boundary lies ahead rather than behind. Until 26 June 2025 the Convention was adopted but not in force: there were no operative obligations on ships or yards to describe, no certificates being issued under it, no yards authorised under it. From that date every one of those things can and must be stated.

The trap is that almost everything written about this Convention was written after it entered into force. A candidate revising from current material, or an author working from a later worked answer, will find the whole subject expressed in the present tense. Converting it back is not a matter of adding ‘will’ in a few places — it changes what the answer is: a description of a regime coming, with a fixed date and a preparation problem, rather than a description of a regime operating. That difference is worth several marks, and it is exactly what an October 2024 examiner was testing.

The corollary is a statistic to leave out. The figure of 24 Parties representing about 57 per cent of world tonnage is the position at entry into force. It is quoted everywhere, and at this sitting it is an anachronism. Say that the conditions were met and the date was fixed; do not quote a count.

blocks.h: The distinction that separates a good answer from a very good one

blocks.p: The Convention does not ban beaching. It requires safe and environmentally sound recycling, authorisation, planning and control — but it does not prescribe the method by which a ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation takes a stricter line and maintains its own list of approved facilities, which is why the acceptability of the Alang yards to European owners has been contested for years and is not settled by entry into force. So the accurate proposition is: Convention compliance is necessary for legitimacy but is not sufficient for European acceptance. A candidate who writes that the Convention has ended beaching, or that compliance automatically opens the EU market, has overstated it in exactly the way the examiner is watching for.

ul: Writing the whole answer in the present tense. At this sitting nothing in the Convention was in force. This is the single biggest error available.
Quoting the 24 Parties / 57 per cent figure, or any Party count. That is the position at entry into force, which had not happened.
Giving the adoption year as the operative date. Adopted 2009, in force 26 June 2025 — the gap is the interesting part and Article 17 explains it.
Reciting only the ship-side obligations and omitting the facility obligations, which are half the Convention and the half that made it hard to bring into force.
Confusing the ICIHM, held through service life, with certification as ready for recycling, which follows the final survey immediately before recycling.
Saying the Convention bans beaching, or that compliance automatically opens the EU market.
Attributing Indian ship recycling law to the merchant shipping statute of any year. It is the separate Recycling of Ships Act, 2019.
Naming the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. At this examination it did not exist even as a Bill.
Quoting a percentage share of world recycling for India. Published figures vary widely; name Alang-Sosiya instead.
Answering only the benefits when the stem says ‘benefit or be impacted’, and giving no concluding judgement.

blocks.p: ‘Is it in force?’ Not at this examination. Adopted May 2009; Article 17 conditions met; enters into force 26 June 2025, eight months after this paper. This is the discriminating answer and the examiner is asking it precisely because most candidates will have read post-2025 material.

‘Why did it take sixteen years?’ Article 17's three conditions, and specifically the 3 per cent recycling-volume threshold, which required the recycling States themselves to join. A tonnage threshold alone could have been satisfied by flag States.

‘Your ship goes for recycling next month. What must be in place?’ A completed Inventory in all three parts, a final survey, certification as ready for recycling, and a ship-specific Ship Recycling Plan approved by the Competent Authority for an authorised yard. Add that at this examination none of that was yet mandatory.

‘By when must an existing ship have an inventory?’ Five years after entry into force, or before going for recycling if earlier — so 26 June 2030. This is a legitimate future date to state even at this sitting, because the entry-into-force date was already fixed.

‘Which Indian statute governs ship recycling?’ The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 with the Rules of 2019 — separate legislation with its own machinery. The general Act standing alongside it here is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

ul: When was the Convention adopted and when does it enter into force? Adopted May 2009; enters into force 26 June 2025.

What are the three entry-into-force conditions? Fifteen States, forty per cent of world gross tonnage, and three per cent combined maximum annual recycling volume over the preceding ten years - then twenty-four months.

Which ships does it apply to? Ships of 500 GT and above flying the flag of a Party, other than those trading throughout their life only in their own flag State's waters; and warships and government non-commercial ships are excluded.
What are the three parts of the Inventory? Materials in the structure and equipment; operationally generated wastes; and stores.

What certificate does a ship in service hold, and what does she need for her last voyage? The International Certificate on Inventory of Hazardous Materials in service; certification as ready for recycling after the final survey.
What must a yard hold? A Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling, valid for not more than five years, and a Ship Recycling Facility Plan.
What must be done to hazardous materials before cutting? Identified, labelled, packaged and removed to the maximum extent possible, by trained and equipped workers.
When did India accede, and why did it matter? 28 November 2019; it took the number of States to fifteen and contributed heavily to the recycling-volume condition.
Does the Convention prohibit beaching? No. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation applies a stricter standard through its own approved list.

blocks.p: STATUS — SHIP — SHORE — INDIA — SCALES. Status: 2009 adopted, 2023 conditions, 2025 in force, not yet (step 1). Ship: inventory, certificates, final survey, 2030 (steps 2 and 3). Shore: authorisation, facility plan, safe for entry and hot work, waste downstream (step 4). India: acceded 2019, Recycling of Ships Act 2019, Alang, competent authority (step 5). Scales: benefit against impact, then a verdict (step 6).

For the dates alone, note that they fall roughly a decade apart each time — adopted 2009, India acceded 2019, in force 2025, existing ships by 2030. Four numbers, evenly spaced, and each one is a scoring point.

blocks.p: The Convention content in this answer is unusually strong: the complete instrument was read at source — Articles 1 to 21 and the whole Annex with its regulations and appendices — so every article and regulation number above is read rather than recalled, and the application scope, the inventory structure, the survey set and the yard obligations are quoted from the text. That is worth stating because it is not the norm for this question: worked answers on this topic commonly rest on IMO briefing material and classification-society guidance.

Two things are weaker and are stated as such. First, the entry-into-force date of 26 June 2025 is not read at source here; it is carried from an earlier MIW verification record whose author read it on the IMO's own briefing, and the June 2023 conditions-met date is derived from Article 17's twenty-four-month rule rather than read from a record of deposit. Both should be confirmed against the IMO status-of-conventions record before being relied on. Second, the Indian instruments are named but not held: the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 and the Rules of 2019 are identified as the implementing legislation on the strength of an earlier MIW record, and no section or rule number is asserted anywhere.

Three quantities are deliberately absent. No Party count and no tonnage percentage, because at this sitting entry into force had not occurred and no October 2024 figure was verified. No share of world ship recycling for India, because published figures differ widely and none could be established. No price or capacity data, because the commercial argument in the last step is a reasoned mechanism rather than a measured outcome — and at this sitting it is necessarily prospective, since the Convention had not yet begun to bite.

notes: THE DEFINING FACT OF THIS QUESTION. The Hong Kong Convention ENTERED INTO FORCE ON 26 JUNE 2025, EIGHT MONTHS AFTER THIS EXAMINATION. At this sitting it was adopted, its Article 17 conditions had been met, its entry-into-force date was fixed and publicly known - and NO OBLIGATION IN IT BOUND ANYBODY. Every requirement is stated in this answer as what the Convention WILL require.

THE DONOR PREDICTED THIS EXACT HAZARD AND NAMED THIS EXACT QUESTION. QP2511-Q8's temporal review records: 'KEPT AFTER ADJUDICATION: the Convention treated as IN FORCE ... This is NOT the position at the October 2024 member of the same family, and that member must not inherit this object unmodified.' It has not.

DELETED FROM THE DONOR: the 24 Parties / 57.15 per cent figure. That is the position AT entry into force, which is a future event at this sitting. No October 2024 count was verified and none is asserted - an anachronistic statistic is a worse defect than a missing one.
DELETED FROM THE DONOR: the word 'now' in the benefits discussion, and every present-tense statement of an operative obligation.

DELETED FROM THE DONOR ENTIRELY: the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. The donor devotes a paragraph, a study-guide trap, a regulation-map entry and a retrieval card to explaining that the 2025 Act had been assented but not commenced. At October 2024 that Act did not exist in any form - the Bill that became it was introduced in the Lok Sabha only on 10 December 2024. The donor's CONCLUSION survives (ship recycling is governed by the separate Recycling of Ships Act, 2019) and its REASONING is replaced by the simpler true one for this sitting.

KEPT DELIBERATELY: 26 June 2030 as the existing-ship inventory deadline. Regulation 5.2 sets it at five years after entry into force, and the entry-into-force date was already fixed and known at this sitting, so the derived date is equally stateable here. A blind post-sitting date strip would have deleted a correct answer point.

ADDED, AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THE OCTOBER 2024 ANSWER DISTINCTIVE: the Convention is in its final run-up. The date is certain and eight months out, owners and yards are preparing against a deadline, and that is a genuinely different commercial position from either 'awaiting conditions' or 'in force'. It is the reason an examiner set the question in October 2024.

CORRECTED AGAINST THE DONOR, FROM SOURCE: application is 500 GT and not-purely-domestic under Article 3.3, not '500 gross tonnage and above on international voyages'. And cybutryne is not named in Appendix 1 of the 2009 text; Appendix 1 controls anti-fouling systems by reference to the AFS Convention as in force at the time of application, which is how later AFS listings are caught.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three demands packed into one running stem, and candidates routinely answer only the first. Discuss the Convention. State its significance FOR INDIA. Then assess how India's shipbreaking industry stands to BENEFIT OR BE IMPACTED. The word 'or' is not offering a choice - it is asking for both sides and, because the command is evaluative, for a reasoned conclusion. Underneath all three sits a temporal question the examiner has not printed but is certainly testing: does the candidate know whether this Convention was in force?
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed against the whole question with no sub-division. Budget roughly a third to the Convention itself, and two thirds to India, split between benefit and impact with an explicit balance at the end. An answer that spends twelve marks' worth of paper reciting Convention machinery and two lines on India has answered a different question.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate can state the Convention's status accurately at the examination date rather than repeating a half-remembered headline; can explain why a Convention adopted in 2009 took sixteen years to bite; understands that this instrument is unusual in regulating a facility ashore as well as a ship; and can weigh a real commercial and industrial argument about India rather than listing advantages.
primary_source_plan: Establish the entry-into-force position FIRST, before any obligation is described, because it governs the tense of every sentence that follows.
Read Article 17 at source and use its own three conditions to explain the delay, rather than asserting a reason.
Read the Annex regulations at source for the ship-side and yard-side obligations, so the answer can carry regulation numbers honestly where the donor could not.
Name the Indian implementing instruments without asserting a section number, and assert no Party count, no tonnage percentage and no share of world recycling.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - and the risk runs backwards, not forwards. Every donor and every piece of commentary a candidate or an author is likely to have read was written after 26 June 2025 and describes a Convention in force. Writing this answer in the present tense is the single most likely way to get it wrong.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: MEDIUM. The question expressly sets an Indian limb, and the trap is to attribute Indian ship recycling law to the general merchant shipping statute of one year or another. It is separate legislation - the Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 - and at this sitting the general Act alongside it is simply the 1958 Act, with no successor in existence.
technical_ambiguities: 'Discuss the Hong Kong Convention' has no natural boundary. Without a plan it becomes an undifferentiated recital; the ship-side and yard-side split gives it one.

'Significance for India' can be read as legal significance or as industrial significance. Both are intended, and the accession is the hinge between them - India's accession is one of the events that made the Convention capable of entering into force at all.
'Benefit or be impacted' reads as alternatives. It is not; it is a two-sided assessment requiring a judgement.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six steps. One establishing what the Convention is and precisely where it stood at this examination, with Article 17 explaining the delay. Two on what it will require of ships. One on what it will require of the yard, flagged as the feature that makes it unlike other IMO instruments. One on India - accession, domestic legislation and competent authority. Then two assessment steps, benefit and impact, closing on an explicit balance.
