quick_revision.critical_regulation: Article 17 is the regulation this question turns on, because it explains both the sixteen-year delay and the status at this sitting. At October 2024 the Convention was adopted with its entry into force fixed for 26 June 2025 and was NOT IN FORCE, so no obligation in it bound any ship or any yard.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing the answer in the present tense. Almost everything published about this Convention was written after it entered into force on 26 June 2025, and an answer that says ships ‘must’ hold a certificate or yards ‘are’ authorised is describing a regime that did not yet exist at this examination. The second trap is quoting the 24 Parties / 57 per cent figure, which is the position at entry into force and is an anachronism here.

questions.memory_cue: STATUS — SHIP — SHORE — INDIA — SCALES. Status: adopted 2009, conditions 2023, in force 2025, not yet (1). Ship: inventory, certificates, final survey, 2030 (2, 3). Shore: authorisation, facility plan, safe for entry and hot work (4). India: acceded 2019, Recycling of Ships Act 2019, Alang (5). Scales: weigh benefit against impact and land a verdict (6). The dates run a decade apart each time — 2009, 2019, 2025 approaching, 2030 ahead — which makes the sequence easy to hold.
questions.understand_first: Almost every IMO instrument regulates the ship — her construction, equipment, certificates and crew. The Hong Kong Convention is one of the very few that reaches ashore and regulates a facility on land, requiring the yard itself to be authorised, planned and inspected. That single feature explains everything else about it, including why it took sixteen years to enter into force: it needed the consent of States whose domestic industry, not merely whose fleet, would be regulated. Article 17's third condition — a recycling-volume threshold — made it impossible to bring the Convention into force over the objections of the recycling States themselves. Read that way, India's accession in 2019 is not a footnote; it is one of the two or three events that made the Convention real. And at this examination the story is at its most interesting point: the conditions are met, the date is fixed, and nothing is yet in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the Hong Kong Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Convention and exactly where it stood at this examination. 2 What it will require of ships. 3 Survey, certification and the last voyage. 4 What it will require of the yard. 5 India's position and domestic implementation. 6 Benefit, impact and the balance.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 4 are roughly a third of the marks on the Convention itself; steps 5 and 6 are the two thirds the stem actually asks about, and step 6 is where the evaluative command is answered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Was the Hong Kong Convention in force at an October 2024 examination?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It was adopted in May 2009; its Article 17 conditions had been met, which fixed entry into force at 26 June 2025 - eight months after this paper. At this sitting it was adopted with a known and certain commencement date, and no obligation in it bound any ship or yard.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the whole temporal content of the question and the single most likely way to lose it. Almost all published commentary was written after June 2025 and is in the present tense.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the three Article 17 entry-into-force conditions.
retrieval_cards.answer: Twenty-four months after: not less than 15 States have consented to be bound; their combined merchant fleets are not less than 40 per cent of the gross tonnage of world merchant shipping; and their combined maximum annual ship recycling volume over the preceding ten years is not less than 3 per cent of their combined tonnage.
retrieval_cards.why: The third condition is the one that matters. It made the Convention impossible to bring into force without the major recycling States, and it is why India's accession was decisive.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three parts of the Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and when is each required?
retrieval_cards.answer: Part I - materials in the ship's structure and equipment, held and maintained throughout the operational life. Part II - operationally generated wastes, and Part III - stores, both incorporated prior to recycling and verified.
retrieval_cards.why: Confusing the inventory held through service life with the pre-recycling completion is the commonest technical error on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships does the Convention apply to?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party or operating under its authority, and ship recycling facilities under a Party's jurisdiction. It does not apply to warships or government non-commercial ships, nor - under Article 3.3 - to ships of less than 500 GT or to ships operating throughout their life only in waters under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of their own flag State.
retrieval_cards.why: The precise scope is 500 GT plus not-purely-domestic. Saying '500 GT on international voyages' is close but is not what Article 3.3 says.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must a recycling yard hold, and what must it do before cutting?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Document of Authorisation to conduct Ship Recycling from the Competent Authority, issued after verification of documentation and a site inspection and valid for not more than five years; and a Ship Recycling Facility Plan adopted by the recycling company's governing body. Hazardous materials identified in the Inventory must be identified, labelled, packaged and removed to the maximum extent possible prior to cutting, by trained and equipped workers.
retrieval_cards.why: The yard-side obligations are half the Convention and are the half candidates omit. Removal before cutting is the operative safety rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does the Hong Kong Convention prohibit beaching, and does compliance open the EU market?
retrieval_cards.answer: No to both. The Convention requires safe and environmentally sound recycling, authorisation, planning and control, but it does not prescribe the method by which a ship is brought ashore. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation applies its own stricter standard through its own list of approved facilities, so a yard may be fully Convention-compliant and still not be EU-listed.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the distinction that separates a good answer from a very good one, and it is the overstatement the examiner is watching for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statute implements the Convention, and when did India accede?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Recycling of Ships Act, 2019 with the Recycling of Ships Rules, 2019, the maritime administration acting as competent authority. India acceded on 28 November 2019, through the Director General of Shipping at the thirty-first IMO Assembly, taking the number of States to the required fifteen.
retrieval_cards.why: Indian recycling law is separate legislation, not part of the general merchant shipping statute. At this sitting the general Act alongside it is simply the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many Parties did the Convention have at this examination?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not established, and not to be quoted. The commonly cited figure of 24 Parties at about 57 per cent of world tonnage is the position AT entry into force on 26 June 2025, which had not happened at this sitting. Say instead that the Article 17 conditions had been met and the entry-into-force date was fixed.
retrieval_cards.why: Quoting a figure from a future event is a straightforward anachronism, and it is exactly the kind of borrowed detail a later worked answer transmits backwards.

blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and what it exists to do

blocks.p: The Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic, 1965 — the FAL Convention — was adopted on 9 April 1965 and entered into force on 5 March 1967. It is IMO's trade facilitation instrument, and it is the odd one out among the conventions a Chief Engineer meets. SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW tell you what the ship, her equipment and her people must be. FAL tells public authorities what they may demand of a ship when she arrives, stays and departs.
Its objectives, in the Organization's own words, are:

ol: to prevent unnecessary delays in maritime traffic;
to aid co-operation between Governments; and
to secure the highest practicable degree of uniformity in formalities and other procedures.

blocks.p: The problem it was written to solve was simple and expensive: every port demanded different documents, in a different format, in a different number of copies, and a ship could lose more time to paperwork than to cargo.

ul: The obligations sit in an annex, expressed as Standards — measures necessary and practicable in order to facilitate international maritime traffic — and Recommended Practices, measures the application of which is desirable.

A Contracting Government that finds it impracticable to comply with a Standard, or that considers it necessary to adopt differing requirements, must notify the Secretary-General of the difference (article VIII). The obligation is therefore not absolute, but a departure must be declared rather than simply operated.

The annex prescribes a maximum, not a minimum. Under Standard 2.1bis public authorities shall not require more information than is provided for in the standardised declarations. This is the single most useful thing in the Convention from the ship's point of view.

Those declarations are the FAL Forms 1 to 7 — the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Ship's Stores Declaration, Crew's Effects Declaration, Crew List, Passenger List and Dangerous Goods manifest — together with the Declaration of Health and the documents required under the Universal Postal Convention.

The annex is amended by tacit acceptance: adopted under article VII(2)(a) and deemed accepted under article VII(2)(b) unless a stated proportion of Contracting Governments objects by a stated date. That mechanism is what makes the dates in step 4 matter.
Time is the cargo owner's money and the ship's cost. Port time is the least productive time a ship has; every hour saved at the interface is earned twice, once in charter hire and once in fuel.
Uniformity is what makes a ship tradeable worldwide. A master and crew cannot learn a different clearance regime for every port, and the FAL Forms mean they do not have to.
A ceiling on demands protects the ship from the port. Standard 2.1bis is a genuine legal protection, not an aspiration: it limits what an authority may lawfully require.

It is the foundation the digital layer was built on. Harmonising what is required had to come before automating how it is submitted, which is why the single window sits in this Convention and not in a new one.

blocks.h: 4. The recent amendments - what is in force, and what is only adopted

blocks.p: This limb is relative to the examination date, and the distinction between adopted and in force is what the examiner is testing. State both, and say which is which.

Already mandatory before either amendment: the electronic exchange of information became mandatory from 9 April 2019, with a minimum twelve-month transitional period. That is the platform the single window was built onto.

IN FORCE at this sitting — resolution FAL.14(46). Adopted 13 May 2022 and, under the article VII(2)(b) tacit acceptance procedure, entered into force on 1 January 2024 — nine months before this paper. It is the amendment that matters, because it made the maritime single window mandatory:

ul: Standard 1.3quin as amended — public authorities shall introduce arrangements enabling the provision of all information required under Standard 2.1 to a single window by electronic means, and shall consider the single window as the channel for communicating decisions.

The annex definition — a single window is ‘an environment that allows for the submission or provision of standardized and harmonized information and declarations to a single entry point, typically by electronic means’. Note standardized and harmonized: those two words are the test of whether a national portal is really a single window.

blocks.p: ADOPTED BUT NOT YET IN FORCE at this sitting — resolution FAL.15(47). Adopted 17 March 2023 under article VII(2)(a). Its operative paragraph determines, under article VII(2)(b), that the amendments enter into force on 1 January 2025 unless, prior to 1 October 2024, at least one third of Contracting Governments notify the Secretary-General in writing that they do not accept them. The amendments concern Recommended Practice 7.11, national facilitation programmes, taking into account the need to combat illicit activities.

So the position at this examination is unusually clean and worth stating in exactly these terms: one annex amendment recently in force, one adopted and waiting — with the waiting one's objection window closing at the very start of this examination month and its entry into force three months away.

One further distinction is worth a mark. Not every recent FAL resolution is an annex amendment. The Committee also adopts guidelines resolutions — for example the 2024 resolution on preventing wildlife smuggling. A guidelines resolution changes no Standard and no Recommended Practice, so however recently adopted it does not answer ‘recent amendments to the FAL Convention’. Approved is not adopted; adopted is not in force; and a guidelines resolution is not an annex amendment at all.

ul: One harmonised submission instead of many. Under the mandatory single window the ship, or her agent, submits the required information once, in an agreed format, to one entry point — and customs, immigration, port health, port authority and security all draw from it. The alternative, which is still the reality in some ports, is the same data typed several times into several systems.

A common data model underneath. The IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, developed with the World Customs Organization, UN/CEFACT and ISO, supplies the reference data model that makes ‘harmonized’ mean something in practice. Without it a single window is a single postbox for several incompatible letters.

Clearance comes off the critical path. Pre-arrival submission means the decisions are taken before the ship is on the berth, so the first hour alongside is a working hour. That is the operational point of the whole exercise.

But the duty falls on the public authority, and the ship's benefit is derivative. The obligation in Standard 1.3quin runs to Governments. Where a State implements well, the ship gains; where a State puts a web form in front of the same unharmonised demands, the ship gains almost nothing and cannot fix it.

And concentration has a cost. A single national entry point holding crew, cargo, security and commercial data is a high-value target and a single point of failure. Cyber resilience and a workable fallback procedure become part of port clearance planning rather than an IT afterthought.

blocks.p: Be precise about the mechanism here, because this is the limb candidates handle worst. FAL sets no emission standard. It prescribes nothing about the ship, her fuel or her machinery. Its environmental benefit is indirect, and it runs through time.

ul: Just-in-time arrival is the main effect. Reliable pre-arrival information exchange, and a clearance decision made before arrival, allow a ship to be given a firm berth time. She can then slow down on passage instead of steaming hard to an anchorage and waiting.

The saving is disproportionate to the speed reduction. Fuel consumption rises very steeply with speed, so a modest reduction over a long passage saves far more fuel than the same number of hours saved at the berth. Time saved in the port is converted into speed not made at sea, and that is where the carbon comes out.

Less congestion, less machinery running for no transport work. A ship at anchor waiting for a berth is burning fuel on generators, boilers and auxiliaries while performing no transport work at all — and, incidentally, scoring badly on any carbon-intensity metric that divides emissions by distance travelled.

The paper saving is real but small. Fewer printed sets, fewer courier movements, fewer launch trips to bring officials on board. Worth a sentence, not a paragraph — the fuel argument is the one that carries the marks.

blocks.h: 7. The limits - what the Convention does not do

ul: The benefit is conditional on implementation. A single window is an outcome, not a website. Where the same information is still demanded in several formats, the Convention has been complied with in form and defeated in substance.

Just-in-time needs the commercial contract to permit it. Laytime and demurrage terms frequently reward arriving early and waiting, and a charterer may be entitled to insist on utmost despatch. FAL removes a technical obstacle to slow steaming; it cannot remove a contractual one.
It imposes no requirement on the ship at all — no construction, equipment, manning or emission standard. It is not a safety or environmental convention and should not be described as one.
It does not override national customs, immigration, quarantine or security law. It harmonises the interface with those regimes; it does not replace them.

A Recommended Practice is not binding, and a notified difference is lawful. Uniformity under FAL is a strong presumption, not a guarantee, and a candidate who claims the Convention makes clearance identical worldwide has overstated it.

blocks.p: The stem prints two sentences and four demands: objectives, importance, recent amendments, and an analysis of their impact — the last narrowed expressly to digitalization and sustainability. Those two words are not decoration; they are the mark scheme for the second half. Make them two headings. An answer that describes the amendments beautifully and never says the word ‘sustainability’ has left marks on the table for no reason.

Budget about half the paper to the Convention and half to the amendments and their impact. Then keep a short closing block for the limits: the command analyse is evaluative, and evaluative answers are marked on whether a judgement appears.

blocks.h: The one thing that makes this answer sitting-specific

blocks.p: ‘Recent’ has no fixed meaning. It means recent at the date of the examination, and the amendment position moves every year or two. At this sitting it is unusually clean and unusually instructive:

rows: IN FORCE since 1 January 2024 — nine months before this paper
ADOPTED, NOT IN FORCE. Objection window closes 1 October 2024; in force 1 January 2025

blocks.p: That table is the answer to ‘recent amendments’ at this sitting, and being able to write it is what separates a candidate who has understood tacit acceptance from one who has memorised a list of resolution numbers. Note in particular that FAL.15(47)'s objection deadline falls in the examination month itself — there is no better live illustration anywhere on this paper of the difference between adopted and in force.

blocks.h: Four states, not two - approved, adopted, in force, and not-an-amendment

ul: Approved — a Committee has agreed a text in principle. It binds nobody.
Adopted — the resolution exists and the tacit acceptance clock is running. It still binds nobody.
In force — the objection window has passed and the amendment has taken effect. Only now does it bind.

Not an annex amendment at all — a guidelines resolution, however recently adopted, changes no Standard and no Recommended Practice. This fourth category is the one candidates never think of, and naming it is worth a mark.
Treating every amendment the candidate has heard of as being in force. At this sitting FAL.15(47) is not.
Describing FAL as a safety or environmental convention. It imposes no requirement on the ship at all.
Saying FAL reduces emissions. It sets no emission standard; the benefit runs through time saved and therefore through fuel.
Answering only digitalization and never reaching sustainability, when the stem names both.
Forgetting that Standard 2.1bis is a ceiling. Candidates routinely describe FAL as prescribing what must be submitted; it prescribes what may not be demanded.
Omitting the article VIII notification of differences, which is the mechanism that reconciles a facilitation convention with national sovereignty.
Quoting a percentage fuel saving for just-in-time arrival. Published figures vary enormously with trade, ship type and port.
Claiming the single window makes clearance identical worldwide. The duty falls on each public authority and implementation varies.

blocks.p: ‘Name the recent amendments and tell me whether they are in force.’ FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, in force 1 January 2024, mandatory single window under Standard 1.3quin. FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, not yet in force — entry into force 1 January 2025, objection window closing 1 October 2024. Giving both, with their status, is the discriminating answer.

‘Our port has a website where we upload the forms. Is that a single window?’ Not necessarily. The definition requires standardized and harmonized information and declarations submitted to a single entry point. Uploading the same unharmonised documents to several agencies through one website is a portal, not a single window.

‘How does a paperwork convention reduce CO2?’ Through time. Reliable pre-arrival clearance enables just-in-time arrival, so the ship slows on passage rather than steaming hard and idling at anchor; and consumption falls steeply with speed. Say plainly that FAL itself sets no emission standard.
‘Whose obligation is Standard 1.3quin?’ The public authority's, not the ship's. This catches candidates out, and it is the reason the ship's benefit is derivative and uneven.
‘Can a Government simply ignore a Standard?’ No — but it may adopt a differing requirement provided it notifies the Secretary-General of the difference under article VIII.

ul: When was the FAL Convention adopted and when did it enter into force? Adopted 9 April 1965; in force 5 March 1967.
What are its three objectives? Prevent unnecessary delays; aid co-operation between Governments; secure the highest practicable degree of uniformity in formalities and procedures.
Standard or Recommended Practice - what is the difference? Necessary and practicable, against desirable.

Name the FAL Forms. General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Ship's Stores Declaration, Crew's Effects Declaration, Crew List, Passenger List and Dangerous Goods manifest - Forms 1 to 7 - plus the Declaration of Health and Universal Postal Convention documents.
What does Standard 2.1bis do? Caps the information a public authority may require.
Which amendment made the single window mandatory, and when did it take effect? FAL.14(46), amending Standard 1.3quin, in force 1 January 2024.

How is the FAL annex amended? Tacit acceptance - adopted under article VII(2)(a), deemed accepted under article VII(2)(b) unless a stated proportion of Contracting Governments objects by a stated date.
What is the IMO Compendium? The harmonised reference data model for single window implementation, developed with the WCO, UN/CEFACT and ISO.
Give one limitation of just-in-time arrival. The charterparty may not permit it - laytime and demurrage terms often reward arriving early.

blocks.p: WHAT — HOW — WHY — WHEN — DIGITAL — GREEN — LIMITS, which is steps 1 to 7 in order. The middle step, WHEN, is the one that changes between sittings and the one to rehearse with dates attached.

For the amendments hold four numbers in two pairs: 14 into 24, 15 into 25. FAL.14(46) in force 2024; FAL.15(47) in force 2025 — and since this paper is sat in 2024, the second one has not yet happened. The mnemonic carries the status, not just the number, which is the whole point.

blocks.p: The two facts that decide this question are strong. Both amending resolutions were read in full at primary level for earlier MIW verification records, including their operative tacit-acceptance paragraphs with both dates — FAL.14(46) adopted 13 May 2022 and in force 1 January 2024, and FAL.15(47) adopted 17 March 2023, objection window to 1 October 2024, entry into force 1 January 2025. Articles VII(2)(a) and VII(2)(b) are primary here too, being recited in the operative text of both resolutions.

What is weaker is stated as such. MIW holds no licensed copy of the FAL Convention or its annex. Standards 1.3quin, 2.1, 2.1bis and 2.1.2 and Recommended Practice 7.11 are therefore cited by number and effect from the resolutions that amend them and from the Organization's own explanatory material, not read in the annex. The itemised list of FAL Forms is at secondary level: the material read confirms that standardised Forms 1 to 7 exist but does not itemise them. And one negative proposition — that no other annex amendment was adopted and awaiting entry into force at this sitting — is inherently harder to establish than a positive one and is stated at a lower evidence grade.

Two things are deliberately absent. No fuel or emission saving percentage is quoted for just-in-time arrival, because published estimates vary widely with trade, ship type and port and none could be verified; the mechanism is explained instead. And no claim is made about any national single window implementation, including India's — the question does not ask for one and none was verified. One boundary is worth recording for honesty: the exact day of this October 2024 examination is not established, so it cannot be said whether the sitting fell before or after FAL.15(47)'s 1 October objection deadline. Nothing turns on it, because entry into force on 1 January 2025 is after any date in October.

classes: BACKWARDS DONOR - LATER AMENDMENT SET REMOVED
notes: The amendment limb is by definition sitting-relative and the position was fixed BEFORE any drafting, from this paper's own temporal anchor rather than from whatever is current now.

IN FORCE at this sitting and answered as such: FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, IN FORCE 1 JANUARY 2024 - nine months before the paper. It is the recent amendment for this sitting, and it is the one that made the maritime single window mandatory.

ADOPTED BUT NOT IN FORCE at this sitting, and stated expressly as such: FAL.15(47), adopted 17 March 2023, amending Recommended Practice 7.11. decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two printed sentences and four demands. First: the OBJECTIVES and the IMPORTANCE of the Convention - two things, not one. Second: the RECENT AMENDMENTS, and an ANALYSIS of their IMPACT on modern shipping operations, expressly 'particularly in relation to digitalization and sustainability'. Those last two words are not decoration; they are the mark scheme for the second half, and an answer that discusses amendments without addressing both of them has answered half the question.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed against the whole question with no sub-division, but the stem divides itself into two sentences of roughly equal demand. Budget about half to the Convention - what it is, how it works, why it matters - and about half to the amendments and their impact, with digitalization and sustainability each getting a labelled block. Reserve a short closing section for the limits, which is where an evaluative answer earns its last marks.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate knows FAL is the odd one out among the conventions - it regulates public authorities rather than the ship - and can state its amendment position accurately at the examination date, distinguishing what is in force from what is merely adopted. The sustainability limb is the discriminating one: the candidate must see that FAL sets no emission standard at all and that its environmental benefit is indirect, running through time saved rather than through paper saved.
primary_source_plan: Fix the amendment position from the paper's own temporal anchor BEFORE drafting, because the limb is sitting-relative and the current position is two amendments further on.
Cite the two amending resolutions by number, adoption date and entry-into-force date from the MIW records that read them in full, including the tacit-acceptance dates in the operative text.
Cite Standards and Recommended Practices by number and effect only, and declare that the annex text is not held.
Quote no fuel-saving or emission-saving percentage for just-in-time arrival.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - The amendment limb goes stale by design: at the authoring date two further sessions and several further instruments exist, and any current source describes them. The whole risk is of importing later material, and it is managed by fixing the position from the anchor first.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is international and asks for no statutory limb. No claim is made about India's own single window implementation, and none is asked for.
technical_ambiguities: 'Recent amendments' has no fixed referent - it means recent AT THE SITTING. This is the whole temporal problem of the question and it must be resolved before drafting rather than during it.
'Impact on modern shipping operations' invites a general essay. The stem then narrows it to digitalization and sustainability, and those two words should become two headings.
'Sustainability' has no obvious connection to a facilitation convention. The connection is real but indirect, through time and therefore through fuel, and finding it is the discriminating step.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Seven steps. Three on the Convention - what it is and what it exists to do, how it works through Standards and Recommended Practices with the information ceiling and the Forms, and why it matters. Then one step separating what is in force from what is only adopted, which is the sitting-specific core. Then two impact steps, one labelled digitalization and one labelled sustainability. Then a short closing step on the limits.

questions.memory_cue: WHAT — HOW — WHY — WHEN — DIGITAL — GREEN — LIMITS. What it is (1), how it works (2), why it matters (3), when the amendments bite (4), then the stem's own two words, digitalization (5) and sustainability (6), then the limits (7). For the amendment limb hold two numbers and two dates: 14 into 24, 15 into 25 — FAL.14(46) in force 2024, FAL.15(47) in force 2025 and therefore not yet.
questions.understand_first: FAL is the odd one out among the conventions a Chief Engineer meets. SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW tell you what the ship, her equipment and her people must be. FAL tells public authorities what they may demand of a ship when she arrives, stays and departs. It is a convention pointed at the shore, and everything odd about it follows from that: its obligations bind Governments, its annex sets a maximum rather than a minimum, and its benefit reaches the ship only indirectly. The problem it was written to solve in 1965 was simple and expensive — every port demanded different documents, in a different format, in a different number of copies, and a ship could lose more time to paperwork than to cargo. Sixty years later the same instrument carries the digital layer, because the single window is the same idea expressed electronically: submit once, in one agreed format, to one place. And once you see that, the sustainability limb becomes obvious rather than mysterious — a ship that knows she will be cleared on arrival does not need to steam hard and then wait at anchor.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the FAL Convention question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What it is and what it exists to do. 2 How it works - Standards, Recommended Practices, the ceiling, the Forms. 3 Why it matters. 4 The recent amendments, split into in force and adopted. 5 Impact on digitalization. 6 Impact on sustainability. 7 The limits.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 5 and 6 are the stem's own two words and must be labelled as such; step 4 is the sitting-specific core and step 7 is where an evaluative answer earns its last marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the FAL Convention's objectives.
retrieval_cards.answer: To prevent unnecessary delays in maritime traffic; to aid co-operation between Governments; and to secure the highest practicable degree of uniformity in formalities and other procedures.
retrieval_cards.why: These are the Organization's own words and the first demand of the stem. Three clauses, three marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between a Standard and a Recommended Practice, and what must a Government do if it cannot comply with a Standard?
retrieval_cards.answer: A Standard is an internationally agreed measure necessary and practicable in order to facilitate international maritime traffic; a Recommended Practice is a measure the application of which is desirable. Under article VIII a Contracting Government which finds it impracticable to comply with a Standard, or considers it necessary to adopt differing requirements, must notify the Secretary-General of the difference.
retrieval_cards.why: The obligation is not absolute, but a departure must be declared rather than simply operated. That is the mechanism that makes a facilitation convention workable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which amendment made the maritime single window mandatory, and when did it take effect?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, amending Standard 1.3quin - public authorities shall introduce arrangements enabling all the information required under Standard 2.1 to be provided to a single window by electronic means, and shall consider the single window as the channel for communicating decisions. It entered into force on 1 January 2024.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the recent amendment for this sitting - in force nine months before the paper - and it is the one that carries the digitalization limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Was FAL.15(47) in force at this examination?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It was adopted on 17 March 2023 and its operative paragraph determines entry into force on 1 January 2025 unless one third of Contracting Governments object prior to 1 October 2024. At an October 2024 sitting it is adopted, its objection window has just closed, and it is not yet in force. It amends Recommended Practice 7.11 on national facilitation programmes.
retrieval_cards.why: Adopted is not in force, and this is the cleanest live example of the distinction on the whole paper - the objection deadline falls in the examination month itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the FAL annex define a single window?
retrieval_cards.answer: An environment that allows for the submission or provision of standardized and harmonized information and declarations to a single entry point, typically by electronic means.
retrieval_cards.why: The words standardized and harmonized are the test. A portal that accepts the same unharmonised forms electronically is not a single window.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does a facilitation convention deliver a sustainability benefit?
retrieval_cards.answer: Indirectly, through time. It sets no emission standard and prescribes nothing about the ship. Reliable pre-arrival clearance makes just-in-time arrival possible, so the ship can slow on passage instead of steaming hard and idling at anchor; because fuel burn falls steeply with speed, the saving is disproportionate. Less congestion also means less machinery running for no transport work.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating half of the second demand. Claiming FAL reduces emissions directly is the standard wrong answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name two reasons the single window may not deliver what it promises.
retrieval_cards.answer: First, implementation: a portal that still demands the same information in the same unharmonised formats moves the paperwork rather than removing it, and the duty falls on the public authority, so the ship cannot fix it. Second, the commercial contract: just-in-time arrival needs the charterparty to permit it, and laytime and demurrage terms often reward arriving early and waiting.
retrieval_cards.why: An evaluative question is marked on judgement. Naming the two conditions on which the benefit depends is worth more than another benefit.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: STANDARD A2.5.2 PARAGRAPH 2, THE DEFINITION - 'a seafarer shall be deemed to have been abandoned where, in violation of the requirements of this Convention or the terms of the seafarers' employment agreement, the shipowner: (a) fails to cover the cost of the seafarer's repatriation; or (b) has left the seafarer without the necessary maintenance and support; or (c) has otherwise unilaterally severed their ties with the seafarer including failure to pay contractual wages for a period of at least two months.'

The system shall provide DIRECT ACCESS, SUFFICIENT COVERAGE AND EXPEDITED FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE to any abandoned seafarer on a ship flying the flag of the Member. Necessary maintenance and support shall include adequate food, accommodation, drinking water supplies, ESSENTIAL FUEL FOR SURVIVAL ON BOARD THE SHIP, and necessary medical care.

P1 PRIMARY VERIFIED, same reading: STANDARD A2.5.2 paragraphs 6 to 8 - ships to which Regulation 5.1.3 applies shall CARRY ON BOARD a certificate or other documentary evidence of financial security issued by the provider, a copy POSTED IN A CONSPICUOUS PLACE where it is available to the seafarers, with the information required in APPENDIX A2-I, in English or with an English translation; where more than one provider gives cover, each provider's document is carried. The cost of repatriation shall cover travel by appropriate and expeditious means, NORMALLY BY AIR, with food and accommodation from leaving the ship until arrival home, necessary medical care, passage and transport of personal effects.

blocks.h: (a) What abandonment is, and why the numbers keep rising — 8 marks
1. What abandonment means - the Convention's own definition

blocks.p: Abandonment is not a matter of impression. Since the 2014 amendments to the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, which entered into force on 18 January 2017, it has had a hard legal definition. Standard A2.5.2, paragraph 2 provides that a seafarer shall be deemed to have been abandoned where, in violation of the requirements of the Convention or the terms of the seafarers' employment agreement, the shipowner:

ol: fails to cover the cost of the seafarer's repatriation; or
has left the seafarer without the necessary maintenance and support; or
has otherwise unilaterally severed their ties with the seafarer, including failure to pay contractual wages for a period of at least two months.

blocks.p: Two features of that definition are worth marks in themselves. First, ‘necessary maintenance and support’ is itself defined — it includes adequate food, accommodation, drinking water supplies, essential fuel for survival on board the ship, and necessary medical care. That last item shows the drafters understood the problem: a ship with no bunkers has no power, no cooling, no fresh water and no lighting. Second, the two-month wage test converts a subjective impression into a legal trigger. Before 2017 a crew could be visibly abandoned and have nothing to point to; now they have a date.

blocks.h: 2. What the seafarer actually suffers, and why it shapes the regime

blocks.p: It is worth a short paragraph, because it explains why the remedy takes the form it does. An abandoned seafarer is stranded rather than endangered, and that is the whole difficulty:

ul: he is unpaid for months, with a family dependent on remittances that have stopped;
he cannot go home — no ticket, frequently no visa, and sometimes no passport;
food, water, fuel and medical supplies run out on a ship with no operating budget;
he often cannot leave the ship even if he could get ashore, because his wage claim is secured on her and walking away may forfeit it;
and no safety instrument reaches him. The ship is afloat, alongside and perfectly safe. He is not in distress in any sense the safety or salvage conventions recognise.

blocks.p: Every ordinary remedy fails at the same moment. He cannot sue an owner who has no money and often no traceable identity; he cannot be rescued, because he is not in danger; and he cannot wait, because the food is running out. That is the gap the financial security regime was written to close, and it is why the Standard insists on direct access and expedited assistance rather than a claims process.

blocks.h: 3. Why the numbers keep rising - the causes

blocks.p: The stem asks for causes, and they are commercial and structural rather than accidental:

ul: Thin capitalisation in a cyclical trade. Marginal owners operate on narrow margins and short-term charters; one bad fixture, one long off-hire or one unexpected repair can end the business, and the ship is where the failure lands.

Single-ship company structures. Each vessel is owned by its own company, so a failure is ring-fenced: the loss stops at that ship and the beneficial owner's other assets are untouched. It is lawful, ordinary and it is also exactly what makes walking away cheap.

Registers with weak inspection, and opaque beneficial ownership. Where a flag State does not inspect and the real owner is hard to identify behind managers and nominees, there is little to deter abandonment and little to pursue afterwards.

Old tonnage at the end of its life. When a ship is worth little more than her scrap value, the cost of lay-up, repair or a proper recycling sale can exceed what she will fetch — and abandoning her becomes the cheapest option available to a failing owner.

Arrest, detention and sanctions. A ship arrested for debt, detained for deficiencies, or caught by sanctions can be frozen in place for months with the crew still aboard, and the owner may simply stop funding her.

Long charter and manning chains. Between the seafarer and whoever really controls the ship there may be a manning agent, a manager, a bareboat charterer and a time charterer. The crew's employer is often the entity with the least money in the chain.
War, sanctions and port closures stranding ships in places where no buyer, no charterer and no bank will engage.

And better reporting. Part of the rise is real and part of it is visibility: the joint IMO/ILO database records more cases because more are being looked for, reported and followed up. That does not diminish the problem, but an accurate answer says so.

blocks.h: (b) The role of the ILO and the ITF, and the provisions within the MLC — 8 marks
4. The MLC financial security regime - the operative answer

blocks.p: This is where the marks in limb (b) mostly are, because it is the part that is law. Regulation 2.5, paragraph 2 requires ships to carry financial security to assist seafarers in the event of abandonment, and Standard A2.5.2 sets out what that means.

ul: Every flag State must ensure a system is in place for ships flying its flag. It may take the form of a social security scheme, insurance, a national fund or a similar arrangement, its form settled after consultation with shipowners' and seafarers' organisations. In practice the provider is usually a P&I club.

The system must provide direct access, sufficient coverage and expedited financial assistance. Those three words are the heart of it: the seafarer calls on the security himself, he does not have to sue anybody, and it must be quick.

A certificate or other documentary evidence of financial security must be carried on board, containing the information required by Appendix A2-I, in English or with an English translation, and a copy posted in a conspicuous place available to the seafarers. Where more than one provider gives cover, each provider's document is carried.

What it must cover: outstanding wages and other entitlements due under the employment agreement, the collective agreement or national law — limited to four months of wages and four months of entitlements; all expenses reasonably incurred by the seafarer, including repatriation; and essential needs — food, clothing where necessary, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board and medical care — from the act or omission constituting the abandonment until the seafarer's arrival at home.
Repatriation is by appropriate and expeditious means, normally by air, with food, accommodation, medical care, passage and transport of personal effects.

The security cannot simply lapse. It may not cease before the end of its period of validity unless the provider has given at least 30 days' prior notification to the competent authority of the flag State.
The provider is subrogated to the seafarer's rights up to the amount paid, and the regime is expressly not exclusive of any other rights, claims or remedies.

And it follows the flag, not the port. The provider must give the agreed assistance wherever the abandonment takes place, including in the territory of a State that has not ratified the Convention. That matters, because abandonment concentrates in exactly the ports least likely to be bound by it.

blocks.p: Behind that sits Standard A2.5 on repatriation itself, which supplies the backstop: where the shipowner fails, the flag State shall arrange the repatriation and may recover the cost from the shipowner — and a State which has paid may detain, or request the detention of, the ships of that shipowner until it is reimbursed. Two propositions in it are worth quoting: the expenses shall in no case be a charge upon the seafarer, and a Member shall not refuse the right of repatriation because of the financial circumstances of a shipowner or the shipowner's inability or unwillingness to replace a seafarer.

ul: The ILO is the source of the law. The MLC is an ILO Convention, adopted by the International Labour Conference in 2006 and in force since 20 August 2013.
Its method is tripartite. Governments, shipowners and seafarers negotiate the text together, which is why the Convention carries the authority it does with the industry as well as with States.

The Special Tripartite Committee amends the Code by a simplified procedure — and the 2014 amendments, which created this entire abandonment regime, were its work. Before them the Convention did not directly address abandonment at all.

It supervises. Member States report; the ILO's supervisory machinery, including the Committee of Experts, examines those reports; and complaints procedures exist where a State is not applying a ratified Convention.

It works jointly with IMO on precisely this problem. The Joint IMO/ILO Ad Hoc Expert Working Group on Liability and Compensation regarding Claims for Death, Personal Injury and Abandonment of Seafarers is the body that identified the gap in the international legal regime in the first place, and the joint Guidelines on Provision of Financial Security in Cases of Abandonment of Seafarers — adopted by both the IMO Assembly and the ILO Governing Body — were the voluntary precursor of the mandatory regime that followed.

blocks.p: The International Transport Workers' Federation is a global federation of transport workers' trade unions. Be precise about what that means: it is industrial, not regulatory. It has no legal authority over a shipowner and it does not enforce the Convention. What it has is presence, money and leverage.

ul: An inspectorate in ports worldwide. ITF inspectors board ships, talk to crews and check wages and conditions — and are very often the first people to identify an abandonment, because they are the only outsiders who routinely go aboard and ask.
Reporting. Cases found are reported into the machinery, including the joint database, which is part of why the recorded numbers have risen.

Collective bargaining agreements. The ITF negotiates agreements fixing wages and conditions, so there is an agreed figure against which arrears can be quantified — which matters when a claim has to be proved.
Pursuit of unpaid wages, including support for the arrest of the ship to secure the crew's claim, and legal assistance in doing it.
The flag-of-convenience campaign, which targets exactly the registers where abandonment concentrates.
Practical relief — food, water, funds, communications and welfare support while the formal machinery grinds. In a real abandonment this is often what actually keeps a crew fed in the first weeks.

blocks.h: 7. What the regime still does not solve

blocks.p: An answer that stops at ‘there is now financial security’ has not finished. The regime is a large improvement and it is not complete:

ul: The four-month cap can be less than what is owed. Where wages have been unpaid for eight months, four months of them are not covered.
It answers the wage and repatriation claim, not the wider loss — the career interrupted, the months of the seafarer's life, the family debt incurred meanwhile.
An uninsured or falsely certificated ship leaves the crew outside the system entirely. The certificate proves cover only if the cover is real.

Non-party flags and lapsed cover. A ship that falls out of class and out of insurance at the same time — which is a common pattern in a failing company — may have no security behind her at the moment she needs it.
Detention, arrest and sanctions can keep a crew aboard even when the money is available, because a port State may not release a ship or its crew until other matters are resolved.
Crews sometimes stay voluntarily, to protect a wage claim secured on the ship. A remedy the seafarer is reluctant to use is only a partial remedy.
And the flag State backstop is only as good as the flag State. The duty to repatriate falls on the same administrations whose weak oversight allowed the situation in the first place.

blocks.p: The marks are 8 + 8, but limb (a) is really two questions of about four marks each: what abandonment is, and why the numbers rise. Candidates habitually merge them and write one long passage of sympathy that answers neither. Label them and answer them separately.

In limb (b), notice what the stem actually asks for: the role of organisations and the available provisions within the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006. The provisions are the law and they are the bulk of the marks. Give Standard A2.5.2 the most paper, then the ILO, then the ITF — and keep a short closing block for what still fails, because that is what makes the answer look like judgement rather than recital.

blocks.h: Define it, do not describe it

blocks.p: This is the single decision that separates a good script from an average one. An average answer says abandonment is when a crew is left on a ship without pay or supplies, which is true and worth almost nothing. A good answer gives Standard A2.5.2 paragraph 2: the shipowner fails to cover repatriation, or leaves the seafarer without necessary maintenance and support, or unilaterally severs ties — including failure to pay contractual wages for at least two months.

The two-month test is the detail to hold above all others. It is the point at which a hardship becomes a legal status, and it is what allows a seafarer, an inspector or a port State to say ‘this is abandonment’ and trigger the machinery. And add the definition-within-the-definition: necessary maintenance and support includes food, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board and medical care.

blocks.h: Why the regime is shaped the way it is

blocks.p: Understand the failure and you can reconstruct Standard A2.5.2 from first principles under exam pressure:

headers: The way the old system failed
What the Standard does about it
rows: The money comes from compulsory financial security, not from the owner
The seafarer cannot enforce a claim against an untraceable company
Direct access — he calls on the security himself, without suing anybody
Everything takes months and the food runs out now
The crew do not know who to call
The certificate is carried on board and posted conspicuously, with Appendix A2-I content
Cover quietly lapses when the owner stops paying premiums
30 days' prior notification to the flag State before it may cease
Abandonment happens in ports outside the Convention
The provider must pay wherever the abandonment takes place
The owner disappears and nobody repatriates
The flag State must arrange it, and may detain that owner's ships to recover

blocks.p: Reproduce two or three rows of that table in the examination room and the answer reads as analysis rather than recall.

ul: Describing abandonment instead of giving the Convention's three-limb definition.
Omitting the two-month wage test, which is the most quotable thing in the whole topic.
Answering the consequences when the stem asks for the causes.
Treating the ITF as a regulator. It is a federation of trade unions with no legal authority over a shipowner.
Treating the ILO as an operational rescue body. It sets and supervises standards.
Not knowing that financial security is mandatory, and has been since 18 January 2017.
Forgetting the four-month cap, which is both the scope of the cover and its main weakness.
Saying the seafarer must claim against the owner. The point of the regime is direct access.
Quoting a number of cases for a given year. Reported counts move with reporting practice as much as with incidence.
Importing the 2022 MLC amendments. They entered into force on 23 December 2024, after this examination.

blocks.p: ‘Your wages are two months late. Are you abandoned?’ Not automatically. Limb (c) of the definition is unilateral severance of ties, including failure to pay wages for at least two months — the two months is the qualifying period for that limb, not a switch that operates by itself. But it is the point at which the question becomes a legal one, and at which the crew should be raising it formally.

‘Where is the certificate and what does it tell you?’ Carried on board and posted in a conspicuous place available to the seafarers, with the Appendix A2-I information, in English or with an English translation. It tells the crew who the provider is and how to contact them — which is the entire practical value of it.

‘The ship is abandoned in a State that has not ratified the MLC. Are you covered?’ Yes, if the flag State is a party and the security is in place. The obligation follows the flag, and the provider must assist wherever the abandonment takes place.

‘Who pays if there is no security at all?’ The flag State must arrange repatriation and may recover the cost from the shipowner, and a State which has paid may detain that owner's ships until reimbursed. The expenses shall in no case be a charge upon the seafarer.

‘What can the ITF actually do for you?’ Find you, report the case, quantify the arrears against a collective agreement, help arrest the ship to secure the claim, and feed you meanwhile. What it cannot do is order the owner to pay.

ul: Give the three limbs of the definition of abandonment. Failure to cover repatriation; leaving the seafarer without necessary maintenance and support; unilateral severance of ties including failure to pay wages for at least two months.
What counts as necessary maintenance and support? Adequate food, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board, and necessary medical care.
Which provision requires financial security? Regulation 2.5 paragraph 2, implemented by Standard A2.5.2.
When did it come into force? 18 January 2017, with the 2014 amendments.
What is the limit on wages covered? Four months of outstanding wages and four months of outstanding entitlements.
How is the seafarer repatriated? By appropriate and expeditious means, normally by air, with food, accommodation, medical care and personal effects.
How much notice before the security can cease? At least 30 days to the flag State competent authority.
Who is usually the provider? A P and I club, though the Convention permits insurance, a social security scheme or a national fund.
What can a State do if it has paid for repatriation? Recover from the shipowner, and detain or request detention of that shipowner's ships until reimbursed.
What is the difference between the ILO and the ITF here? The ILO makes and supervises the standard; the ITF is a trade union federation that finds cases and pursues owners industrially.

blocks.p: Limb (a): WHAT — WHO SUFFERS — WHY. Limb (b): CONVENTION — ILO — ITF — GAPS.

For the definition, three verbs in order: FAILS to repatriate, LEAVES without support, SEVERS ties — and the number attached to the third is two months. For the cover, three more: FOUR months, THIRTY days, BY AIR. Five items in total and they carry most of what is quotable in the answer.

For the causes, work outward from the ship: the owner (thin capital, single-ship company), the flag (weak inspection, opaque ownership), the ship (old tonnage near scrap value), the situation (arrest, detention, sanctions, war), and the record (better reporting).

blocks.p: The Convention content in this answer is read at source, and the edition is the right one for this sitting rather than the newest available — which is worth stating, because on this topic those are not the same thing. The ILO consolidated text of 2020, ‘including the Amendments of 2014, 2016 and 2018’, is the operative edition at October 2024: Regulation 2.5, Standard A2.5 and Standard A2.5.2 were read in full from it. The 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, two and a half months after this examination, and although a consolidation including them is available it was deliberately not used as law here. The 2025 amendments, adopted in June 2025, are further away still.

The dates are also primary: the ILO Compendium of maritime labour instruments was read at source and records the Convention's adoption on 23 February 2006, its entry into force on 20 August 2013, and the entry into force of the 2014 amendments on 18 January 2017 — together with the Office's own observation that before that date the Convention did not directly address the serious problem of abandonment. The same source establishes that the provider may be a P&I club and must assist wherever the abandonment occurs, and it carries the 2006 Conference resolution on the Joint IMO/ILO working group.

What is weaker is stated as such. MIW holds no ITF constitutional document, collective agreement or inspectorate procedure, so the ITF's role is described by function and no clause, membership figure or number of inspectors is asserted. The establishing instrument of the joint IMO/ILO abandonment database was not identified and no resolution number is given for it. And no number of abandonment cases is quoted for any year — deliberately. The stem asserts an ever-increasing number, the answer accepts that framing and explains why, but reported counts move with reporting practice as much as with incidence, and giving a figure would put false precision on the least measurable part of the subject.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two limbs of eight marks each, and limb (a) contains two separate demands that candidates routinely merge. First, WHAT abandonment IS - and the examiner expects the Convention's own definition, not a description of hardship. Second, WHY the number keeps increasing - a causes question, requiring commercial and structural analysis rather than sympathy. Limb (b) is institutional and legal: the role of the ILO and the ITF, and the AVAILABLE PROVISIONS WITHIN THE MLC - which is an invitation to name and explain Standard A2.5.2.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as 8 + 8. Within limb (a) the two demands are worth about four marks each, so the definition must be tight and the causes must be a real list rather than one sentence. Within limb (b) the MLC provisions are the substantial part - probably five of the eight - because the stem says 'the available provisions within the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006' and that is where the operative law is; the ILO and ITF share the remainder.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate can state the three-limb definition, including the two-month wage test, rather than describing abandonment impressionistically; can explain the commercial structure that produces abandonment, which is the difference between an analytical and a sentimental answer; and knows that since 2017 there has been a MANDATORY FINANCIAL SECURITY regime with a certificate on board, direct access and a four-month wage cap - which is the single most useful thing a Chief Engineer can know about this subject.
primary_source_plan: Read Standard A2.5.2 at source in the edition operative at the sitting, and take the definition and the scope of cover from it verbatim.
Establish from the Compendium that the financial security regime entered into force on 18 January 2017, so it is unambiguously available at this sitting.
Confirm that the 2022 amendments are AFTER the sitting and use the 2020 consolidated edition.
Describe the ITF and the joint database BY FUNCTION and assert no constitutional document, no resolution number and no case count.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The MLC Code is amended on a regular cycle and two later amendment sets exist, both after this sitting. The risk is entirely of importing later material; the abandonment regime itself has been stable since 2017.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is international and names international organisations. No Indian statutory limb is set and none is imported.
technical_ambiguities: 'What do you understand by abandonment' invites a description of the hardship. The Convention gives it a hard legal definition with three limbs and a two-month test, and that is what scores.
'What is cause of the ever-increasing number' asks for causes, not for consequences. An answer that describes what abandoned crews suffer has answered the wrong half.
'Available provisions within the Maritime Labour Convention' is narrower than 'the MLC generally'. It points at Regulation 2.5 and Standard A2.5.2, not at the whole Convention.
The ITF is a trade union federation, not a regulator. Treating it as though it enforced the Convention is a category error the examiner will notice.

The second trap is treating the ITF as a regulator: it is a federation of trade unions with no legal authority over a shipowner — its power is industrial, practical and reputational, and saying so precisely is worth more than overstating it.

questions.understand_first:
Abandonment is not a shipwreck and it is not a strike. It is what happens when a commercial failure ashore leaves a crew stranded on an asset that nobody will pay for — and the reason it needed its own legal regime is that every ordinary remedy fails at once. The seafarer cannot sue an owner who has no money and often no traceable identity. He cannot go home, because he has no ticket, frequently no visa, and sometimes no passport. He cannot leave the ship, because leaving may forfeit the wage claim that is secured on her. And he cannot simply be rescued, because he is not in distress in any sense the salvage or safety conventions recognise: the ship is afloat, alongside, and perfectly safe. The crew are stranded rather than endangered, and no instrument written for danger reaches them.

That is the gap the 2014 amendments closed, and understanding what they did explains the whole shape of Standard A2.5.2. If the problem is that the owner has no money, then the money must come from somewhere other than the owner — hence compulsory financial security. If the problem is that the seafarer cannot enforce a claim, then he must be able to call on the security directly, without suing anybody — hence direct access. If the problem is delay, the assistance must be expedited and the certificate must be posted where the crew can read it, so they know who to call. Every element of the Standard is an answer to a specific way the old system failed, and an answer that shows that is worth far more than one that recites the paragraph.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the abandonment of seafarers question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 The Convention's definition. 2 What the seafarer actually suffers. 3 The causes of the rising numbers. (b) 4 The MLC financial security regime. 5 The role of the ILO. 6 The role of the ITF. 7 What the regime still does not solve.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) contains two demands - what it is and why it increases - and the causes list is half its marks. In limb (b) the Convention provisions are the substantial part; the two organisations share the rest.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is a seafarer deemed to have been abandoned under the MLC?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Standard A2.5.2 paragraph 2, where in violation of the Convention or of the seafarers' employment agreement the shipowner (a) fails to cover the cost of the seafarer's repatriation; or (b) has left the seafarer without the necessary maintenance and support; or (c) has otherwise unilaterally severed their ties with the seafarer, including failure to pay contractual wages for a period of at least two months.
retrieval_cards.why: Three limbs and a hard two-month test. Reciting this instead of describing hardship is the single largest scoring decision on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does 'necessary maintenance and support' include?
retrieval_cards.answer: Adequate food, accommodation, drinking water supplies, essential fuel for survival on board the ship, and necessary medical care.
retrieval_cards.why: Essential fuel for survival on board is the detail that shows the drafters understood the problem - a ship with no bunkers has no power, no cooling and no water.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the financial security cover, and up to what limit?
retrieval_cards.answer: Outstanding wages and other entitlements due under the employment agreement, the collective bargaining agreement or national law, limited to four months of each; all expenses reasonably incurred by the seafarer including repatriation; and essential needs - food, clothing where necessary, accommodation, drinking water, essential fuel for survival on board and medical care - until arrival home. Repatriation is by appropriate and expeditious means, normally by air.
retrieval_cards.why: Four months is the number to hold, and it is also the regime's main limitation: it can be less than what is actually owed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does an abandoned seafarer actually get the money?
retrieval_cards.answer: Directly. The system must provide direct access, sufficient coverage and expedited financial assistance; assistance is granted promptly on request by the seafarer or a nominated representative with the necessary justification of entitlement; and the certificate of financial security, containing the Appendix A2-I information, is carried on board and posted in a conspicuous place available to the seafarers.
retrieval_cards.why: Direct access is the mechanism that makes the regime work, because the seafarer does not have to sue a company that has no money. The posted certificate tells him who to call.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When did the MLC financial security regime for abandonment come into force?
retrieval_cards.answer: 18 January 2017, when the 2014 amendments entered into force and introduced Standard A2.5.2. Before that date the MLC, 2006 did not directly address abandonment, although some of its provisions bore on it. The Convention itself was adopted on 23 February 2006 and entered into force on 20 August 2013.
retrieval_cards.why: The date is the proof that the regime existed and was fully available at this examination. It also explains why older material on abandonment reads so differently.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between what the ILO does and what the ITF does?
retrieval_cards.answer: The ILO is the standard-setting body: the MLC is an ILO Convention, negotiated tripartitely between governments, shipowners and seafarers, and amended through the Special Tripartite Committee - the 2014 amendments that created this regime were its work. It supervises through reporting and expert examination. The ITF is a global federation of transport trade unions with no legal authority over a shipowner: its inspectorate boards ships in ports, finds and reports cases, negotiates collective agreements, pursues unpaid wages and supports arrest of the ship, and provides practical relief.
retrieval_cards.why: One makes the law, the other finds the ships. Treating the ITF as a regulator is a category error and treating the ILO as an operational body is the mirror of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The ship is abandoned in a State that has not ratified the MLC. Is the crew covered?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, if the flag State is a party and the security is in place. The financial security provider - which may be a P and I club - must provide the agreed assistance wherever the abandonment takes place, including in the territory of a State that has not ratified the Convention or is not bound by the 2014 amendments. The obligation follows the flag, not the port.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the feature that makes the regime useful, because abandonment concentrates in exactly the ports least likely to be bound by the Convention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name three reasons abandonment cases keep rising.
retrieval_cards.answer: Thin capitalisation and single-ship company structures, so one bad charter ends the business and isolates the liability; registers with weak inspection and beneficial ownership that is hard to trace; and old tonnage near the end of its life, where walking away can be cheaper than lay-up or recycling. Add arrest, detention and sanctions freezing ships with crews aboard - and better reporting, since the joint IMO/ILO database records more cases because more are looked for.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks for causes. Structural and commercial causes score; describing the suffering answers a different question.
