blocks.h: 1. Why propeller efficiency is worth pursuing

blocks.p: The propeller is the final energy conversion in the propulsion chain and one of the least efficient links in it: a large proportion of the delivered power never becomes useful thrust. Because resistance rises steeply with speed, a modest improvement in propulsive efficiency releases a disproportionate saving in fuel and therefore in emissions.

The stem supplies its own framing — ‘improving efficiency of propellers is recognized as a growing means to improve energy efficiency of ships’ — and that framing is sound at this sitting. The 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI has been in force since 1 November 2022, and it bites in two directions at once: a propeller change reduces the attained EEXI (regulation 23) against the required EEXI (regulation 25), which is a design-index requirement assessed once; and the same change improves the attained operational carbon intensity under regulation 28, which is assessed every year. Very few measures do both. And unlike reducing speed — the other large lever — a propeller change costs the operator no time.

blocks.h: 2. Where the losses occur, and the ceiling on recovering them

blocks.p: A useful answer explains what each device is attacking before describing it. Overall propulsive efficiency is the product of hull efficiency, open-water (propeller) efficiency and relative rotative efficiency. The devices in this question act chiefly on the second, where the energy is lost in four ways:

ul: Axial or slipstream loss. The propeller works by accelerating water aft; the kinetic energy left in that accelerated column is lost. It falls as the disc area is increased and the acceleration reduced.

Rotational loss. A single propeller leaves the race rotating. That swirl carries energy which does nothing to propel the ship, and it is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation.
Frictional loss. Viscous drag over the blade surfaces — irreducible, and worsened by roughness and fouling.

Tip vortex loss. At the blade tip the pressure difference between face and back equalises around the edge, shedding a strong vortex which carries away energy and is a principal source of pressure pulses, hull vibration and cavitation erosion.

blocks.p: Cavitation sets the ceiling. Blade loading cannot simply be increased, because local pressure falling to vapour pressure produces cavities whose collapse causes erosion, vibration and radiated noise. Every device below is an attempt to recover one of these losses without breaching that ceiling: the duct attacks axial and tip loss, Kappel attacks tip vortex loss, contra-rotation attacks rotational loss, and azimuth propulsion attacks the quality of the water arriving at the disc.

Principle. The propeller runs inside an annular aerofoil — a nozzle, the classic form being the Kort nozzle. In an accelerating duct the internal section converges, so flow is accelerated into the disc; each blade then has to generate less thrust for the same total, and the duct itself, being a lifting surface with circulation, produces additional forward thrust. The close tip clearance also largely suppresses the tip vortex. A decelerating duct reverses the section to raise pressure at the disc and suppress cavitation and radiated noise — mainly a naval application.

The governing parameter is thrust loading. The duct earns its keep where the propeller is heavily loaded at low speed: tugs, trawlers, pushers, and slow full-form ships whose diameter is limited by draught.

ul: Merits. Substantial thrust augmentation at high loading, which is why bollard-pull vessels are almost universally ducted; improved efficiency where the propeller would otherwise be overloaded; suppression of the tip vortex and its associated erosion; physical protection of the propeller from debris and quay contact; improved course stability with a fixed nozzle; and, with a steerable nozzle, a genuine manoeuvring gain that can remove the need for a separate rudder.

Demerits. The duct is an appendage with its own drag, and at light loading and higher speed that drag exceeds the benefit — a duct can make a fast, lightly loaded ship worse. It fouls and corrodes, and marine growth inside the nozzle degrades performance quickly; it can be damaged or blocked by debris or ice; internal cavitation erosion occurs on the inner surface and at the tip gap; clearances are critical and alignment must be maintained; it adds weight and structure; and it complicates survey, inspection and propeller removal in dry dock.

blocks.p: Principle. A Kappel propeller is a conventional-diameter propeller whose blade tips are curved smoothly towards the suction side, forming an integrated, continuous winglet rather than a bolted-on end plate. The curvature allows blade loading to be carried further outboard while the tip vortex is weakened and displaced away from the blade. The aeronautical analogy is exact: it is the marine equivalent of an aircraft winglet, and it recovers energy from the same mechanism.

ul: Merits. It reduces tip vortex loss for the same diameter, which matters when draught or aperture fixes the diameter. There is no additional appendage, so no added drag, no added fouling surface and no new maintenance item. The weakened tip vortex produces a more uniform wake into the rudder, reducing pressure pulses, hull vibration and radiated noise — a real habitability and structural benefit as well as an efficiency one. And it is retrofittable as a straight propeller replacement at a scheduled dry docking.

Demerits. The gain is modest and is highly dependent on the hull wake field, so the blade must be designed for the specific ship — which means CFD and model testing, and a high design cost that is hard to justify on a single vessel. The curved tip geometry is complex to cast, dearer than a conventional blade, and more difficult to repair, straighten or re-pitch after damage; the tip is also relatively vulnerable. And the benefit is design-point dependent: a ship trading persistently away from the draught and speed for which the blade was designed may realise little of it.

blocks.p: Principle. Two propellers are mounted coaxially on the same axis and turn in opposite directions. The forward propeller leaves a rotating race; the after propeller, turning the other way, is designed to recover that rotational energy and convert it into additional thrust. Because rotational loss is the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation, this attacks the biggest target directly. Mechanically it requires either concentric inner and outer shafting with epicyclic gearing, or a podded after unit driven electrically in the hybrid arrangement.

ul: Merits. The highest theoretical efficiency gain of the four, because it recovers swirl rather than merely avoiding a loss. The total thrust is divided between two propellers, so loading per propeller falls — which reduces cavitation risk, pressure pulses and induced vibration, and permits a smaller diameter for a given thrust, valuable where draught constrains the aperture. Torque reaction is largely cancelled, improving course keeping and reducing rudder correction.

Demerits. The objection is mechanical, and it is serious. The arrangement demands concentric inner and outer shafting with complex reduction and reversing gearing, and the sealing of two concentric shafts at the stern tube is a recognised reliability weak point. Capital cost is high; alignment, maintenance and dry-dock withdrawal are all substantially harder; there are more components to fail in a system whose failure immobilises the ship. Service experience in the large merchant fleet remains limited, so spares support and operator confidence lag the theory — which, more than the engineering, is why adoption has been slow.

blocks.p: Principle — and note first that this item is a different kind of answer from the other three. Ducted, Kappel and contra-rotating are propeller or duct designs. Azimuth propulsion is a propulsion arrangement: a thruster unit rotatable through 360 degrees, producing thrust in any direction, in mechanical Z-drive or L-drive form with bevel gearing, or as an electrically driven pod with the motor inside the underwater housing. In the pulling or tractor configuration the propeller is ahead of its own housing and strut, so it works in undisturbed flow rather than in the disturbed wake behind them.

ul: Merits. Inflow quality — the tractor arrangement gives a clean, uniform inflow, which raises open-water efficiency and reduces the wake non-uniformity that drives cavitation and pressure pulses. No shaft line, no rudder, no stern tube, which removes shafting losses and stern tube sealing, frees the after end for cargo or machinery, and allows the prime movers to be placed where they suit the ship. Outstanding manoeuvring: full thrust in any direction, so astern power without reversing the engine, and station-keeping and dynamic positioning capability that a shaft-and-rudder ship cannot approach. With diesel-electric drive the engines run at their own most efficient load independent of ship speed, and surplus sets can be shut down.

Demerits. The housing and strut are appendages with their own drag, which offsets part of the inflow gain, and the transmission or electrical conversion chain adds losses that a direct-coupled shaft line does not have. Capital cost is high and the unit is complex. Maintenance is the real objection: the whole unit generally must be withdrawn in dry dock, and the steering gear, slip rings, seals and thrust bearings inside the pod are new failure modes with limited redundancy. Fleet familiarity, spares support and repair capability are thinner than for conventional shafting, and on a straightforward deep-sea trade the manoeuvring advantage — which is the main prize — is worth very little.

blocks.p: The four are not competitors for the same ship. The choice follows the thrust loading coefficient and the operating profile:

rows: Heavily loaded, low speed, high thrust — tug, trawler, pusher, slow full-form ship
The duct earns its drag several times over at high thrust loading, and a steerable nozzle adds manoeuvring
Moderately loaded single screw with a reasonably clean wake, diameter fixed by draught
Recovers tip vortex loss with no new appendage and no new maintenance item; retrofittable at a scheduled docking
Large recoverable swirl and acceptable mechanical complexity
Attacks the largest single loss directly — the most on offer, at the highest engineering and commercial risk
Manoeuvring, station-keeping or an awkward machinery arrangement
Clean inflow plus arrangement freedom, and manoeuvring capability nothing else matches
None of them — and certainly not a duct
Appendage drag exceeds the benefit. This is the trap in the question

blocks.p: Two points on answering. First, this sitting prints ‘Discuss the following’, so all four are required and an answer that treats three has left about four marks unclaimed — whatever a worked answer to an earlier sitting of this question may advise. Second, give no percentage figures: published gains are manufacturer-sourced and depend entirely on hull form, wake field, loading and trade. A correctly explained mechanism is worth more than a number you cannot defend.

Four devices, sixteen marks, and a three-part demand on each — principle, merits, demerits. That is about four marks per device and it is tight. The structure that makes it fit is to establish the four loss mechanisms once, in a short block, and then open each device section with the loss it attacks. Done that way, each device needs only a compact principle and two short lists, and the answer is complete.

The alternative — a long theoretical preamble on propulsive efficiency followed by three devices in loving detail and the fourth in a sentence — is the commonest failure, and it is a planning failure rather than a knowledge failure. Decide the four-way split before you start writing.

blocks.h: The three words that change this question

blocks.p: An earlier sitting printed ‘Discuss any three of the following high-efficiency propellers’. This paper does not. It prints ‘Discuss the following’, and the three missing words move about four marks from optional to compulsory.

This matters for revision as much as for the examination room. A candidate working from a worked answer to the earlier sitting will have learned three devices thoroughly and will have seen azimuth propulsion demoted to an appendix — along with advice, entirely correct for that paper, that three treated properly beats four treated superficially. Read the stem, not the note. The general lesson is worth more than this one question: an examiner who recycles a stem often edits it, and the edit is where the marks move.

blocks.h: Why azimuth propulsion is the odd one out

blocks.p: Three of the four items are designs — changes to the blade or a duct around it. Azimuth propulsion is an arrangement, and its efficiency argument is correspondingly different. Very little of its gain comes from the blade: it comes from inflow quality in the tractor configuration, from deleting the shaft line, rudder and stern tube, and, with diesel-electric drive, from decoupling engine load from ship speed. Saying that explicitly shows the examiner you read the list rather than pattern-matched it, and it opens the manoeuvring and dynamic-positioning merits that no blade design can claim.

It also has the most honest set of demerits, and they are worth stating properly: the housing and strut are appendages with drag, the transmission chain adds losses, and the maintenance objection is real — the unit generally comes off in dry dock, and the seals, slip rings and steering gear inside it are failure modes a shaft line does not have.

ul: Answering only three devices. This sitting requires four.
Describing what each device looks like instead of naming the loss it recovers.
Giving merits only. The stem asks for merits and demerits, so half the marks are in the second list.
Treating a device as high-efficiency in the abstract. A duct makes a fast, lightly loaded ship worse.
Quoting percentage gains. They are vendor-sourced and hull-specific.
Naming manufacturers or products. Kappel is named only because the stem names it.
Forgetting cavitation as the ceiling. Without it, the answer implies blade loading could simply be increased.
Using the pre-2021 MARPOL Annex VI numbering in the framing paragraph. Regulation 21 is functional requirements; attained EEXI is 23, required EEXI 25 and operational CII 28.
Confusing contra-rotating (two propellers on one axis turning opposite ways) with twin screw (two independent shafts) or with a counter-rotating pod behind a conventional propeller.

blocks.p: ‘Would you fit a nozzle to a container ship?’ No. Thrust loading is low and speed is high, so the duct's own drag would exceed any benefit. This is the single best question in the topic because it tests whether the candidate understands the condition rather than the device.

‘Contra-rotating gives the biggest gain. Why is your ship not fitted with it?’ Because the gain is bought with concentric shafting, complex gearing and a stern tube seal on two concentric shafts — a recognised reliability weak point — at high capital cost, with harder alignment and dry-dock withdrawal and limited merchant service experience.
‘What does a winglet on a propeller actually do?’ It weakens and displaces the tip vortex, allowing load to be carried further outboard for the same diameter. The same physics as an aircraft winglet.

‘You have fitted a new propeller. What happens to your engine?’ The propeller demand curve moves, and the engine's operating point moves with it — which is why this question and the propeller-demand-curve question on the same paper are two halves of one topic. A propeller that absorbs more torque at a given speed makes the engine run heavy.

‘How much fuel will it save?’ The correct answer is that it depends on hull form, wake field, loading and trade, and that any single figure is manufacturer-sourced. Saying why the number cannot be given scores better than giving one.

ul: What are the components of propulsive efficiency? Hull efficiency, open-water efficiency and relative rotative efficiency.
Which loss is the largest recoverable one? Rotational loss - the swirl left in the race.

What is a Kort nozzle, and what is the difference between an accelerating and a decelerating duct? An annular aerofoil around the propeller; the accelerating form converges to speed flow into the disc, the decelerating form raises pressure at the disc to suppress cavitation and noise.
On what parameter does the value of a duct depend? Thrust loading coefficient.
What is a Kappel propeller? A propeller with tips curved smoothly to the suction side as an integrated winglet, weakening the tip vortex.
How is a contra-rotating arrangement driven? Concentric inner and outer shafting with epicyclic gearing, or a podded after unit driven electrically.
What is the difference between a Z-drive and a pod? A Z-drive transmits mechanically through bevel gearing from an inboard engine; a pod carries the electric motor in the underwater housing.
What is the tractor configuration and why is it efficient? The propeller is forward of its own housing and strut, so it works in undisturbed flow.
Name one demerit of azimuth propulsion. Housing and strut drag; transmission or conversion losses; or the need to withdraw the unit in dry dock.
Why does cavitation matter to all of these? It sets the ceiling on blade loading, and its collapse causes erosion, vibration and noise.

blocks.p: LOSSES — FOUR DEVICES — CHOOSE. Fix the four losses first (step 2) and each device then announces itself by the loss it attacks: duct = axial and tip, Kappel = tip vortex, contra-rotating = swirl, azimuth = inflow and arrangement. Four devices, four attacks, in the printed order a) b) c) d).

For the closing section hold one word: loading. High loading and slow → duct. Moderate loading, diameter fixed → Kappel. Large swirl, complexity acceptable → contra-rotating. Manoeuvring → azimuth. Light loading and fast → leave it alone.

MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76) — in force 1 November 2022. This supplies the stem's energy-efficiency framing
Regulation 23 attained EEXI and regulation 25 required EEXI — a propeller change is one route to a design-index reduction
Regulation 28 operational carbon intensity — the same change improves the annual rating, which is why a propeller retrofit is one of the few measures that pays twice

Naval architecture references for propulsive efficiency, the loss mechanisms, duct and winglet theory, contra-rotating arrangements, podded propulsion and cavitation. No manufacturer, product or percentage gain is cited

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the numbers that are deliberately absent

blocks.p: Engineering judgement is the dominant provenance class on this question and that is stated rather than disguised. No instrument prescribes a propeller, so there is nothing regulatory to verify in the four device sections; the content is settled naval architecture, explained by mechanism, and it would properly be reviewed by a naval architect rather than by a regulatory check. The one part of the answer that is primary-verified is the framing paragraph: MARPOL Annex VI was read at source for this paper, which is why the regulation numbers appear here at all — an earlier worked answer to this same question deliberately asserted none, because the Annex had not been read.

No percentage efficiency gain is quoted for any of the four devices, and that is deliberate. Published figures for ducts, tip-modified propellers, contra-rotating arrangements and podded drives vary widely, depend entirely on hull form, wake field, loading and operating profile, and originate largely from manufacturers. The same applies to the drag penalty of a pod housing and strut and to the transmission losses of a Z-drive: both are real, both are installation-specific, and neither is given a number here. No claim is made about the installed population of any device or about the relative adoption of mechanical azimuth drives against electric pods, neither of which was established from a held source.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Four losses, four devices. Axial, rotational (the biggest), frictional, tip vortex — with cavitation as the ceiling. Duct attacks axial and tip loss; earns its drag only at high thrust loading and low speed, and makes a fast light ship worse. Kappel is an integrated winglet attacking the tip vortex; no appendage, modest and wake-dependent gain. Contra-rotating recovers swirl, the largest loss, at a serious mechanical price. Azimuth is an arrangement, not a blade: clean inflow and superb manoeuvring, against housing drag and transmission losses. This paper wants all four.
critical_numbers: FOUR devices are required at this sitting - the earlier sitting of this question allowed any three
Sixteen marks over four devices is about four marks each, each carrying principle plus merits plus demerits
Four loss mechanisms: axial, rotational, frictional, tip vortex - rotational is the largest recoverable one
NO percentage efficiency gain is quoted for any device - published figures are vendor-sourced and hull-specific
MARPOL Annex VI: attained EEXI reg 23, required EEXI reg 25, operational CII reg 28 - the framing the stem supplies
quick_revision.critical_regulation: No instrument prescribes a propeller type. The regulatory framing the stem supplies is MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022 — attained EEXI regulation 23 against required EEXI regulation 25, and operational carbon intensity regulation 28. A propeller change is one of the few measures that improves both. Regulation 21 is Functional requirements, not EEDI.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering only three. This paper prints ‘Discuss the following’, not ‘any three of the following’ — a candidate revising from a worked answer to an earlier sitting of this same question will drop azimuth propulsion and lose four marks. The second trap is treating a device as high-efficiency in the abstract: a duct on a fast, lightly loaded ship makes her worse.

questions.memory_cue: LOSSES FIRST, THEN FOUR DEVICES, THEN CHOOSE. Establish the four losses once (2) and every device section then opens with the loss it attacks: duct = axial and tip (3), Kappel = tip vortex (4), contra-rotating = swirl (5), azimuth = inflow quality plus the whole arrangement (6). Close by matching device to thrust loading (7).
questions.understand_first:
Every one of these devices is an answer to the same question: where does the energy go? A propeller does not lose its efficiency in one place, it loses it in four, and each device in this list attacks a different one. Establish the four losses first and the whole answer becomes short and orderly — a duct is an attack on axial and tip loss, a Kappel blade on tip vortex loss, contra-rotation on swirl, and azimuth propulsion on the quality of the water arriving at the disc together with everything the arrangement itself frees up.

The second idea is the one that separates a Class I answer from a catalogue: none of these is high-efficiency in the abstract. The duct is the clearest case. At high thrust loading and low speed it earns its own drag several times over, which is why every tug has one; on a fast, lightly loaded ship the same duct is a drag-producing appendage that makes her worse. So the honest form of every answer here is conditional — this device, on this hull, in this trade — and the closing section that matches device to operating profile is where the examiner finds out whether the candidate understands that.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the high-efficiency propellers question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why propeller efficiency is worth pursuing. 2 Where the losses occur and the cavitation ceiling. 3 Ducted. 4 Kappel. 5 Contra-rotating. 6 Azimuth. 7 Choosing between them.
retrieval_cards.why: Establishing the losses once in step 2 lets each device section open with the loss it attacks, which keeps four devices inside sixteen marks. Step 7 is where the judgement is.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many of the four propeller types does this paper require?
retrieval_cards.answer: All four. This sitting prints 'Discuss the following high-efficiency propellers with its merits and demerits'. An earlier sitting of the identical question printed 'Discuss any three of the following' - those three words are absent here, so azimuth propulsion cannot be dropped.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate revising from a worked answer to the earlier sitting will treat three thoroughly and lose about four marks for the fourth.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four loss mechanisms in a propeller race and say which is the largest recoverable one.
retrieval_cards.answer: Axial or slipstream loss - kinetic energy in the accelerated column of water. Rotational loss - swirl left in the race, and the largest single recoverable loss in a conventional installation. Frictional loss - viscous drag over the blades. Tip vortex loss - pressure equalising around the blade edge. Cavitation sets the ceiling on how hard a blade may be loaded.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the loss each device attacks is what distinguishes an explanation from a description, and it makes four device sections fit inside sixteen marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When does a duct help, and when does it hurt?
retrieval_cards.answer: The governing parameter is thrust loading. At high loading and low speed - tugs, trawlers, pushers, slow full-form ships whose diameter is limited by draught - the duct accelerates flow into the disc, generates its own forward thrust and suppresses the tip vortex, earning its drag several times over. On a fast, lightly loaded ship its appendage drag exceeds the benefit and it makes the ship worse.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating point of the whole question and the clearest demonstration that no device is high-efficiency in the abstract.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a Kappel propeller and what does it recover?
retrieval_cards.answer: A conventional-diameter propeller whose blade tips are curved smoothly towards the suction side to form an integrated, continuous winglet rather than a bolted-on end plate. It allows blade loading to be carried further outboard while weakening the tip vortex and displacing it from the blade, so it recovers tip vortex loss without adding an appendage.
retrieval_cards.why: The aeronautical analogy is exact and it is the fastest way to hold the principle. The no-appendage point carries several of the merits.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Contra-rotating propellers offer the highest theoretical gain. Why are they rare?
retrieval_cards.answer: The objection is mechanical and it is serious. They need concentric inner and outer shafting with complex reduction and reversing gearing, and sealing two concentric shafts at the stern tube is a recognised reliability weak point. Capital cost is high; alignment, maintenance and dry-dock withdrawal are all substantially harder; and there are more components whose failure immobilises the ship. Merchant service experience remains limited, so spares support and operator confidence lag the theory.
retrieval_cards.why: The theory-versus-practice gap is the mark-scoring observation, and the stern tube seal is the specific answer an examiner wants.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is azimuth propulsion a different kind of answer from the other three?
retrieval_cards.answer: The other three are blade or duct designs that change how the propeller works. Azimuth propulsion is a propulsion arrangement - a unit rotatable through 360 degrees. Its efficiency argument is different too: the gain comes largely from inflow quality in the pulling configuration, from removing the shaft line, rudder and stern tube, and, with diesel-electric drive, from letting the engines run at their own best load independent of ship speed.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying this explicitly shows the candidate has read the list rather than pattern-matched it, and it opens the manoeuvring and dynamic-positioning merits the other three do not have.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regulations make a propeller retrofit attractive, and which regulation is NOT EEDI?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex VI as revised by MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022: attained EEXI is regulation 23 and required EEXI regulation 25, so a propeller change is one route to a design-index reduction; and operational carbon intensity is regulation 28, so the same change improves the annual rating. Regulation 21 is Functional requirements - it is not EEDI. Attained EEDI is regulation 22.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem supplies an energy-efficiency framing and it can now be cited correctly. Using the pre-2021 numbering is a known error in circulating material.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How much efficiency does each of these devices gain?
retrieval_cards.answer: No figure should be quoted. Published gains are manufacturer-sourced and depend entirely on hull form, wake field, loading and operating profile, so a number quoted without those conditions is not defensible. Explain the mechanism instead and state that the gain is hull-specific.
retrieval_cards.why: An unverifiable quantity is omitted rather than given false precision, and an examiner is more impressed by a candidate who says why the number cannot be given.

blocks.h: (a) Design features adopted to comply with EEXI — 8 marks
1. Where EEXI sits in law, and what the printed Phase 2 framing refers to

blocks.p: EEXI is the technical half of the IMO short-term GHG measure, introduced by the 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI (resolution MEPC.328(76)), which was deemed accepted on 1 May 2022 and entered into force on 1 November 2022. Two regulations carry it:

ul: Regulation 23 — attained EEXI. The attained value is calculated for each ship in the listed categories, is specific to the ship, is accompanied by an EEXI technical file containing the information necessary for the calculation and showing the process of calculation, and is verified on the basis of that file by the Administration or an organisation duly authorised by it. Where the ship already has a verified attained EEDI at or below the required EEXI, that value may be taken as the attained EEXI.
Regulation 25 — required EEXI. The requirement is Attained EEXI ≤ Required EEXI = (1 − Y/100) × EEDI reference line value, where Y is the reduction factor in Table 3.

blocks.p: Compliance is assessed once, against the design, at the first annual, intermediate or renewal IAPP survey on or after 1 January 2023, and the outcome is recorded on the International Energy Efficiency Certificate. It is a design index, not a performance measurement: the calculation uses reference conditions, not the ship's actual trading.

One point of precision on the printed stem. Read at source, EEXI is not phased. Regulation 25 Table 3 sets a single fixed reduction factor per ship type and size band — 20 per cent for a bulk carrier or tanker between 20,000 and 200,000 DWT and 15 per cent above that; 30 per cent for a gas carrier, general cargo ship or LNG carrier; 20 to 50 per cent for containerships by size; 5 per cent for ro-ro ships. The phases — Phase 0, 1, 2 and 3 on dated windows — belong to the required EEDI in regulation 24 Table 1. The two are connected, which is why the phase language attaches itself to EEXI in practice: the EEXI factors were derived from the EEDI reference lines at broadly phase 2 stringency, and for most merchant ship types they land in the 20 to 30 per cent band the question names. So the figure in the stem is right; the phase label belongs to EEDI.

blocks.h: 2. The design measures that reduce the attained EEXI

blocks.p: The index is a ratio of CO2 emitted to transport work, so every measure either cuts the numerator or raises the denominator. Group them by where they act — a list organised by mechanism scores better than a list of product names.

ul: Hull. Low-friction and foul-release coatings reduce frictional resistance, which is the dominant component for most full-form ships. Where a major conversion is being done anyway, bulbous bow replacement to suit the ship's actual operating draught and speed, and fairing of appendages, are available.

Propeller. Retrofit or redesign to the ship's real operating point, larger diameter turning more slowly where the aperture allows it, tip-modified blades, and propeller boss cap fins to recover hub vortex energy.

Energy saving devices. Pre-swirl ducts, stators and wake-equalising fins ahead of the propeller; rudder bulbs and twisted rudders behind it. Each conditions the flow into or out of the disc and each must be designed for the specific hull — none is universally worthwhile.

Machinery and heat. Waste heat recovery from exhaust gas; shaft generators to remove auxiliary engines from the load; variable-frequency drives on pumps and fans; efficient turbochargers and engine tuning to the new operating point.
Air lubrication where the hull form suits it, reducing frictional resistance by a carpet of microbubbles under the flat of bottom.
Wind assistance — rotor sails, rigid wing sails and kites — which the EEDI/EEXI calculation methodology expressly recognises through an availability factor.

Fuel. Because the numerator is CO2 and not fuel mass, moving to a fuel with a lower carbon conversion factor — LNG, methanol, a biofuel blend — reduces the attained value directly for the same energy delivered.

blocks.h: 3. Power limitation - what most existing ships actually did

blocks.p: The honest answer to ‘what design features were adopted’ is that for the great majority of existing ships the compliance route was not a design change at all. The index is computed from a reference power, so capping that power reduces the attained EEXI arithmetically, immediately, and without a shipyard.

ul: EPL — engine power limitation. A mechanical stop or a software limit on the fuel index or governor setting, restricting the maximum power the main engine can develop.

ShaPoLi — shaft power limitation. The limit is imposed and monitored on the shaft rather than on the engine, using a torsion meter, which suits electronically controlled and shaft-generator installations.

In both cases the limit is sealed and verified, and is overridable so that full power remains available for the safety of the ship in adverse conditions — with the override, its reason and its duration recorded and reported.

blocks.p: Its attractions are obvious: it is by far the cheapest route, needs no drydocking, and can be arranged between voyages. Its drawbacks are equally real and are what an examiner is looking for:

ul: it caps sea speed, which is a commercial loss on trades where speed is sold;
it may conflict with charterparty speed and consumption warranties, so the limitation has to be disclosed and the description of the ship amended;
it reduces reserve power in heavy weather and, on some installations, the margin available for manoeuvring — which is precisely why the override exists;

and, most importantly, it improves the index without improving the ship. The vessel is no more efficient than she was; she is simply restrained. The regulation accepts that outcome deliberately, because the operational half of the measure is meant to pick up what the technical half cannot.

blocks.h: (b) The CII rating, AER and EEOI, and improving the rating — 8 marks

blocks.p: CII is regulation 28, the operational half. It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above in the cargo and passenger categories listed in the regulation. Where EEXI is assessed once against the design, CII is assessed every year against how the ship was actually run.

ul: Attained annual operational CII — calculated after the end of each calendar year over 1 January to 31 December, using the fuel oil consumption data already collected under regulation 27 (the IMO DCS, running since calendar year 2019), and reported to the Administration within three months of the year end.
Required annual operational CII — regulation 28.4: Required CII = (1 − Z/100) × CIIR, where CIIR is the reference value for the ship type on the 2019 reference line under the G2 guidelines.
Z, the annual reduction factor, is what makes the standard tighten. Under G3, resolution MEPC.338(76) Table 1, relative to the 2019 line:

rows: expressly not yet set — to be further strengthened and developed

blocks.p: Under regulation 28.6 the attained value is verified against the required value to give a rating of A, B, C, D or E — major superior, minor superior, moderate, minor inferior, inferior — and the middle point of rating level C is the required CII itself. The G4 guidelines place four boundaries around that midpoint, set on the 2019 fleet distribution so that the middle 30 per cent of a segment would have been C, the next 20 per cent either side B and D, and the outer 15 per cent either side A and E.

The consequences are in regulations 28.7 to 28.10. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E in any single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions; the SEEMP is reviewed to incorporate it and submitted for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained CII; and the ship must then duly undertake those actions. Administrations, port authorities and other stakeholders are encouraged to provide incentives to ships rated A or B. Note what the regulation does not do: there is no fine, no detention and no certificate withdrawn. The pressure is administrative, through the SEEMP, and commercial, through charterers, financiers and cargo owners who read the rating.

The position at this examination is worth stating. 2023 was the first calculation year and the attained value fell due for reporting by 31 March 2024, six months before this paper. The first CII ratings in the history of the measure have therefore already been assigned, and owners are now managing a real rating rather than an anticipated one. Regulation 28.11's review, due by 1 January 2026, had not reported at this sitting.

The G1 guidelines, resolution MEPC.352(78), draw the distinction the question is really about. A demand-based CII uses the actual mass or volume of cargo carried. A supply-based CII uses the ship's capacity as a proxy for cargo.

ul: AER — the Annual Efficiency Ratio — is the supply-based CII using deadweight as the capacity: total CO2 for the year divided by (capacity × total distance travelled). The variant using gross tonnage is cgDIST, applied to cruise passenger ships, ro-ro cargo ships including vehicle carriers, and ro-ro passenger ships.
EEOI — the Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator — is demand-based: CO2 per tonne of cargo actually carried per mile, as defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684.

blocks.p: Their regulatory status is not equal, and this is the discriminating fact. AER (or cgDIST) is the metric regulation 28 is satisfied by. EEOI is not a regulatory metric at all: G1 section 5 lists it, with EEPI, cbDIST and clDIST, among indicators encouraged to be used for trial purposes. A candidate who presents them as two official alternatives has not read the guideline.
The critical case against AER is real and should be made:

ul: It rewards distance, not cargo. A long ballast leg improves AER; days idle at anchor, burning fuel while travelling no distance, worsen it. Neither movement reflects transport efficiency.

It is blind to utilisation. Two identical ships, one full and one half empty, score identically if they burn the same fuel over the same distance — so the metric cannot reward the commercially efficient operator, and a truly efficient trade can be penalised.
It penalises short-sea and multi-port trades, where port time and manoeuvring are a large share of consumption and sea distance is small.

It can be gamed at the margin. Slow steaming with more ships lowers each ship's AER while the cargo moves no more efficiently overall — and, as with engine power limitation in limb (a), the index improves without the underlying efficiency improving.

blocks.p: The case for choosing it anyway is equally real, and stating it is what turns criticism into critical discussion. EEOI needs cargo mass data that the DCS does not collect, that is commercially confidential, that an Administration cannot verify in the way it verifies bunker and distance figures, and that is not comparable across trades — a car carrier, a container ship and a crude tanker cannot sensibly be ranked on tonne-miles. IMO therefore chose the metric that could be audited and enforced over the one that is conceptually correct. That trade-off — enforceability bought at the cost of validity — is the answer the examiner wants, and regulation 28.11's inclusion of the Z and CIIR values in its review is the Organization's own acknowledgement that the matter is not settled.

blocks.h: 6. Measures to improve the rating, administered through the SEEMP

blocks.p: Because AER is fuel over capacity-distance, there are only two levers: burn less, or travel further for it. Operational measures dominate because they are available now and cost little.

ul: Speed and voyage management. Consumption rises far faster than speed, so optimising speed to the required arrival time is the single largest lever. Just-in-time arrival converts waiting at anchor — which burns fuel and adds no distance — into a slower, cheaper passage.
Hull and propeller condition. In-water cleaning and propeller polishing scheduled against measured performance rather than against a calendar.
Trim, draught and ballast. Optimise trim against the ship's own trim tables or CFD-derived guidance, and carry no more ballast than is required.
Weather routeing to avoid added resistance, and autopilot tuning to reduce rudder-induced drag.

Auxiliary and port load. Shut down surplus generators, use the shaft generator, run pumps and fans on variable-frequency drives, manage cargo heating and inert gas use, control accommodation load, and take shore power where it is available.
Technical retrofit and fuel — the same measures as limb (a), which is the point at which the two halves of the measure meet: a device fitted for EEXI also improves the attained CII.
Data quality. The attained CII is only as good as the reported fuel and distance, so flowmeter calibration, consistent bunker figures and correct noon-report distances change the rating directly.

G5 voyage adjustments and correction factors, resolution MEPC.355(78), for defined cases such as ice conditions and ship-to-ship operations — used within their own stated limit, that their use should in no way undermine the goal of reducing carbon intensity.

blocks.p: All of it is administered through the SEEMP. Under regulation 26.3.1 an affected ship's SEEMP had to contain, on or before 1 January 2023, the CII calculation methodology and reporting process, the required CII for the next three years, an implementation plan documenting how it will be achieved, and a procedure for self-evaluation and improvement — and the SEEMP is subject to verification and company audit. Where a ship is rated D for three consecutive years or E, the corrective action plan goes into that same document. The examiner expects the measures above to live in the SEEMP, not in a loose list.

The marks are 8 + 8 and the commonest failure on this question is arithmetic, not knowledge: candidates know more about CII than about EEXI, so limb (b) grows and limb (a) shrinks, and half the paper is lost in a limb that could only ever have earned eight marks. Give each limb equal paper. Three sections each is a workable discipline.

Inside limb (b) there are three printed demands, not one — the concept of the rating, the critical comparison of AER and EEOI, and the improvement measures. Eight marks across three demands means the improvement measures are a short organised list, not an essay. Organise them by mechanism (speed, condition, trim, weather, auxiliary load, retrofit, data, adjustments) and finish by placing them in the SEEMP, which is the sentence that shows you know where the regulation puts them.

blocks.h: The single idea that ties both limbs together

blocks.p: Both halves of this measure share one weakness, and a candidate who names it is answering at Class I level rather than reciting. Engine power limitation improves the EEXI without making the ship more efficient. Slow steaming with more ships improves AER without making the trade more efficient. In each case the index moves and the reality does not. That is not an accident and it is not a scandal: it is the price of choosing measures that can be calculated from data an Administration can verify. Say it once in limb (a) and refer back to it in limb (b), and the whole answer reads as an argument rather than as two lists.

blocks.h: EEXI and CII — keep the two halves apart

rows: What the ship did, from reported data
Ships of 5,000 GT and above in the listed categories
(1 − Y/100) × EEDI reference line, Y fixed per ship type
(1 − Z/100) × CII<sub>R</sub>, Z tightening every year
Pass, recorded on the IEE Certificate
D three years or E → corrective action plan in the SEEMP

blocks.p: A ship can pass EEXI comfortably and still be rated E. A certificate about design says nothing about how she was traded, and saying so out loud is worth a mark.

blocks.h: The numbering trap — this one has bitten a solved paper in this corpus

blocks.p: The 2021 revised Annex VI renumbered chapter 4 when it entered into force on 1 November 2022. Read off the annex itself: 21 functional requirements, 22 attained EEDI, 23 attained EEXI, 24 required EEDI, 25 required EEXI, 26 SEEMP, 27 fuel oil consumption data, 28 operational carbon intensity.

The pre-2021 scheme ran reg 20 attained EEDI, reg 21 required EEDI, reg 22 SEEMP, and it is still circulating in notes and in older worked answers. Writing ‘regulation 21 (EEDI)’ or ‘regulation 22 (SEEMP)’ is the tell that a candidate is working from superseded material, and an examiner who has read the Annex will see it immediately. Learn the four that matter as a block: 23 attained EEXI, 25 required EEXI, 26 SEEMP, 28 CII.

ul: Letting limb (b) swallow the answer. The marks are 8 + 8.
Listing only physical retrofits in limb (a) and never mentioning engine or shaft power limitation, which is how most of the existing fleet actually complied.
Using the pre-2021 regulation numbers. Regulation 21 is functional requirements, not EEDI.
Treating EEXI as phased without qualification. The phases belong to the required EEDI; EEXI has a single fixed factor per ship type and size band.
Presenting EEOI as a regulatory metric. It is encouraged for trial purposes only.
Explaining how AER is calculated instead of criticising it. The stem says critically.
Inventing a penalty for a poor CII rating. There is no fine, no detention and no certificate withdrawn.
Quoting percentage savings for coatings, devices or air lubrication. Published figures are vendor-sourced and hull-specific.
Quoting a numeric rating boundary from the G4 tables. They are ship-type specific and cannot be recalled reliably.
Importing anything from MEPC 83, the IMO Net-Zero Framework or the GFI. None of it existed at this sitting.

blocks.p: ‘Your ship is rated D for the third year running. What must you do, and what happens if you do not?’ Develop a plan of corrective actions under regulation 28.7; have the SEEMP reviewed to include it and submitted for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained CII, under 28.8; and duly undertake the actions under 28.9. What happens if you do not is a flag State non-conformity and a commercial problem — not a fine, and not detention. Candidates routinely invent a penalty.

‘How did your last ship comply with EEXI?’ The expected answer names EPL or ShaPoLi and then says how the override works and where it is recorded. An answer that describes a bulbous bow replacement is describing the exception.
‘Which is the better metric, AER or EEOI?’ EEOI is the better measure of transport efficiency and AER is the better regulatory instrument, and the reason is verifiability. Say both halves.
‘What is the Z factor this year?’ For calendar year 2024, 7 per cent relative to the 2019 reference line. The series runs 5, 7, 9, 11 for 2023 to 2026, and 2027 onwards is expressly not yet set.
‘Where does the middle of band C sit?’ Exactly at the required annual operational CII. That is regulation 28.6 and it is the sentence that shows the rating is a comparison, not a measurement.

ul: Which regulation is attained EEXI, and which is required EEXI? 23 and 25.
What document supports the attained EEXI, and who verifies it? The EEXI technical file, verified by the Administration or an organisation duly authorised by it.

What is EPL, what is ShaPoLi, and why must the limit be overridable? A limit on engine power and on shaft power respectively; overridable so full power remains available for the safety of the ship in adverse conditions, with the override recorded.
From what year is the attained CII calculated, and by when is it reported? Calendar year 2023 onwards; within three months of the year end.
What is the CII formula? Required CII = (1 - Z/100) times the reference value CII-R.
What are the five ratings and where does C sit? A to E - major superior to inferior - with the middle point of C equal to the required CII.
What is AER, and what does cgDIST use instead of deadweight? CO2 over capacity times distance, capacity being deadweight; cgDIST uses gross tonnage.
Is EEOI mandatory? No - it is encouraged for trial purposes under G1 section 5, and is defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684.
Which regulation requires the SEEMP to carry the required CII for the next three years? Regulation 26.3.1, on or before 1 January 2023.
When is the review of the CII regulation due? By 1 January 2026, under regulation 28.11 - and it had not reported at this sitting.

blocks.p: DESIGN ONCE, OPERATE EVERY YEAR. Limb (a) is the ship as built: law, measures, power limit. Limb (b) is the ship as run: mechanism, metrics, measures. Three and three.

Two number strings carry most of the recall. For the regulations: 23, 25, 26, 28 — attained EEXI, required EEXI, SEEMP, CII. For the reduction factor: 5, 7, 9, 11 — odd numbers climbing by two from 2023, and this paper sits in the 7 year. For the rating bands, the 2019 distribution reads outward from the middle: 30 in C, 20 either side, 15 at each end.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, currency and the one boundary this paper cannot resolve

blocks.p: The regulatory content of this answer is unusually well supported: the Annex and the guidelines were read at source. Regulations 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 and 28 were read in full, with Tables 1 and 3; the Z factors come from G3 Table 1; the AER, cgDIST and EEOI definitions and EEOI's trial-purpose status come from G1 sections 2.4, 2.5 and 5; and the five-band rating structure comes from G4 section 3. Every regulation number above is read rather than recalled.

One boundary cannot be resolved, and it is declared rather than guessed. The 2024 SEEMP Guidelines, resolution MEPC.395(82), were adopted on 4 October 2024 — at the close of MEPC 82, which sat from 30 September — and their operative paragraph 5 revokes the 2022 Guidelines, MEPC.346(78). This examination was sat in October 2024 and no source establishes the day. It is therefore not possible to say which edition of the SEEMP Guidelines was operative on the examination date. This answer is deliberately anchored on regulation 26 itself, which has been in force since 1 November 2022 and is edition-independent, and names the guideline chain with the revocation date stated. No proposition in this answer depends on which side of 4 October the sitting fell, and a candidate who can explain why that boundary matters has understood the difference between a regulation and a guideline.

Three things are deliberately absent. No numeric rating boundary from the G4 tables and no reference-line coefficient from G2, because they are ship-type specific and quoting one wrongly is worse than naming the guideline that carries them. No percentage saving for any design measure, because published gains are vendor-sourced and depend entirely on hull form, wake field and operating profile. And no claim about the distribution of ratings actually assigned for 2023 — that the first ratings had been assigned by this sitting follows from the regulation 28.2 reporting deadline of 31 March 2024, but what those ratings were was not established.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two equally weighted limbs on the two halves of the short-term measure, and they are not the same kind of question. Limb (a) is TECHNICAL: what does a shipowner actually DO to an existing ship to bring her attained EEXI below the required value. Limb (b) is REGULATORY AND CRITICAL: explain the CII rating, critically discuss AER and EEOI as measuring metrics, and say what the vessel must do to improve. The word 'critically' in limb (b) is the instruction that decides the marks - the examiner wants the case against the chosen metric, not a recital of how it is calculated.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16 printed as 8 + 8, reconciling exactly. Equal weight, so equal paper. Within limb (b) the three demands - the concept of the rating, the critical comparison of AER and EEOI, and the improvement measures - split the eight marks roughly evenly, which means the improvement measures must be a SHORT ORGANISED LIST rather than an essay. The commonest failure is to let limb (b) become the whole answer because the candidate knows more about CII.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That a management-level candidate knows the difference between the technical and operational halves of the measure; knows that most existing ships met EEXI by LIMITING POWER rather than by rebuilding, and can say why that is acceptable to the regulation and awkward on board; and can make the AER-versus-EEOI argument properly - that IMO chose the auditable metric over the conceptually correct one, and that this is a deliberate trade-off rather than an oversight.
primary_source_plan: Read the chapter 4 regulation list off the annex itself before writing any regulation number, because a solved paper in this corpus carries the pre-2021 numbering.
Read regulation 25 and Table 3 at source to establish that the EEXI reduction factor is a single fixed value, so the printed 'Phase 2' framing can be explained rather than repeated.
Read G1 sections 2.4, 2.5 and 5 at source, because the whole critical comparison turns on EEOI being a trial-purpose metric.
Establish the SEEMP guideline boundary before writing the improvement limb, and anchor that limb on regulation 26 rather than on a guideline edition.
Quote no percentage saving for any design measure and no numeric rating boundary.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: HIGH - This is the most actively moving area in the whole syllabus. The risks run in both directions: forward, from the April 2025 Net-Zero Framework and everything after it, which must not appear; and backward, from the January 2024 donor, whose statement that no ship had yet been rated is false here.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The question is international and sets no Indian limb. Flag State implementation varies in detail but nothing in the answer depends on any one administration.
technical_ambiguities: The printed stem says 'the EEXI framework under Phase 2 (of 20% - 30% reduction)'. Read at source, EEXI is NOT phased - regulation 25 Table 3 sets a single fixed factor per ship type and size band, and the phases belong to the required EEDI in regulation 24 Table 1. The printed wording is preserved and the position explained; the question is not corrected away.

'Design features adopted in the existing vessels to comply' could mean physical modification only. In practice the dominant compliance route was power limitation, which is a certificated operational restriction rather than a design change, and an answer that omits it has missed what actually happened.
'Measuring metrics of AER and EEOI' invites two definitions. The command is 'critically discuss', which requires the comparison and the trade-off.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Six steps in two labelled limbs. Limb (a): one step placing EEXI in law and disposing of the phase framing, one on the design measures proper, one on power limitation as the dominant route with its trade-offs. Limb (b): one on the CII mechanism and the rating, one on AER versus EEOI as the critical comparison, one on the improvement measures organised under the SEEMP.

steps.title: Where EEXI sits in law, and what the printed Phase 2 framing refers to
points: the 2021 revised Annex VI, MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022
regulation 23 attained EEXI, with the EEXI technical file, verified by or for the Administration
regulation 25 required EEXI - attained EEXI <= (1 - Y/100) x EEDI reference line value
Y is a single fixed factor per ship type and size band in Table 3, typically 15 to 30 per cent
EEXI is NOT phased - the phases belong to the required EEDI in regulation 24 Table 1
compliance assessed once against the design, at the first annual, intermediate or renewal survey after 1 January 2023

steps.title: The design measures that reduce the attained EEXI
points: the index is a ratio of CO2 emitted to transport work, so cut the numerator or raise the denominator
hull - low-friction and foul-release coatings, hull form refinement where a conversion allows it
propeller - retrofit or redesign, boss cap fins, larger diameter at lower revolutions
energy saving devices - pre-swirl ducts and stators, rudder bulbs, wake-equalising fins
waste heat recovery, shaft generators and air lubrication where the ship suits them
wind assistance - rotor sails and rigid wings - recognised in the calculation methodology
fuel with a lower carbon factor, since the numerator is CO2 and not fuel mass

steps.title: Power limitation - what most existing ships actually did
points: the index uses a reference power, so limiting that power reduces the attained EEXI directly
EPL - engine power limitation, a mechanical or software stop on the fuel index
ShaPoLi - shaft power limitation, monitored at the shaft
an overridable limit, sealed, with recording, for use in adverse conditions and for safety
it is the cheapest route and requires no shipyard time - hence its dominance
but it caps sea speed, may erode charter warranties and cuts margin in heavy weather
and it improves the index without improving the ship - a criticism the regulation accepts

steps.title: The CII rating - the mechanism
points: regulation 28, the operational half; ships of 5,000 GT and above in the listed categories
attained annual operational CII from 1 January to 31 December using regulation 27 DCS data
reported to the Administration within three months of the year end
required CII = (1 - Z/100) x CIIR, CIIR being the 2019 reference line value under G2
Z under G3 - 5 per cent 2023, 7 per cent 2024, 9 per cent 2025, 11 per cent 2026
rating A to E under G4, the middle point of band C being the required CII itself
bands set on the 2019 distribution - 15, 20, 30, 20, 15 per cent across A to E
at this sitting the first ratings, for calendar year 2023, have already been assigned

steps.title: AER and EEOI critically compared
points: G1 distinguishes demand-based from supply-based indicators
AER is the supply-based CII using DWT as capacity; cgDIST uses GT
EEOI is demand-based - CO2 per tonne of cargo actually carried per mile
AER is the regulatory metric; EEOI is encouraged for TRIAL PURPOSES only
the case against AER - it rewards distance not cargo, and is blind to utilisation
ballast legs and idle days at anchor both worsen it; short-sea trades are penalised
the case for AER - every input is already reported, auditable and comparable
EEOI needs cargo mass that DCS does not collect, is commercially confidential and is not comparable across trades
IMO chose enforceability over validity, and regulation 28.11's review acknowledges it is not settled

steps.title: Measures to improve the rating, administered through the SEEMP
points: speed and voyage management - consumption rises far faster than speed
just-in-time arrival converts waiting at anchor into a slower, cheaper passage
hull and propeller condition managed against measured performance, not a calendar
trim and draught optimisation; carry no more ballast than is needed
weather routeing and autopilot tuning; shut down surplus auxiliary load; shore power
technical retrofit and lower-carbon fuel, as in limb (a)
data quality - flowmeter calibration and correct noon distances change the rating directly
G5 voyage adjustments and correction factors, whose own limit is that they must not undermine the goal
all of it lives in the SEEMP under regulation 26.3, and a D-for-three-years or E ship must add a corrective action plan

quick_revision.recall_15s: Two halves of one measure. (a) EEXI — technical, assessed once against the design. Reg 23 attained, reg 25 required, attained ≤ (1 − Y/100) × EEDI reference line, Y a fixed factor per ship type. Comply by hull, propeller, energy saving devices, waste heat, wind, fuel — or, as most ships did, by LIMITING POWER (EPL / ShaPoLi). (b) CII — operational, every year. Reg 28: attained from DCS data; required = (1 − Z/100) × CIIR, Z = 7 per cent for 2024; rating A to E, middle of C is the required value; D three years running or E triggers a corrective action plan in the SEEMP. AER is the regulatory metric; EEOI is trial-purpose only.

EEXI reduction factor Y: a single fixed value per ship type and size band, typically 15 to 30 per cent - NOT a phased scheme
CII reduction factor Z relative to the 2019 reference line: 2023 5%, 2024 7%, 2025 9%, 2026 11%; 2027-2030 not yet set
CII applies to ships of 5,000 GT and above; DCS data collected since calendar year 2019
Attained CII reported within three months of the year end; revised SEEMP within one month of that report

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI, 2021 revised (MEPC.328(76)), in force 1 November 2022. Reg 23 attained EEXI, reg 25 required EEXI, reg 26 SEEMP, reg 27 fuel oil consumption data, reg 28 operational CII. Regulation 21 is Functional requirements — it is NOT EEDI; attained EEDI is regulation 22. Using the pre-2021 numbering is a known and recurring error.
quick_revision.major_trap: Two. First, letting limb (b) swallow the answer — the marks are 8 + 8 and the EEXI limb is worth exactly as much as the CII limb. Second, reciting how AER is calculated instead of criticising it. The stem says critically discuss: the marks are in the argument that AER rewards distance rather than cargo, that EEOI is not the regulatory metric at all but a trial-purpose one, and that IMO deliberately chose the auditable measure over the conceptually correct one.

questions.memory_cue: DESIGN ONCE, OPERATE EVERY YEAR. Limb (a) is the ship as built — law, measures, power limit (1, 2, 3). Limb (b) is the ship as run — mechanism, metrics, measures (4, 5, 6). For the CII arithmetic hold one line: attained from DCS, required = reference line less Z, rated A to E about the middle of C. For Z hold the odd numbers climbing by two from five: 5, 7, 9, 11 for 2023 to 2026, and this paper sits in the 7 year.
questions.understand_first:
The short-term measure is one policy with two halves, and almost every mark on this question comes from keeping them apart. EEXI is technical and it is assessed once: it asks what the ship is, on paper, against a reference line derived from ships built years ago. CII is operational and it is assessed every year: it asks what the ship actually did last year, and the target moves every January. A ship can pass EEXI comfortably and still be rated E, because a certificate about design says nothing about how she was traded.

The second thing to see is why most owners complied with EEXI by limiting power. The index uses a reference power in its numerator, so capping that power reduces the attained value arithmetically, immediately, and for the price of an engine-shop visit rather than a drydocking. It is a lawful and expressly contemplated route — and it makes the index better without making the ship more efficient. Once you have said that out loud, the criticism of AER in limb (b) is the same criticism wearing different clothes: a metric that can be improved without improving anything real is the recurring weakness of this whole regime, and a candidate who joins those two observations is answering at Class I level.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the EEXI and CII question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 Where EEXI sits in law and what the Phase 2 framing refers to. 2 The design measures that reduce the attained EEXI. 3 Power limitation - what most ships actually did. (b) 4 The CII rating mechanism. 5 AER and EEOI critically compared. 6 Measures to improve the rating, administered through the SEEMP.
retrieval_cards.why: Three steps per limb keeps the 8 + 8 split honest. The commonest failure is to write four sections on CII because the candidate knows more about it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the chapter 4 regulation numbers of the 2021 revised MARPOL Annex VI.
retrieval_cards.answer: 21 functional requirements; 22 attained EEDI; 23 attained EEXI; 24 required EEDI; 25 required EEXI; 26 SEEMP; 27 collection and reporting of fuel oil consumption data; 28 operational carbon intensity.
retrieval_cards.why: Regulation 21 is functional requirements, not EEDI. The pre-2021 scheme - reg 20 attained EEDI, 21 required EEDI, 22 SEEMP - was superseded when the revised Annex entered into force on 1 November 2022, and it still appears in circulating notes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is EEXI phased, like EEDI?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Regulation 25 Table 3 sets a single fixed reduction factor Y per ship type and size band - typically 15 to 30 per cent, and up to 50 per cent for the largest containerships. The phases - Phase 0, 1, 2 and 3 on dated windows - belong to the required EEDI in regulation 24 Table 1. The EEXI factors are derived from the EEDI reference lines, which is why the phase language attaches itself to EEXI in conversation.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed stem uses phase language for EEXI. Explaining the position accurately, without contradicting the question, is what a Class I answer does with a loosely worded stem.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How did most existing ships comply with EEXI, and what are the drawbacks?
retrieval_cards.answer: By limiting power - engine power limitation (EPL), a mechanical or software limit on the fuel index, or shaft power limitation (ShaPoLi) monitored at the shaft. The limit is sealed and overridable for safety in adverse conditions, with the override recorded. It is cheap and needs no shipyard time. The drawbacks: it caps sea speed, it may conflict with charterparty speed and performance warranties, it reduces reserve power in heavy weather, and it improves the index without improving the ship.
retrieval_cards.why: An answer that lists only physical retrofits has described what was theoretically available rather than what the fleet actually did.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the CII reduction factor Z for 2023 to 2026, and which applies at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.answer: Relative to the 2019 reference line: 2023 5 per cent, 2024 7 per cent, 2025 9 per cent, 2026 11 per cent. Factors for 2027 to 2030 are expressly not yet set. This paper sits in calendar year 2024, so 7 per cent applies.
retrieval_cards.why: From G3, resolution MEPC.338(76), Table 1. The numbers climb by two from five, which makes them easy to hold, and the reason a ship's rating decays on unchanged operation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between AER and EEOI, and which one does regulation 28 use?
retrieval_cards.answer: AER is a supply-based indicator: CO2 divided by the ship's capacity in deadweight times distance travelled - capacity is used as a proxy for cargo. EEOI is demand-based: CO2 per tonne of cargo actually carried per mile. Regulation 28 uses the supply-based indicator, AER for most cargo ship types and cgDIST where gross tonnage is the capacity. EEOI is not a regulatory metric at all - G1 section 5 lists it among indicators encouraged for trial purposes, defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the discriminating fact in the whole limb. A candidate who thinks EEOI is one of two official metrics has not read the guideline.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Make the critical case against AER in three lines.
retrieval_cards.answer: It rewards distance, not cargo: a long ballast leg improves it and days idle at anchor worsen it, neither of which reflects transport efficiency. It is blind to utilisation: two identical ships, one full and one half empty, score the same if they burn the same fuel over the same distance. And it penalises short-sea and multi-port trades, where port and manoeuvring consumption is large and sea distance is small.
retrieval_cards.why: The command is critically discuss. Three specific failure modes score; a general remark that the metric is imperfect does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did IMO choose AER anyway?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it is auditable and comparable. Every input - fuel consumed and distance run - is already collected and verified under the regulation 27 data collection system. EEOI needs cargo mass, which DCS does not collect, which is commercially confidential, which an Administration cannot verify in the same way, and which is not comparable between a car carrier, a container ship and a crude tanker. Enforceability was bought at the cost of validity, and regulation 28.11 puts the Z and CIIR values into the review due by 1 January 2026.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the trade-off, rather than just the fault, is what turns a criticism into a critical discussion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a ship rated D three years running, or E in one year?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under regulation 28.7 she must develop a plan of corrective actions to achieve the required CII; under regulation 28.8 the SEEMP is reviewed to include it and submitted to the Administration for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained CII; and under regulation 28.9 the ship must duly undertake those actions. There is no fine, no detention and no certificate withdrawn - the pressure is administrative and commercial. Regulation 28.10 encourages incentives for A and B.
retrieval_cards.why: The teeth of the regime are in the SEEMP and in the charter market, not in enforcement. Candidates commonly invent a penalty that does not exist.

reverify_before_publication.why: It follows from regulation 28.1 and 28.2 read at source - calendar year 2023 was the first calculation year and the attained value fell due within three months of the year end, i.e. by 31 March 2024, six months before this sitting.
