blocks.h: (a) ‘General average is based on certain essential features’ — 8 marks
1. What a general average act is, and how the Rules apply

blocks.p: The statement in the question is correct, and the features are not a matter of opinion: they are drawn from the definition itself. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules provides that there is a general average act ‘when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure’.

Note first how the Rules apply, because it is a point candidates routinely get wrong. They are not law. They take effect by incorporation into the contract of carriage — the bill of lading or the charterparty — and the Rule of Interpretation then makes them apply ‘to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith’. It follows that the version which governs any given adventure is the version the contract incorporates, which need not be the latest. In India the concept is separately recognised by statute, in the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 — not the English Act of 1906.

blocks.h: 2. The essential features, drawn out of Rule A

blocks.p: Every phrase of Rule A is doing work, and each yields one essential feature. Present them that way and the list is defensible rather than remembered:

ol: Extraordinary. The sacrifice or expenditure must be outside the ordinary performance of the contract of carriage. Fuel burned on a normal passage, or wear on machinery in ordinary service, is not extraordinary however costly.

Intentional and voluntary. The loss must be deliberately incurred. Cargo washed overboard by a sea is accidental and lies where it falls; cargo jettisoned by decision is a sacrifice. This is the single feature that most sharply separates general from particular average, and it is the one limb (b) turns on.
Reasonable. Reinforced by the Rule Paramount, which overrides everything else: ‘In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.’
Peril. There must be real danger — not necessarily immediate, but genuine and substantial, and more than the ordinary risk of the sea.

Common safety of a common adventure. The act must benefit the whole adventure, not one interest alone, and there must be more than one interest at risk. A ship in ballast with no cargo on board has no common adventure and can have no general average.
Preservation of property. The purpose must be to preserve the property from that peril, and success matters: there must be something saved to contribute.

blocks.h: 3. The lettered rules that qualify the definition

ul: Rule C — only losses which are the direct consequence of the general average act are allowed. It expressly excludes demurrage, loss of market, loss caused by delay whether on the voyage or subsequently, and any indirect loss whatsoever, and excludes damage to the environment and loss in consequence of the escape or release of pollutant substances.

Rule D — rights to contribution are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties to the adventure, without prejudice to any remedies or defences open in respect of that fault. So the adjustment proceeds first, and blame is fought separately.

Rule E — the onus of proof is on the party claiming, who must give notice in writing to the average adjuster and supply particulars of value, with a twelve-month period after which the adjuster may estimate.

blocks.h: 4. How the loss is shared, and what general average is not

blocks.p: Under Rule A.2 the sacrifice is borne by the different contributing interests — ship, cargo and freight at risk — rateably in proportion to their values at the termination of the adventure. The adjustment is prepared by an average adjuster, and security is taken before cargo is released: normally an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter.
Two distinctions complete the picture and are worth a mark each:

ul: General average is not particular average. Particular average is accidental damage; it falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared.

General average is not insurance. It is a rule of contribution between the parties to the adventure, which predates marine insurance entirely — though in practice the contribution is recoverable under the policy.

blocks.h: (b) The refloating scenario — can the burnt bearings be included? — 8 marks
5. The rule written for exactly these facts

blocks.p: This situation is dealt with expressly, by a rule written for precisely these circumstances. Rule VII, ‘Damage to Machinery and Boilers’, provides:

‘Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.’
Rule VII is materially unchanged from the 1994 and 2004 texts, so the answer is the same whichever version the contract of carriage incorporates.

blocks.h: 6. Applying it - the four conditions, the one that decides it, and the converse

blocks.p: Yes, the burnt bearings can be allowed in general average — provided four things are shown.

ol: The ship was ashore. She was aground, so the first condition is met on the facts given.

She was in a position of peril. This must be established, not assumed — and the question does not say it. A vessel lying safely aground on soft mud in fine weather, in no danger and simply awaiting the tide, is not in peril; one working on a hard bottom, or exposed to weather, tide, swell or the risk of breaking her back, is. This is the condition on which the claim will actually turn, and an answer that does not identify it has missed what the examiner left out on purpose.

The machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety. Running the main engine ahead and astern to shake her off the ground is precisely that — a deliberate act directed at the safety of the whole adventure, not a routine manoeuvre.

The damage arose at the risk of such damage. The master must have accepted the risk of damaging the engine as the price of refloating. That acceptance is real and identifiable, because the engineering risk is well known: working an engine hard ahead and astern against a grounded hull applies sustained high torque at low or zero shaft speed with repeated reversals, so the hydrodynamic oil film in the main and crankpin bearings is degraded exactly when the load is highest — and if the sea suctions are silted, cooling is impaired at the same time. It is that knowing acceptance of a foreseeable risk that makes the loss a sacrifice rather than an accident.

blocks.p: The damage then satisfies Rule A as well: it is extraordinary (not ordinary service), intentional (the engine was deliberately worked in a way likely to damage it), reasonable if refloating was a sensible response to the situation, and directed at the common safety. It is also the direct consequence of the act, as Rule C requires. And under Rule D it makes no difference to the right of contribution that the grounding may have been somebody's fault — that is dealt with separately.

The converse must be stated, because it is the trap. Rule VII closes with an absolute prohibition: where the ship is afloat, damage from working the propelling machinery is ‘in no circumstances’ allowed. So if she had already come off and the bearings burnt while manoeuvring clear, or if she were merely touching the bottom and not in peril, the same physical damage would be particular average — the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo. The engine damage is identical; the legal answer is opposite; and what decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

The marks are 8 + 8 and the temptation is to spend twelve of them on limb (a), because the doctrine is comfortable and the scenario is not. Resist it. Limb (b) is not a one-word answer: it is a four-condition analysis, an identification of the condition the examiner deliberately left out, and the converse case, and that is a full eight marks of writing.

In limb (a), present the essential features as phrases of Rule A rather than as a remembered list. It takes no longer, it is far easier to reconstruct under pressure, and it answers the printed statement directly — the features are ‘essential’ precisely because the definition says ‘when, and only when’.

blocks.h: The one thing the examiner has deliberately left out

blocks.p: Read the facts again: ‘A large vessel ran aground.’ That is all. It does not say she was in danger. Rule VII requires the ship to be ashore AND in a position of peril, and those are two conditions, not one.

So the correct answer is a qualified yes, and the qualification is where the marks are. A ship lying safely on soft mud in fine weather, waiting for the tide with tugs ordered, is aground but is not in peril; if her master works the engine and burns the bearings, that is his own particular average. A ship pounding on a hard bottom with a swell running, or one whose hull is taking the ground unevenly with the tide falling, plainly is. Say which facts you would need and why, and the justification the stem asks for writes itself.

blocks.h: Sacrifice or accident - the question underneath both limbs

blocks.p: The whole of general average turns on one distinction, and this paper tests it twice. In limb (a) it is the second essential feature. In limb (b) it is the entire analysis. Physically identical damage is a sacrifice or an accident depending on the circumstances and the intention — and Rule VII makes the point unusually cleanly, because it gives both answers in one sentence: allowed when she is ashore and in peril and the engine is worked knowing it may be damaged; never allowed when she is afloat.

If you can articulate that in the examination room, you can answer any general average scenario, including the ones this paper does not set — jettison, voluntary stranding, damage in extinguishing fire, port of refuge expenses.

ul: Answering limb (b) with a flat yes and no conditions.
Assuming peril because the ship went aground. Aground is not the same as in peril, and the question does not say.
Describing the York-Antwerp Rules as law or as an IMO convention. They bind by contractual incorporation.
Citing the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 in an Indian examination. The Indian statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Forgetting the converse in Rule VII — afloat, and it is in no circumstances allowed.
Saying the claim fails because the grounding was the master's fault. Rule D says otherwise.
Listing the essential features from memory rather than deriving them from Rule A, which is what the printed statement invites.
Confusing general average with particular average, or treating general average as a species of insurance.
Forgetting that something must be saved. If the adventure is a total loss there is nothing to contribute.
Letting limb (a) grow to twelve marks' worth of paper.

blocks.p: ‘She came off the ground and the bearings burnt ten minutes later. Same answer?’ The opposite answer. Rule VII: where the ship is afloat, no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery is in any circumstances allowed. This is the single best follow-up in the topic because it isolates the legal variable from the engineering one.

‘Was she in peril?’ The correct response is to say what would decide it — nature of the bottom, state of weather and swell, state of tide, hull stresses, whether she was working, whether assistance was available. Do not simply assert it.

‘The grounding was a navigational error by the master. Does the claim fail?’ No. Rule D preserves the right to contribution notwithstanding the fault of a party, without prejudice to remedies and defences in respect of that fault. Cargo interests may have a separate claim; that is a different fight.

‘Who pays, and how do you get the cargo released?’ Ship, cargo and freight at risk contribute rateably on values at the termination of the adventure; an average adjuster prepares the adjustment; and security is taken before release — an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter.

‘Which version of the Rules applies to your ship?’ Whichever the bill of lading or charterparty incorporates. On Rule VII it does not matter: the 1994, 2004 and 2016 texts are materially identical on this point.

ul: State Rule A. There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
Are the York-Antwerp Rules law? No - they apply by incorporation into the contract of carriage.
Which Indian Act recognises general average? The Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
What does the Rule Paramount say? No allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.
Name three things Rule C excludes. Demurrage, loss of market, and any loss by reason of delay or any indirect loss - and environmental damage and pollutant escape.
Who bears the onus of proof? The party claiming in general average, under Rule E.
Which rule governs machinery damage in refloating? Rule VII.
Name the four conditions in Rule VII. Ashore; in a position of peril; an actual intention to float her for the common safety; at the risk of such damage.
What happens if she is afloat? No such damage is in any circumstances allowed as general average.
Give an example of a general average sacrifice other than machinery damage. Jettison of cargo, voluntary stranding, damage done in extinguishing a fire, or expenses at a port of refuge.

blocks.p: Limb (a): Rule A taken apart, then C, D, E, then who pays. The six essential features are the six phrases of one sentence, so learn the sentence and the features come out of it: EXTRAORDINARY — INTENTIONAL — REASONABLE — PERIL — COMMON — PRESERVED.
Limb (b): four words in order, then the sting. ASHORE — PERIL — INTENTION — RISK, and then AFLOAT — NEVER. Five items, and they carry the whole of Rule VII including its converse.

Two limitations are declared rather than disguised. First, MIW does not hold the Indian Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It is named, as an Indian marine insurance answer must name it in preference to the English Act of 1906, but no section number is asserted anywhere and nothing in the analysis depends on the statute — the whole of it runs on the Rules. Second, the statement that Rule VII is materially identical in the 1994 and 2004 texts rests on published versions of those texts rather than on a line-by-line collation. That matters because the Rules apply by contractual incorporation and an older version may govern the adventure in front of you.

The temporal position was re-checked in both directions for this sitting and is nil. General average is among the most stable doctrines in maritime law: the 2016 Rules were the current CMI text throughout 2024, no revision fell in the window, and no Indian statutory change touched the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. Finally, the engineering explanation of why the bearings burn is given to show that the risk was foreseeable and therefore capable of being knowingly accepted; it supports the legal analysis rather than deciding it, and no bearing load or torque figure is quoted, because both are entirely installation-specific.

Limb (b) is APPLIED: a short set of facts, a yes-or-no question, and an express demand for justification. The examiner is testing whether the candidate can find the rule that governs and then apply it to the facts given, including the facts that are NOT given.

for the purpose of preserving from peril the property in a common maritime adventure
the Rules are NOT law - they apply by incorporation into the bill of lading or charterparty
the Rule of Interpretation then excludes any inconsistent law and practice
in India the concept is also recognised by the Marine Insurance Act, 1963

steps.title: The essential features, drawn out of Rule A
points: extraordinary - outside the ordinary performance of the contract of carriage
intentional and voluntary - a sacrifice, not an accident; this is the sharpest divider
reasonable - reinforced by the Rule Paramount, which overrides everything else
real and substantial peril, more than the ordinary risk of the sea
for the common safety of a common adventure - more than one interest must be at risk
preservation of property - something must be saved to contribute

steps.title: The lettered rules that qualify the definition
points: Rule C - only the direct consequence of the act is allowed
demurrage, loss of market, loss by delay and any indirect loss whatsoever excluded
environmental damage and the escape or release of pollutants excluded
Rule D - fault does not affect the right to contribution
so the adjustment proceeds first and blame is fought separately
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the claimant; written notice and particulars to the adjuster

steps.title: How the loss is shared, and what general average is not
points: Rule A.2 - borne by the contributing interests: ship, cargo and freight at risk
rateably in proportion to values at the termination of the adventure
an average adjuster prepares the adjustment
security before cargo is released - average bond from the receiver, guarantee from the underwriter
not particular average - accidental damage lies where it falls and is not shared
not insurance - a rule of contribution between the parties, older than marine insurance

steps.title: The rule written for exactly these facts
points: Rule VII, Damage to Machinery and Boilers, is directly in point
damage to machinery and boilers of a ship ASHORE and IN A POSITION OF PERIL
in endeavouring to refloat
shown to have arisen from an ACTUAL INTENTION to float her for the common safety
AT THE RISK OF SUCH DAMAGE
but where the ship is AFLOAT, such damage is in no circumstances allowed

steps.title: Applying it - the four conditions, the one that decides it, and the converse
points: 1 she was ashore - satisfied on the facts given
2 she was in a position of peril - NOT stated, and this is what the claim turns on
3 an actual intention to refloat for the common safety - working ahead and astern is exactly that
4 at the risk of such damage - the master knowingly accepted a foreseeable engineering risk
the engineering: sustained torque at low shaft speed, repeated reversals, loss of oil film
it then satisfies Rule A too - extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, for the common safety
Rule C is satisfied - the damage is the direct consequence of the act
Rule D - it makes no difference that the grounding may have been somebody's fault
THE CONVERSE - afloat, or aground without peril, and the identical damage is particular average

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) Rule A: extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, peril, common safety of a common adventure, preservation of property. The Rules bind by contract, not as law; in India the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 also recognises the concept. Rule C direct consequence only; Rule D fault is irrelevant to contribution; Rule E onus on the claimant. (b) Rule VII — machinery damage in refloating is allowed if she was ashore AND in peril, with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety, at the risk of such damage; afloat, it is in no circumstances allowed. Yes — provided peril is proved.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: York-Antwerp Rules 2016, Rule A for limb (a) and Rule VII for limb (b). Rule VII is written for exactly these facts and is the complete answer. Remember that the Rules bind by contractual incorporation, not as law, and that in India the concept is also recognised by the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 — not the English Act of 1906.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) with a flat ‘yes’. Rule VII requires the ship to be ashore AND in a position of peril, and the question does not say she was in peril — that omission is deliberate and it is what the claim turns on. The mirror trap is forgetting the converse the rule expressly provides: where the ship is afloat, damage from working the propelling machinery is in no circumstances allowed, so identical engine damage a few minutes later is the owner's own particular average.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is Rule A taken apart word by word (1, 2), then C, D, E (3), then who pays (4). Limb (b) is Rule VII quoted (5) then four conditions and the converse (6). For Rule VII hold four words in order: ASHORE — PERIL — INTENTION — RISK, and then the sting: AFLOAT — NEVER.
questions.understand_first:
General average is older than marine insurance and is not insurance at all. It is a rule of contribution between the parties to one adventure: if the ship, the cargo and the freight are all in danger together and something belonging to one of them is deliberately given up to save them all, the loss is shared among all of them in proportion to what each had at stake. The idea is ancient and its logic is simple — nobody should be worse off for having been the one chosen to be sacrificed.

That is why the essential features are what they are, and why they are not really a list. Every one of them is a phrase of Rule A doing a job: extraordinary keeps ordinary voyage costs out; intentional separates a sacrifice from an accident; reasonable keeps panic out; peril keeps ordinary sea risk out; common ensures there is more than one interest to share; and preservation ensures there is something saved to contribute. Learn Rule A and you have the features.

Limb (b) then tests one thing only: can you tell a sacrifice from an accident? The engine damage is physically identical whether she was in danger or not. What changes the legal answer is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked — and Rule VII says so in one sentence, with the converse attached.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the general average question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 What a general average act is and how the Rules apply. 2 The essential features drawn out of Rule A. 3 The lettered rules C, D and E. 4 How the loss is shared, and what general average is not. (b) 5 Rule VII quoted. 6 The four conditions applied, the one that decides it, and the converse.
retrieval_cards.why: Four steps for eight marks in limb (a) and two for eight in limb (b) - limb (b)'s steps are heavier because the applied analysis is where the marks are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: The words 'when, and only when' are the reason the essential features are not a matter of opinion - every feature is a phrase of this sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Are the York-Antwerp Rules law?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. They take effect by incorporation into the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty - and the Rule of Interpretation then applies them to the exclusion of any inconsistent law and practice. Which version applies is therefore a question of what the contract incorporates. In India the concept of a general average loss is separately recognised by the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates commonly describe the Rules as international law. Getting this right also explains why an older version may govern, and Rule VII is materially identical in the 1994, 2004 and 2016 texts.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What most sharply separates general average from particular average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Intention. A general average loss is deliberately incurred - cargo jettisoned by decision, an engine worked knowing it may be damaged. Particular average is accidental damage, which lies where it falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared.
retrieval_cards.why: This one distinction decides limb (b) as well as limb (a), because the burnt bearings are either a sacrifice or an accident depending on the circumstances.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Quote the effect of Rule VII of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.
retrieval_cards.why: It is written for exactly these facts and is the complete answer to limb (b), including the absolute prohibition in its second half.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The vessel ran aground and burnt her bearings trying to come off. Is it general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, provided four things are shown: she was ashore; she was in a position of peril; the machinery was worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety; and the damage arose at the risk of such damage. The question states the grounding but does NOT state peril, and that is what the claim actually turns on - a ship lying safely on soft mud in fine weather awaiting the tide is not in peril.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner has left out the condition that decides the case. Supplying it, and saying so, is what earns the justification marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: She comes off the ground and burns her bearings ten minutes later while manoeuvring clear. Same answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - the opposite answer. Rule VII provides that where a ship is afloat, no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average. The damage is identical; it is now particular average, the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy.
retrieval_cards.why: The converse is expressly in the rule and it is the neatest demonstration that the legal answer follows the ship's condition and the master's purpose, not the engineering.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does it matter that the grounding was the master's own fault?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not to the right of contribution. Rule D provides that rights to contribution in general average are not affected though the event may have been due to the fault of one of the parties to the adventure, but without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against or to that party in respect of that fault. The adjustment proceeds first; blame is fought separately.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely assume fault destroys the claim. It does not - it is dealt with elsewhere, and saying so shows command of the lettered rules.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who bears the loss, and how is it collected?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under Rule A.2 it is borne by the contributing interests - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably in proportion to their values at the termination of the adventure. An average adjuster prepares the adjustment, and security is taken before cargo is released: normally an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter. Under Rule E the onus of proof is on the party claiming.
retrieval_cards.why: The practical machinery is a scoring block in limb (a) and is what makes the doctrine real rather than theoretical.

The point matters because the Rules apply by contractual incorporation and an older version may govern. Confirm by collation before publication.

It supports the legal analysis rather than deciding it, and no bearing load or torque figure is quoted because both are entirely installation-specific.
